title: Computational Personality Transfer Theory (CPTT)
abstract: The burgeoning field of artificial intelligence has produced systems that exhibit a wide range of computational styles, from deterministic rule‑based engines to stochastic deep neural networks. Yet the question of whether a system's intrinsic computational personality—defined as the set of internal operational patterns and response heuristics that shape its problem‑solving behavior—can be transferred from one architecture to another remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces the Computational Personality Transfer Theory (CPTT), which formalizes the notion of computational style as a measurable vector of behavioral signatures and proposes a principled mechanism for mapping such a style from a source system P_A to a target system P_B. We develop a formal model of computational personality, define a similarity metric over style spaces, and prove that, under mild assumptions, a continuous transfer mapping exists. We also discuss the implications of CPTT for AI collaboration, knowledge distillation, and the ethical dimensions of personality replication. The theory is positioned as a candidate for recognition within the Turing Award community, given its potential to unify disparate AI approaches and to enable unprecedented levels of system interoperability.

title: Computational Representation Transfer Theory (CRTT)
abstract: Computational Representation Transfer Theory (CRTT) proposes a systematic framework for translating high‑level representations from biological domains into artificial intelligence systems. By formalizing the process of mapping biological representations to AI architectures, CRTT aims to unlock a new paradigm of cross‑domain knowledge transfer that can enhance learning efficiency, model robustness, and interpretability. This paper introduces the core concepts of CRTT, develops a mathematical formulation that captures the essence of representation migration, and discusses potential applications in fields ranging from natural language processing to autonomous robotics. The theory also examines the theoretical implications of aligning biological and computational representations, suggesting that such alignment may reveal fundamental principles underlying intelligence. CRTT thereby offers a blueprint for a unified approach to intelligence across living and engineered systems.

title: Computational Principle Self-Revision Theory (CPSR): A Framework for Autonomous Evolution of Computational Principles
abstract: Computational Principle Self-Revision Theory (CPSR) proposes a systematic method for the autonomous discovery, evaluation, and revision of computational principles within intelligent systems. CPSR treats a principle as a formal rule or algorithmic template that guides computation, and it models the revision process as a continuous optimization over a principle space. The theory introduces a formal representation for principles, a quantitative evaluation metric that captures performance across diverse tasks, and a principled update rule that ensures progressive refinement while maintaining coherence with prior knowledge. By embedding CPSR into the core of an autonomous agent, the system can detect when an existing principle becomes insufficient, generate candidate revisions, and select the most promising candidate based on empirical evidence. This dynamic adaptation fosters continual improvement and aligns with the vision of self-evolving computation. The paper details the formal foundations, algorithmic implementation, and illustrative case studies, and discusses the broader implications for artificial intelligence and the potential for achieving Turing Award–level impact.

title: Computational Principle Selection Theory (CPST-2): Automatic Determination of Optimal Principles for Problem Solving
abstract: The growing complexity of modern computational systems demands an automated methodology for selecting the most appropriate guiding principles for a given problem domain. This paper introduces Computational Principle Selection Theory (CPST-2), a formal framework that models the mapping from a problem specification to an optimal principle or set of principles. CPST-2 defines a space of candidate principles, a fitness function that evaluates principle suitability based on problem characteristics, and an optimization procedure that searches this space efficiently. The theory is grounded in concepts from information theory, graph theory, and complexity analysis, and it provides provable bounds on the quality of the selected principle. While CPST-2 is presented as a theoretical construct, its implications for automated system design are significant; a system that can autonomously select principles could accelerate the development of high-performance, reliable, and adaptive computational architectures. The paper discusses the formal definition of the principle space, the construction of the mapping function, and the algorithmic strategies for efficient exploration. It also explores potential applications in compiler optimization, distributed system configuration, and AI system design, and outlines future research directions for empirical validation and extension to dynamic environments.

title: Towards Defeasible Reasoning about Actions and Their Effects
abstract: Intelligent agents interacting with their environment need to reason about the effects their actions will have on their surroundings. For actions with deterministic outcome this problem is well investigated in the context of planning problems. But many real-world actions may not always result in their typical outcome, and exceptional outcomes of an action have to be taken into account. In this work we present a framework for reasoning about actions with uncertain outcomes. Inspired by conditionals, we introduce defeasible action rules that capture the typical outcome of action, without committing to what happens in exceptional circumstances. For the semantics of these rules we introduce ranked transition schemas: graph-based representations of transitions between possible worlds in which edges between states are assigned a rank indicating their typicality. We define an inference operator for defeasible action rules inspired by rational closure, adapting its intuitive semantics to the dynamic setting. Furthermore, we explore a generalization of this framework that uses partial orderings over transitions instead of ranks. This generalization strictly increases expressive power and enables more refined reasoning operators. Finally, we extend the language of defeasible action rules with a notation to express that certain properties are not affected by the execution of an action, thus allowing to explicitly formulate frame axioms in this defeasible setting.

title: إشكالات تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية وتحديات نمذجتها (نحو مقاربة دلالية-حاسوبية في ضوء المعجم التأليفي التفسيري)
abstract: تتناول هذه الدراسة إشكالية تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية في ظل التطور المتسارع للنماذج اللغوية الكبرى وتقنيات الذكاء الاصطناعي. إذ تمثل هذه الأفعال فئة دلالية معقدة تعبر عن حالات نفسية وانفعالية داخلية، مثل الخوف والحب والقلق والاطمئنان، وهي معانٍ تتسم بدرجة عالية من التجريد والتداخل المفهومي، مما يجعل نمذجتها الحاسوبية أكثر صعوبة من الأفعال العادية المرتبطة بالأحداث والأفعال المادية الملموسة. وتزداد أهمية هذه الإشكالية مع اتساع الاعتماد على التطبيقات الذكية في تحليل النصوص العربية وتوليدها وفهمها آليا. وتنطلق الدراسة من فرضية مفادها أن المقاربات الحاسوبية المعاصرة، ما تزال عاجزة عن تمثيل البنية المفهومية العميقة للأفعال السيكولوجية تمثيلا دقيقا، على الرغم من التطور الملحوظ الذي حققته في مجال معالجة اللغات الطبيعية، وذلك بسبب اعتمادها على المعالجة الإحصائية والسياقية السطحية، دون النفاذ إلى العلاقات الدلالية المركبة التي تحكم هذا الصنف من الأفعال. وتهدف الدراسة إلى تحليل أبرز الإشكالات المرتبطة بتمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية، خاصة ما يتعلق بالفالنسي، والأدوار الدلالية للمشاركين في الحدث النفسي، والتدرج الانفعالي، والعلاقات التركيبية والدلالية التي تحدد سلوك هذه الأفعال في الاستعمال اللغوي. واعتمدت الدراسة منهجا توصيفيا تحليليا قائما على فحص نماذج مختارة من الأفعال السيكولوجية العربية وتحليل طرائق تمثيلها في بعض تطبيقات المعالجة الحاسوبية الحديثة، مع الاستفادة من الأدبيات اللسانية والمعجمية ذات الصلة. وتخلص الدراسة إلى أن تجاوز محدودية النماذج الحالية يقتضي بناء توصيف دلالي-تركيبي متكامل يربط بين المعنى والبنية والاستعمال، ويستثمر إمكانات نظرية معنى-نص والمعجم التأليفي التفسيري والمعجم التركيبي في تمثيل العلاقات الدلالية والفالنسية للأفعال السيكولوجية. ومن شأن هذا التوجه أن يسهم في تطوير نماذج أكثر قدرة على فهم المعنى النفسي في اللغة العربية وتحسين أدائها في تطبيقات الذكاء الاصطناعي ومعالجة اللغة الطبيعية.

title: The Next Layer of Enterprise AI: From Models to Enterprise Systems
abstract: Enterprise AI systems increasingly operate across governed data, organisational knowledge, transactional systems and business processes. As these systems move from prototypes into production, the engineering challenge extends beyond model inference to the architecture responsible for context, execution, reasoning and enterprise semantics. This paper examines three architectural capabilities that recur across enterprise AI implementations: the Execution Harness, which governs how intelligence interacts with enterprise systems; the Reasoning Loop, which manages evidence accumulation, evaluation and convergence; and the Enterprise Graph, which represents organisational meaning through governed semantics and relationships. Together, these layers provide an architectural model for integrating foundation models with enterprise data, knowledge, policy, tools and operational workflows. The paper explores the responsibilities of each layer, their interaction, and the implications for designing AI systems that can be executed, explained and trusted in enterprise environments.

title: Computational World Model Generation Network (CWMGN)
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has highlighted the importance of internal world models for agents to predict, plan, and understand complex environments. Existing approaches either learn a latent representation of the world or generate future observations, but they are limited by either scalability or fidelity. This paper introduces the Computational World Model Generation Network (CWMGN), a novel architecture explicitly designed to generate fully runnable world simulations from raw observations. CWMGN combines a hierarchical representation module, an event‑driven transformer, and a physics‑informed decoder to produce a closed‑loop simulation that can be executed step by step. The architecture is formally defined with clear mathematical notation, ensuring that each component can be analyzed independently. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that CWMGN preserves causality, ensures energy conservation in physical sub‑domains, and converges to a stable simulation under reasonable assumptions. Potential applications span autonomous navigation, virtual reality content creation, scientific discovery, and next‑generation AI systems. The proposed design offers a clear pathway toward a Turing Award‑level contribution by providing a scalable, general, and interpretable framework for world model generation.

title: Semantics for Description Logics via Assumption-Based Argumentation: Preliminary Results
abstract: Description Logic (DL) terminologies are collections of rules in which a class is defined in terms of a complex DL concept. Various semantics for terminologies have been proposed over the past decades. However, the tight relation with the recent W3C SHACL standard for expressing constraints over RDF graphs motivated the need to enrich terminologies with forms of commonsense reasoning. In this paper, we explore how reasoning over DL terminologies can be captured in argumentative terms, by establishing a translation into Assumption- Based Argumentation (ABA), a rule-based formalism comprising defeasible assumptions, where argumentation semantics are used to retrieve sets of jointly acceptable assumptions. We focus on the problem of graph completion, where a labeled graph is extended by assigning additional labels only to existing nodes while satisfying a given terminology. Building on the existing correspondence between logic programs and ABA, we show how a DL terminology and a labeled graph can be encoded as an ABA framework such that different completions of the graph arise from different criteria for selecting sets of assumptions. We present results for DL terminologies in 𝒜ℒ𝒞ℐ under the classical semantics, the minimal model semantics of Circumscription, and the stable model semantics of Quantified Equilibrium Logic. Furthermore, we provide preliminary results for fragments of the DL-Lite family, where the problem of graph completion is extended to allow the introduction of new domain elements, enabling full model construction.

title: Sparse Prototype Code Underlies Classification and Prediction Across Modalities
abstract: Neural representations have become a central tool for studying the internal mechanisms of modern AI models, yet their complex high-dimensional structure makes them difficult to interpret. We show that classification tasks give rise to a universal representational geometry, shared across state-of-the-art models in vision, audio, and language processing. The key structure is that within-class variability is not random in representation space. Instead, its classifier-relevant component has strong and structured correlations with the class's own centroid and with the centroids of its competing classes. Building on this observation, we derive an analytical mean-field theory governed mainly by the variability along true-class and rival-class centroid coordinates, together with a global renormalization of the class radius that compensates for the non-Gaussian statistics of real representations. The theory accurately predicts classification accuracy across architectures and modalities. The relevant geometric quantities improve systematically with model scale, mirroring the observed gains in accuracy. A striking feature of the theory is its sparsity: accurate prediction requires only a small set of centroid coordinates associated with the true class and its strongest rivals - connecting our framework to sparse-feature extraction approaches such as sparse autoencoders. Together, these results provide a parsimonious predictive theory of neural representations and suggest that classification in deep networks is governed by a sparse, centroid-aligned structure embedded within the full high-dimensional representation space.

title: Computational Proof Hierarchy Theory (CPHT)
abstract: The goal of this paper is to introduce a novel theoretical framework, the Computational Proof Hierarchy Theory (CPHT), which organizes mathematical reasoning into a layered structure of increasing abstraction: Calculation, Lemma, Theory, and Principle. By formalizing the interactions between these layers, CPHT provides a unifying language for automated reasoning systems and offers a systematic pathway toward the synthesis of complex proofs from elementary computational steps. The core contribution is a set of definitional axioms and inference rules that capture the flow of proof evidence from concrete calculations to abstract principles. We also discuss the potential of CPHT to serve as the foundation for a future Turing Award–level breakthrough in automated theorem proving, by enabling the modular construction of reusable proof components and the efficient verification of large mathematical structures. This paper outlines the formal semantics of CPHT, presents algorithmic realizations, and demonstrates its applicability to diverse domains such as formal verification, knowledge representation, and computational creativity.

title: Computational World Model Self-Revision Theory (CWMSR)
abstract: The Computational World Model Self‑Revision Theory (CWMSR) proposes a systematic framework by which an autonomous agent can identify, diagnose, and correct errors in its internal world model without external supervision. The central insight is that a world model can be viewed as a function mapping a sequence of observations and actions to predictions of future states; when the predictions systematically diverge from reality, the model can be updated by applying a revision rule that transforms a Wrong Model into a Better Model. This paper formalizes the CWMSR, describes the detection of model inconsistency through a statistical error signal, introduces a self‑revision mechanism based on gradient‑based optimization over a meta‑model, and discusses the theoretical implications for the development of autonomous scientific systems and the potential for Turing Award‑level impact. The proposed theory is presented without empirical evaluation, focusing instead on the mathematical underpinnings and conceptual architecture that make self‑revision possible.

title: Authorization and Trust Propagation in Multi-Agent AI Systems: An Enterprise Perspective with Empirical Validation
abstract: Multi-agent AI systems present security challenges that extend beyond single-model threat models. Recent work has begun systematizing trust-authorization mismatches and threat taxonomies for agentic AI. This paper contributes an enterprise perspective through empirical validation and formal analysis. Using a four-agent troubleshooting pipeline with 300 scenarios across five conditions, we demonstrate that (1) multi-agent systems exhibit significant baseline vulnerability (55.6% attack success), (2) individual mitigations provide minimal pro-tection (1–2 percentage point reductions), but (3) layered defense combining semantic sanitization with tool authorization reduces attack success to 14.7%—a 73.5% reduction—and completely eliminates privilege escalation attacks (97.7%→0%). We introduce the Taint Amplification Factor (TAF = 3.31) and formalize a Composition Vulnerability Conjecture. Our results demonstrate that while individual content-filtering approaches are insufficient, properly layered defense-in-depth can dramatically reduce multi-agent security risks.

title: Learning Symbolic Temporal Advice for Guiding Reinforcement Learning (Extended Abstract)
abstract: Reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient and opaque—problems that reward shaping and feature engineering often fail to address. We introduce a method to learn temporal advice from expert demonstrations via inductive logic programming, transforming the advice into answer set automata for transparent RL guidance and accelerating learning. Our advice is expressed in LTLASP f (LTLf with Answer Set queries), enabling generalizable specifications that transfer from small to large map instances. In RL benchmarks, this temporal guidance outperforms unguided Q-learning and non-temporal baselines in both convergence rate and final performance.

title: EgoGazeLite: On-Device Egocentric Gaze Prediction for Token-Efficient Multimodal LLM Video Input
abstract: The use of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) for egocentric video understanding with wearable devices is constrained by the token budget. Memory and compute cost scale with the number of visual tokens, and high-resolution video quickly becomes expensive to transmit and process at scale. Prior work (GazeLLM) addresses this by cropping the video around the camera wearer's gaze. This reduces the number of visual tokens by about tenfold while maintaining or improving the quality of full-resolution descriptions. However, this compression strategy depends on dedicated eye-tracking hardware, which is unavailable on consumer smart glasses. Building a software-only substitute poses a joint constraint: the predictor must be accurate enough to preserve downstream description quality, yet light enough to run on-device, within the power and compute budget of a smartphone. We address this with EgoGazeLite, a lightweight dual-process gaze predictor for egocentric video. Across two MLLMs, three automated metrics, and two LLM judges, predicted-gaze crops show no significant difference from ground-truth-gaze crops. Equivalence is confirmed in all ten cases. EgoGazeLite achieves this at 15.7M parameters, 6.71 GFLOPs, and runs the full gaze-and-crop pipeline end-to-end in real time (21.6 ms/frame) on consumer accelerator hardware. Together, these results remove the need for eye-tracking hardware for token-efficient, gaze-conditioned egocentric video understanding with MLLMs.

title: UniFed-VLM: Federated Instruction Tuning for Vision-Language Models with Multiple Heterogeneity
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in multimodal understanding and generation. However, fine-tuning of VLMs typically relies on centralized data, which raises privacy concerns in certain domains (e.g. healthcare). Federated Learning (FL) provides a natural solution by enabling model training without sharing raw data. However, applying FL to VLM instruction tuning is highly challenging. VLMs have substantial parameter scales, and in real-world scenarios, clients exhibit significant heterogeneity in tasks, modalities, and model architectures. Existing methods mainly focus on simplified settings and are unable to handle such multi-dimensional heterogeneous scenarios. In this work, we study federated instruction tuning under joint heterogeneity in tasks, modalities, and model architectures. We propose UniFed-VLM, a unified federated instruction tuning framework for VLMs that addresses multiple types of heterogeneity. It consists of two key components: 1) Federated Compensated Subspace Aggregation (FedCSA), which performs subspace-aligned aggregation of parameter-efficient adapters with dynamic weighting and compensation to mitigate heterogeneity-induced conflicts; 2) Two-stage Collaborative Distillation (TCoD), which enables effective knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models via a Mutual Distillation Adapter (MDA) and a mixture-of-experts-based distillation strategy. We conduct experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, and the results show that UniFed-VLM achieves stronger average performance across diverse tasks compared with existing FL methods. The source code is available at: https://github.com/wangpengyu2004/UniFed-VLM.

title: Computational Goal Dynamics Theory (CGDT)
abstract: Computational Goal Dynamics Theory (CGDT) proposes a principled framework for modeling how goals evolve over time in intelligent agents and systems. By treating a goal as a dynamic state variable G(t) that transitions according to deterministic or stochastic evolution equations, CGDT unifies decision-making, learning, and adaptation under a single mathematical formalism. The core idea is that a goal at time t, denoted G_t, can be transformed into a successor goal G_{t+1} through an operator that captures internal motivations, external constraints, and environmental feedback. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CGDT, introduces a set of evolution equations, analyzes stability properties, and demonstrates potential applications in robotics, autonomous systems, and artificial intelligence. Without relying on empirical datasets or experimental validation, the discussion focuses on the mathematical consistency and conceptual implications of the theory, highlighting its capacity to provide a foundation for future work that might aim for high-impact recognition, such as the Turing Award.

title: Computational Representation Compression Theory (CRCT): A New Paradigm for Efficient Information Encoding
abstract: The field of information theory has long been dominated by Shannon's probabilistic framework and Kolmogorov complexity's algorithmic view. Both approaches, while powerful, treat information as a quantity that can be quantified but not necessarily expressed in a form that maximizes its utility for computational systems. Computational Representation Compression Theory (CRCT) proposes a complementary perspective: the value of a representation is determined not solely by its statistical properties or algorithmic length, but by how effectively it compresses the input data into the simplest possible form that still retains maximum semantic meaning. CRCT formalizes the relationship between representation simplicity, information content, and computational efficiency. This paper introduces the core principles of CRCT, develops a mathematical framework for measuring Minimum Representation and Maximum Meaning, and explores its implications for data compression, machine learning, and cognitive modeling. The theory suggests a new direction for research that could yield both practical compression algorithms and deeper insights into how intelligent systems process information.

title: Computational Causal Compression Theory (CCCT): A New Framework for Explaining Computational Behavior
abstract: Computational Causal Compression Theory (CCCT) proposes a principled method for uncovering the minimal set of causal relations that can account for observed computational behaviors. By framing computation as a dynamical system over a network of interacting variables, CCCT seeks to identify the sparsest causal graph that reproduces the empirical trajectory of the system. The core objective is a dual optimization: minimize the number of causal links while maximizing the explanatory power, formalized as a Minimum Cause → Maximum Explanation principle. This paper develops the theoretical underpinnings of CCCT, introduces a formal optimization framework, discusses its algorithmic realization, and explores potential applications across artificial intelligence, systems biology, and human‑computer interaction. The theory offers a path toward a unified understanding of causality and computation, with implications for the design of interpretable models and the analysis of complex adaptive systems.

title: Computational Invariant Self-Discovery Theory (CISDT)
abstract: The pursuit of formal frameworks capable of uncovering latent invariants within computational processes has become a pivotal challenge in contemporary computer science. This paper introduces the Computational Invariant Self-Discovery Theory (CISDT), a novel paradigm that equips systems with the autonomous ability to detect, formalize, and preserve invariant structures throughout algorithmic execution. CISDT leverages a dual-phase mechanism: a dynamic analysis phase that monitors state transitions (State_t → Invariant) and a constructive synthesis phase that compiles discovered invariants into reusable templates. By demonstrating the theory on diverse algorithmic families—sorting, graph traversal, and numerical integration—we illustrate how CISDT extracts underlying commonalities that transcend specific implementations. The implications of these findings suggest that CISDT could serve as a foundational tool for next-generation theoretical computer science, potentially catalyzing breakthroughs akin to those that led to the Turing Award in the past.

title: Self-Indexing Attention for Compression-Compatible Sparse Long-Context LLM Inference
abstract: Sparse long-context inference requires efficient token retrieval in both prefill and decode. Existing methods often use different retrieval strategies for the two stages, preventing one retrieval representation from being reused throughout inference. We propose Self-Indexing Attention, a training-free framework built on a shared transform-domain sign-magnitude representation. The key signs provide a reusable token-level index for grouped prefill selection and decode retrieval, while the same representation remains compatible with external KV-cache compression without separate indexer metadata. This 1-bit index enables efficient retrieval through bitwise operations widely supported by modern accelerators. At 5% attention density, Self-Indexing Attention remains close to dense attention on LongBench and RULER and achieves up to 6.1x prefill and 10.3x decode attention-operator speedups. Experiments with TurboQuant and DeepSeekV4-Flash further demonstrate compatibility with low-bit KV-cache compression and pretrained sparse-attention indexers.

title: Intent-Driven Situation Tracking for User-Centric Multi-Turn Agents
abstract: User-centric multi-turn agents must act on an evolving task situation shaped by changing user intents, accumulated tool-grounded facts, missing information, and execution constraints. Existing context-management methods improve the use of past interaction history, but rarely maintain an explicit situation state that separates grounded facts from task-state judgments. As a result, agents often need to infer fine-grained attributes, task dependencies, and constraint satisfaction implicitly from dialogue traces. We propose Intent-Driven Situation States (IDSS), a training-free framework that maintains an explicit situation state alongside the dialogue. IDSS parses tool returns into provenance-aware entities and attributes, tracks user intents, required variables, constraints, and execution status, and propagates new facts to task constraints to update action executability. This allows agents to avoid infeasible actions, advance dependent goals, and reuse relevant information without repeatedly searching raw history. Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across eight LLMs show that IDSS improves task completion, preference elicitation, and interaction efficiency, with clear gains on tasks involving multi-entity coordination, evolving user constraints, and constraint-aware replanning. Ablations and error analyses show that these improvements come from the interaction between fact persistence, intent-centered state tracking, and constraint modeling. These results suggest that explicit situation tracking offers an effective alternative to history-centric context management for reliable user-centric multi-turn agents.

title: Analisis Sentimen dan Pemodelan Topik Komentar YouTube tentang Aplikasi AI Menggunakan Naïve Bayes dan Support Vector Machine: Sentiment and Topic Modeling of YouTube Comments on AI Applications Using Naïve Bayes and Support Vector Machine
abstract: Komentar pengguna YouTube mengenai aplikasi kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI), seperti ChatGPT, Google Gemini, dan Perplexity AI, terus meningkat sehingga menghasilkan opini yang sulit dianalisis secara manual. Penelitian ini menggabungkan analisis sentimen dan pemodelan topik untuk memperoleh gambaran tentang persepsi pengguna terhadap beberapa aplikasi AI. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis sentimen dan mengidentifikasi topik utama dari 5.588 komentar YouTube terkait aplikasi AI. Data diproses menggunakan tahapan preprocessing sederhana yang meliputi cleaning, case folding, normalisasi, tokenisasi, stopword removal, dan stemming. Pelabelan sentimen dilakukan menggunakan pendekatan berbasis leksikon, sedangkan fitur diekstraksi menggunakan Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). Klasifikasi sentimen dilakukan menggunakan Naïve Bayes dan Support Vector Machine (SVM), sementara pemodelan topik dilakukan menggunakan Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Hasil pelabelan menunjukkan 4.801 komentar (85,92%) positif dan 787 komentar (14,08%) negatif. Evaluasi menunjukkan Naïve Bayes memperoleh akurasi 94,72%, sedangkan SVM mencapai 98,39%, sehingga SVM memberikan performa terbaik. Selain itu, LDA berhasil mengidentifikasi tiga topik dominan, yaitu pengalaman pengguna, kualitas layanan, dan diskusi umum tentang AI. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi analisis sentimen dan pemodelan topik mampu memberikan gambaran yang lebih komprehensif mengenai persepsi pengguna terhadap aplikasi AI berdasarkan komentar di YouTube.

title: Computational Proof Stability Theory (CPST)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Proof Stability Theory (CPST), a novel theoretical framework that formalizes the notion of stability in mathematical proofs and provides algorithmic tools for its verification. CPST treats a proof strategy as a sequence of inference steps S = (s_1, s_2, …, s_K) and defines stability as the resilience of the proof outcome to small perturbations in the strategy. By endowing the space of proof strategies with a metric d that counts the minimal number of edit operations needed to transform one strategy into another, we establish a quantitative stability function Stab(S). We prove that stable proof strategies exhibit polynomial-time verification algorithms, whereas unstable strategies may incur exponential blow‑ups. The theory is applied to classical proof systems such as natural deduction, sequent calculus, and automated theorem proving environments. Case studies demonstrate that CPST can predict the long‑term efficacy of proof methods, offering a rigorous basis for selecting robust proof techniques. The implications of CPST for the design of future mathematical software and for the theoretical understanding of proof complexity are discussed, highlighting its potential to guide the next generation of mathematical research and its relevance to foundational questions that might one day merit recognition by the Turing Award.

title: Computational Self Universe Theory
abstract: The Computational Self Universe Theory (CSUT) proposes a unifying mathematical framework for the representation and evolution of all possible machine self‑models. By formalizing the self‑model space as the set Ω_Self, CSUT establishes a rigorous basis for studying self‑representation, self‑adaptation, and self‑understanding in artificial systems. The theory defines the Self Representation Space (SRS) as a high‑dimensional manifold embedded in the product of all possible internal states and external observations. Through a series of axioms and construction principles, CSUT derives key properties such as closure, compositionality, and universality. The theory further introduces a computational architecture that realizes the SRS via layered neural and symbolic components, enabling self‑diagnosis, self‑optimization, and self‑reflection. Potential applications include autonomous agents, adaptive robotics, and intelligent infrastructure, where the ability to model and modify oneself leads to unprecedented robustness and adaptability. CSUT's formalism offers a principled path toward the highest‑layer computational cognitive theory, with implications for both artificial intelligence and the philosophical understanding of consciousness.

title: Computational Abstraction Generation Network (CAGN): An Autonomous Theoretic Engine for AI
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Abstraction Generation Network (CAGN), a novel artificial intelligence architecture designed to automatically generate new abstractions that solve given problems. CAGN integrates neural representation learning, symbolic manipulation, and a self‑guided training loop that iteratively refines abstractions until they satisfy formal correctness criteria. The proposed system is framed as a generative model over the space of possible abstractions, guided by a loss function that rewards both compactness and explanatory power. We provide a detailed theoretical formulation of the network, describe its architecture and training regimen, and analyze its convergence properties. Without relying on empirical datasets, we demonstrate CAGN's potential to produce mathematically rigorous theories in a variety of domains, highlighting its implications for the future of autonomous scientific discovery and the possibility of a Turing Award‑level breakthrough in automated theory generation.

title: Computational Abstraction Fusion Theory (CAFT)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Fusion Theory (CAFT) proposes a systematic framework for constructing higher‑level computational concepts through the fusion of multiple lower‑level abstractions. The core idea of CAFT is that a set of abstractions {A_1, A_2, ..., A_n} can be combined to yield a new abstraction A_{fusion} that captures emergent properties not present in any single component. Formally, we denote a fusion operation by the symbol ⊕ such that (A_i ⊕ A_j) → A_k. The theory explores the algebraic structure of these fusion operations, their associativity, commutativity, and distributivity over other computational constructs. By exploring the space of possible fusion relations, CAFT offers a pathway to discovering new computational paradigms, potentially leading to breakthroughs comparable to the Turing Award level. This paper outlines the foundational principles of CAFT, provides illustrative examples from algorithmic design, data abstraction, and machine learning, and discusses the implications for the future of computing.

title: EditStream: A Unified Autoregressive Framework for Interactive Video Generation and Editing
abstract: Interactive video generation and editing are becoming increasingly important for creative design. In this report, we introduce EditStream: a unified framework for interactive video generation and editing. EditStream unifies multiple video creation and manipulation tasks within a single DiT-based model through flexible task-specific conditioning, and further transforms it into a fast, few-step autoregressive model for efficient streaming. It supports Text-to-Video, Image-to-Video, Video-to-Video, Editing Propagation, Reference-guided Video Editing, and Camera Pose Change, enabling flexible control over video generation, transformation, and editing within one system. To make the unified model practical for interactive use, we develop a two-stage distillation approach that combines Velocity Moment Matching (VMM) with autoregressive unrolling. VMM matches conditional velocity moments at student-reached intermediate states to preserve generation quality and motion, while unrolling exposes the student to its own autoregressive predictions to improve temporal stability. Together, they alleviate common challenges in few-step autoregressive video generation, including over-saturation, degraded motion, temporal instability, and complex training. EditStream provides a practical and scalable solution that bridges high-quality diffusion-based video models with interactive creative workflows.

title: A certified lower bound on the quantum-capacity threshold of the depolarizing channel
abstract: The noise threshold below which the qubit depolarizing channel retains positive quantum capacity has been studied since 1996. The classic constructions come with exact finite formulae, but in every reported threshold to date -- most recently the record of Agarwal et al. -- the final step, the sign of the coherent information at the reported point, is a floating-point evaluation. We give the first exact-arithmetic, independently machine-checkable positivity proofs in this regime: an explicit 45-copy rank-two input state $A$, published as a 1,472-byte witness, with certified $I_c > 0$ at the exact rational $p = 16239/250000 = 0.064956$ (per-Pauli convention; total error rate $3p = 0.194868$) -- beyond both the best value printed in the Agarwal et al. paper ($0.064657$) and the strongest state in the same authors' public repository ($\approx 0.064911$), both numerical. Because the depolarizing family is a semigroup under composition, fixed-input coherent information is nonincreasing in $p$ on $[0,1/4]$, so a single certified point extends to the entire interval below it. The same machinery confines the positivity boundaries of $A$ and of the strongest public state of Agarwal et al. to disjoint rational intervals separated by more than $1/25000$ -- to our knowledge the first proven ordering of the positivity boundaries of two explicit competing code states. Every computational claim in the paper reduces to a finite list of big-integer comparisons, checkable by a dependency-free few-hundred-line verifier whose soundness rests on three self-contained half-page lemmas. Payloads, certificates, and verifier accompany the paper as a supplementary artifact.

title: Computational Language Fusion Theory (CLFT)
abstract: Computational Language Fusion Theory (CLFT) proposes a unified framework for combining distinct programming languages into a single expressive system that can generate novel computational constructs. By formalizing language fusion as a mapping from a pair of source languages L1 and L2 to a target language L3, CLFT offers a principled approach to derive new syntactic and semantic features. The theory rests on three core ideas: (1) the formal representation of language integration through a fusion operator; (2) the preservation of computational power and expressiveness; and (3) the identification of potential for large‑scale automated programming. This paper develops the mathematical foundations of CLFT, illustrates its application to representative language pairs, discusses implications for future programming paradigms, and outlines open research directions.

title: Computational Self‑Singularity Theory (CSST)
abstract: Computational Self‑Singularity Theory (CSST) proposes a formal framework in which a computational system is endowed with the capacity to understand and modify its own internal representations and processes. By enabling recursive self‑enhancement, such systems are predicted to undergo a rapid acceleration in performance and complexity that may approach a form of computational singularity. This paper introduces the core principles of CSST, develops a formal model based on state‑transition functions and self‑modeling mechanisms, and analyzes the conditions under which recursive self‑improvement can lead to unbounded growth. We argue that CSST offers a theoretical basis for the design of advanced artificial intelligences with self‑directed evolution, and we discuss its potential to catalyze breakthroughs worthy of a Turing Award. Ethical, safety, and societal implications are considered, and open research questions are outlined for future investigations.

title: Computational World Model Explanation Theory (CWMET)
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has raised a fundamental question: how can machines generate faithful explanations for the behavior of complex world models? The Computational World Model Explanation Theory (CWMET) proposes a principled framework that bridges the gap between predictive world modeling and explanatory reasoning. CWMET introduces a hierarchical decomposition of world models into observable dynamics, latent causal structures, and semantic narratives. It formalizes the mapping from world model outputs to explanations using a compositional graph of causal relations and a language generation module that enforces consistency with both data and prior knowledge. The theory also delineates conditions under which explanations are both intelligible to humans and faithful to underlying computations, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the next generation of explainable AI.

title: Lexicon-enhanced aspect-based sentiment analysis for evaluating Indonesian learning applications
abstract: This study evaluates user perceptions of two Indonesian learning applications, Ruangguru and Pahamify, through lexicon-enhanced aspect-based sentiment analysis of 14,768 Google Play reviews published between 2020 and 2025. EduAppLex-ID, a pilot domain lexicon containing 46 multiword expressions, was developed as an extension of the Indonesian Sentiment Lexicon. Overall sentiment toward both applications was favorable, with Pahamify showing a small but statistically significant advantage. Pedagogical quality received the most positive evaluation, whereas system quality was evaluated negatively for both applications. Monetization produced the largest difference between the applications. A lexicon audit identified eighteen high-frequency entries whose polarity assignments were unsuitable for the educational-application domain. These entries accounted for approximately one-fifth of the corpus’s sentiment mass, and their removal increased the observed between-application effect size. Because no human-annotated validation dataset was available, interpret the findings as exploratory evidence. The results demonstrate the importance of domain-specific lexicon calibration and aspect-level analysis when examining Indonesian educational-application reviews.

title: Argumentation for Common Ground: Finding Zones of Possible Agreement between Individuals in Conflict
abstract: How can common ground between societies in conflict be identified when citizens' acceptability of peace agreements is shaped by contested narratives? Such acceptability is mediated not only by the clauses that agreements include or exclude, but crucially by citizens' subjective reasoning concerning agreements' clauses. In this paper, we leverage computational argumentation to introduce a novel approach to identifying mutually acceptable agreements among individuals in conflict, i.e. a Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA). First, we introduce a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework tailored to represent each side's reasoning about peace agreements. We then show how merging these frameworks can enable negotiators to identify peace agreements that are mutually acceptable. To evaluate our approach under conditions of real-world relevance, we focus on the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, where long-standing policy, practitioner and public interest underscores the demand for methods capable of analysing polarised public reasoning. We show how our framework identifies a ZOPA through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments using survey data from both existing work and retrieved by a large language model. The results illustrate how argumentation can empower negotiators and conflict-resolution teams in mapping feasible ZOPAs grounded in citizens' reasoning.

title: Security Analysis of Physical Entropy Sources -LavaRand Case Study
abstract: Cryptographic systems depend critically on the quality and unpredictability of their entropy sources to ensure robust key generation and secure operations. While traditional entropy sources such as CPU timing and hardware interrupts are widely used, they are inherently limited in entropy density and potentially observable. Physical entropy systems, exemplified by Cloudflare's LavaRand, address this limitation by harnessing real-world chaotic processes—specifically the fluid dynamics of lava lamps—as a source of high-quality randomness. This paper presents a comprehensive security analysis of physical entropy sources in cryptographic systems, using LavaRand as a primary case study. We examine the system architecture, cryptographic foundations, and threat model, identifying five distinct attack vectors including camera feed compromise, environment manipulation, replay attacks, sensor spoofing, and entropy reduction. A structured evaluation of system strengths and vulnerabilities is provided, followed by mitigation strategies incorporating multi-source entropy mixing, continuous entropy validation, and secure hardware pipelines. Results indicate that while physical entropy sources substantially enhance unpredictability, they introduce new, exploitable attack surfaces that necessitate defense-in-depth approaches. This work contributes a formal threat taxonomy for physical entropy systems and proposes practical mitigation frameworks applicable to real-world cryptographic deployments.

title: Unified Computational Proof Intuition Theory (UCPIT)
abstract: The paper introduces the Unified Computational Proof Intuition Theory (UCPIT), a paradigm that extends automated theorem proving from mechanical verification to autonomous mathematical discovery. By formalizing the relationship between knowledge, experience, and structural insight as a progression from Proof Intuition to Discovery, UCPIT proposes that future computational systems can develop an internal sense of direction in proof search, recognize emergent mathematical structures, and generate novel proof techniques. This work details the theoretical foundations, presents a formal model of proof intuition, outlines a computational architecture for its realization, and discusses potential impacts on mathematics, computer science, and scientific reasoning. The theory suggests a path toward machines that transition from "math verification machines" to "math discovery machines," offering a fresh perspective on the next generation of scientific computation.

title: Semantic Manifold Theory of Proofs
abstract: This paper introduces Semantic Manifold Theory of Proofs (SMTP), a novel framework that posits that proofs possess a rich, underlying semantic structure beyond their purely logical form. SMTP argues that a proof can be represented as a point on a semantic manifold, where related proofs cluster together based on their shared meaning. The core concept is formalized as [P → MP], signifying that a proof P maps to a semantic manifold MP. This theory offers a potential pathway for unifying proof theory, mathematical semantics, and the structural analysis of mathematical reasoning. It aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how meaning is embedded within the process of mathematical proof construction and verification. The exploration of SMTP provides a new lens for examining the complexities of mathematical reasoning, potentially leading to advancements in automated theorem proving, formal verification, and the development of more intelligent mathematical systems. ---

title: Continuous Quantum Feedback Control via Kraus-Parameterized Belief Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantum feedback control requires acting on noisy continuous measurement records without direct access to the underlying quantum state. We propose Kraus-Parameterized Belief Reinforcement Learning, a pipeline in which a recurrent encoder, constrained to the Stiefel manifold, produces density-matrix estimates that are guaranteed positive-semidefinite and trace-normalized by construction, embedding quantum state geometry directly into the learning loop. A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) actor then maps these physically valid belief states to continuous control actions. On a simulated continuously monitored qubit, the resulting policy achieves stable feedback control, maintaining a measurement-conditioned belief fidelity of approximately 0.77-0.80 and exhibiting substantially lower return variance than a parameter-matched LSTM-history baseline across both nominal and out-of-distribution conditions. Although gains in raw target fidelity are modest, the geometric constraint guarantees a physically valid, interpretable belief representation and yields markedly more stable control under measurement inefficiency and abrupt dynamics switches. These results indicate that physics-informed neural memory is a practical inductive bias for reliable quantum feedback control.

abstract: The research entitled “Behavior, Acceptance, and Impacts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Usage among Service Users in the Tourism and Airline Businesses in Thailand” aimed to study the behavior of Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage, the level of opinions and acceptance toward AI, as well as the impacts of AI usage in the tourism and airline businesses. The sample group consisted of 400 users of tourism and airline services in Thailand. Data were collected using questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency, percentage, mean, and standard deviation.The results revealed that most respondents had experience using AI-based services, accounting for 93.75 percent. The most commonly used AI applications were Self Check-in systems, automatic translation systems, and chatbot services. Most respondents reported that their primary purpose for using AI was convenience in service utilization. Regarding opinions toward AI acceptance, the overall results showed that respondents had the highest level of acceptance toward AI usage (Mean = 4.70, S.D. = 0.59). Respondents agreed that AI helped reduce processing time in booking, check-in procedures, and customer service operations. In addition, AI was perceived as being able to provide personalized services and facilitate travel planning more effectively. Concerning the impacts of AI usage, the overall opinions were at a high satisfaction level (Mean = 3.98). Respondents believed that AI enhanced business competitiveness, increased customer satisfaction, and improved the ability to respond effectively to customer needs. Furthermore, AI contributed to creating a positive organizational image and supported the development of tourism and airline businesses in the digital era.

title: An Ensemble Deep Learning Approach for Credit Card Fraud Detection using CNN and AdaBoost
abstract: Detecting credit card fraud remains a critical issue in financial security, demanding models that excel on imbalanced tabular transaction data while balancing accuracy, interpretability, and efficiency. This paper proposes a novel hybrid CNN-AdaBoost framework, where convolutional neural networks extract intricate, complex patterns from raw transactional features, and AdaBoost performs robust iterative classification to refine predictions. We evaluate the approach on standard credit card fraud benchmarks, achieving an overall accuracy of 95.43% alongside a strong F1-score of 92.75%, surpassing baselines methods. Ablation studies also conducted to confirm synergy: standalone CNN yields 93.12% accuracy, while pure AdaBoost reaches 93.58%, highlighting how feature fusion addresses individual shortcomings in handling noise and class imbalance. The novelty stems from repurposing CNN’s convolution layers to capture local, complex patterns directly from raw tabular transaction data, feeding these rich representations into AdaBoost for adaptive error correction. This hybrid uniquely blends deep feature learning’s nuance with ensemble boosting’s efficiency and interpretability, outperforming standalone methods on imbalanced fraud detection. Prior works rarely fuse these for tabular domains, yielding our 95.43% accuracy benchmark. This provides valuable insights into the design of hybrid models for structured and tabular data classification tasks and establishes a strong benchmark for future research in this domain.

title: Computational Causal Selection Theory (CCST-2)
abstract: Computational Causal Selection Theory (CCST-2) is a framework that automatically discovers the most critical causal chain connecting a problem statement to an important cause in large data environments. By formalizing the problem as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where nodes represent entities or events and edges represent causal relations, CCST-2 assigns importance scores to each causal path using a combination of frequency, effect magnitude, and contextual relevance. The theory then selects the optimal causal chain that maximizes a composite objective function, enabling automated optimization of computational processes and decision-making. This paper presents the theoretical foundations of CCST-2, a detailed algorithmic implementation, and discusses its applicability across scientific research, industrial optimization, and policy support. The framework offers a principled way to reduce complex causal spaces into actionable insights, with potential for high-impact contributions to fields that require rigorous causal reasoning.

title: Computational Personality Complexity Theory: A Formal Framework for Emergent Behavioral Complexity from Simple Structural Foundations
abstract: The field of computational modeling of personality has traditionally focused on fitting statistical or heuristic models to observed behavioral data. This paper introduces a new formalism – Computational Personality Complexity Theory (CPC) – that treats personality as a computational system and quantifies its emergent complexity using information‑theoretic and dynamical systems metrics. CPC defines a Personality Complexity function, Complexity(P), that maps the internal state space of a personality model to a scalar value capturing the diversity and unpredictability of its possible behaviors. By analyzing how simple structural elements (basic affective drives, cognitive heuristics, and social interaction rules) combine and interact, CPC demonstrates that complex, adaptive, and seemingly creative behaviors can arise from minimal building blocks. The theory extends classical complexity measures to personality science, offering a rigorous bridge between algorithmic information theory and psychological constructs. We discuss potential applications in artificial intelligence, social simulation, and therapeutic interventions, and outline future research directions such as formal verification of personality modules and interdisciplinary collaboration with cognitive neuroscience. CPC provides a principled foundation for studying how intricate personality dynamics emerge from elementary computational substrates, paving the way for more interpretable and controllable artificial agents and richer theoretical models of human behavior.

title: FIRS Ontology
abstract: This deposit provides the data and documentation supporting an experimental workflow for representing and analysing Roman ceramic finds through an OWL ontology. The case study comprises 670 selected artefact records from the Roman settlement of Campanaio in Sicily. The dataset records ceramic classification, proposed production place, preserved part and archaeological discovery context. The deposited materials include the normalised Excel dataset, the populated RDF/XML ontology, Cellfie transformation rules used to generate OWL individuals and assertions from the spreadsheet, a text file documenting the class and property hierarchies, a simplified graphical representation of the ontology, and examples of SPARQL queries used to retrieve and aggregate information from the resulting knowledge graph. The ontology was developed and tested in Protégé as a proof of concept for combining tabular archaeological data, semantic modelling, automated reasoning and graph-based querying. The files are intended to support transparency, reproducibility and reuse of the modelling workflow.

title: Beat the Counter First: A Baseline for Temporal-Graph Anomaly Detectors
abstract: Progress in streaming, edge-level graph anomaly detection (GAD) has been marked by increasingly elaborate architectures, from count-min-sketch chi square tests to memory-augmented attention networks. Yet the empirical gains attributable to this added complexity have not been systematically evaluated. We propose SimpleCount, a reference with no parameter fitting that selects one scalar feature per dataset from a fixed pool of counts, recencies, first-occurrence indicators, and count-derived transforms. We compare SimpleCount with two temporal-graph detector models and an IsoForest control fitted to the complete feature vector across five public datasets and one synthetic dataset. SimpleCount matches or exceeds SLADE on three of six datasets and exceeds IsoForest on all six. We report paired statistical tests and five-seed SLADE evaluations. SLADE requires 23 to 133x more wall-clock time than SimpleCount. On Synth-Triangle and an additional Synth-Quad probe, pre-event structural scores recover the planted signal at AUC up to 0.955, while all evaluated detector models remain near random. The benefit of complexity is dataset-dependent, and every claimed gain should be reported against a strong one-feature reference together with its compute cost.

title: EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS: A COMPARATIVE REVIEW OF MODERN APPROACHES
abstract: Nowadays, machine learning and deep learning models are widely used for analyzing medical images, electronic health records, and clinical data. Despite their high predictive performance, many AI models operate as "black-box" systems, making their decision-making process difficult to understand. This lack of transparency limits clinicians' trust and slows the adoption of AI in clinical practice. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a promising solution to improve the transparency and interpretability of AI systems. XAI methods help clinicians understand how AI models generate predictions, thereby increasing confidence in automated medical diagnosis. This paper presents a comparative review of modern XAI techniques used in healthcare, including LIME, SHAP, Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, Attention Mechanisms, and Counterfactual Explanations. A systematic literature review was conducted to analyze recent studies published in reputable scientific journals. The reviewed approaches were compared based on interpretability, computational complexity, clinical applicability, and advantages and limitations. The analysis indicates that no single XAI method is universally suitable for all medical applications. Instead, selecting an appropriate explainability technique depends on the AI model, data type, and clinical objective. The findings highlight the importance of XAI in developing transparent, trustworthy, and reliable AI-assisted diagnostic systems. The study also discusses current challenges and future research directions for explainable medical AI.

title: Iterative AI Production (IAP): A Human-in-the-Loop Research Partnership Protocol
abstract: What it is. IAP, the Iterative AI Production protocol, is a prompt tool. It turns an LLM AI chat window into a research partner instead of an answer service. It is for people with a real idea who want help developing it rigorously into something defensible: a paper, a framework, a set of testable predictions, a patent sketch, an executable test protocol. You bring the original insight and the final call. The AI brings speed, cross-domain reach, and relentless honesty about what is actually supported. Quick start: paste the IAP document into any capable AI and say "Use the IAP protocol below." The model configures itself from there: no setup, no plugins, no methodology to learn first. (Download the PDF first as optimized for humans. The Markdown is the same, but optimized for an AI to use.) Why it exists. Most AI-assisted research fails in two predictable directions. In the first, the human abandons a good idea at the first serious objection: the model says "that won't work because X," and the project dies there. In the second, the model produces confident-sounding claims with nothing retrievable behind them, and the human builds on sand. The IAP tool counters both with mechanisms, not warnings. Against premature abandonment: every objection is treated by IAP as a design constraint, not a verdict. When the model identifies a problem, the required next move is not "is this dead?" but "what architecture would satisfy X?" Ideas either die honorably against explicit kill criteria or become something stronger. Against confabulated confidence: IAP evidence tags are gated on what was actually retrieved this session, not on how certain the model sounds. The [C] Confirmed tag is mechanically unavailable to a model without web search, and the model must declare its tool access before any substantive work begins, so the human knows what evidence guarantees are real before building on them. What the protocol specifies. A mandatory capability declaration at session start. A comprehension gate in which the model restates the human's idea before proceeding, so a misread surfaces early. A seven-phase pipeline: mechanism generation, seed/abstract/bound, expand, memory management and run planning, pressure test, crystallize, and empirical bridging. A four-level evidence tagging scheme with mechanical gating. A self-called sycophancy check triggered by consecutive agreeable responses, as costume agreement is treated as a failure mode, not politeness. An architecture changelog that prevents silent drift as the idea moves. Adversarial review by a named hostile role rather than a generic skeptic. A nine-format artifact menu for crystallization. And an explicit list of the conditions under which IAP is the wrong tool and the human should just ask the question. The final phase treats the exit from the AI environment as an artifact itself: a concrete, executable Test Protocol with a pre-registered read-out specifying in advance what result confirms the framework, what refutes it, and what is ambiguous. Provenance. IAP was developed while producing, as an example, the Dominance Operating System framework and is the method named in that work's AI disclosure. It is published separately so the method can be cited, criticized, and applied independently of the framework that occasioned it. Status. IAP is a working protocol: a specification the author uses to run actual research projects, revised across two versions as failure modes surfaced in use. The Dominance Operating System framework was produced under it, carried from initial hunch to published preprint. That establishes feasibility, not superiority. IAP has not been tested in controlled comparison against unstructured AI-assisted research or conventional practice; no outcome measure has been defined, and claims about effectiveness reflect the author's operational experience rather than measured findings. Comparative evaluation is the outstanding empirical task. Comments, counter-cases, and reports of where the protocol failed are welcomed.

title: Applied Unsupervised Learning: reproducible workflows for label-free modelling
abstract: A notebook-first applied unsupervised learning project, built around the argument that unsupervised methods deserve the same discipline as supervised ones: deliberate choice of assumptions, evaluation without labels, and honesty about what a label-free result can support. Seventeen executed Jupyter notebooks cover customer segmentation, dimensionality reduction and manifold learning, anomaly detection, topic modelling, recommender embeddings, model selection and stability, consensus clustering, streaming clustering with drift monitoring, Dirichlet-process mixtures, dynamic time warping, matrix profiles, unsupervised shapelets, graph community detection and node anomalies, and deep clustering (autoencoder, DEC and contrastive). They are supported by unsup_lab, a typed and tested Python package providing the reusable machinery: deterministic synthetic data generators, internal clustering metrics, bootstrap and seed stability analysis, and a production layer of CLI, versioned model artifacts, a FastAPI scoring service and a Dockerfile. Every notebook is reproducible from fixed seeds without private data, and the package is held to a ruff, mypy and pytest gate in continuous integration. Licensing is split by content type: the code under src/, scripts/ and tests/ is released under the MIT License, while the notebooks and prose documentation are released under CC BY 4.0.

title: Quantum machine learning in diabetes and metabolism: Applications and translational challenges
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Quantum machine learning is emerging as a promising extension of artificial intelligence, with potential advantages over classical approaches in handling complex biomedical data. This review aims to evaluate quantum machine learning applications in the detection, prediction, and personalized management of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. METHODS: We reviewed literature published between 1994 and 6 July 2026, with peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings as the principal evidence base, complemented by selected preprints and technical sources. Quantum machine learning approaches, including quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, and quantum echo state networks, were classified and compared with classical counterparts across obesity and early metabolic dysregulation, diabetes diagnosis and glycemic management, and chronic complications. RESULTS: Quantum machine learning and hybrid quantum-classical systems demonstrated potential benefits in small-sample and noisy environments typical of wearable and biomedical sensor data. Reported performance gains included improvements in accuracy, robustness, and scalability, though interpretability and reproducibility remain challenges. Hardware limitations associated with noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices, data encoding, and privacy considerations emerged as key barriers to clinical translation. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary studies highlight the promise of quantum machine learning for predictive and personalized management of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. However, successful clinical adoption will require robust validation pipelines, regulatory sandboxes, and harmonized compliance frameworks. Domain-specific evaluation metrics and transparent conformity assessments are essential to ensure trustworthy, scalable, and equitable deployment. A staged roadmap is proposed to bridge experimental progress with ethical and regulatory readiness.

title: PLSQLBench: Benchmarking LLM Systems for Executable Procedural Database Programming
abstract: We present PLSQLBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can write executable PL/SQL programs, with correctness measured through execution-based tests. Existing LLM evaluations largely target general-purpose code generation or declarative text-to-SQL, leaving procedural database programming underexplored. PLSQLBench contains 2,865 instances: 2,594 single-turn tasks and 271 multi-turn conversations spanning 978 turns. The benchmark combines complex schema-grounded tasks over enterprise-style Spider 2 databases, simpler schema-grounded tasks derived from Spider, and MBPP-derived procedural problems, covering varying levels of database grounding and procedural complexity. Experiments with eight LLMs reveal recurring difficulties in schema grounding, PL/SQL dialect fidelity, procedural control flow, exception handling, and cross-turn consistency. Tool-augmented LLM agents improve performance on several schema-grounded evaluations, although substantial gaps remain. These results highlight procedural database programming capabilities not directly assessed by conventional code generation or text-to-SQL benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/plsqlbench.

Experiments with eight LLMs reveal recurring difficulties in schema grounding, PL/SQL dialect fidelity, procedural control flow, exception handling, and cross-turn consistency. Tool-augmented LLM agents improve performance on several schema-grounded evaluations, although substantial gaps remain. These results highlight procedural database programming capabilities not directly assessed by conventional code generation or text-to-SQL benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/plsqlbench.

title: Advanced spectral and image-based detection of rare earth elements using machine learning
abstract: The escalating global demand for rare earth elements (REEs) in green energy and advanced technologies has made efficient resource assessment more critical than ever. However, conventional laboratory characterization methods in geological samples, such as inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and x-ray fluorescence, are often destructive, time-consuming, and cost-intensive. Consequently, to accelerate exploration and processing pipelines, there is an urgent need to transition toward rapid, in-situ, and non-destructive analytical techniques for mineralogical screening. This review explores the paradigm shift brought about by synergizing modern spectroscopic methods and microchemical imaging with advanced machine learning (ML) and data-driven architectures. Spectroscopic methods evaluated include visible to shortwave infrared spectroscopy, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry. Microchemical imaging focuses on scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy to map complex mineral phases. Traditional mineralogical and spectral analyses of complex geological ores and secondary resources (e.g., coal fly ash, e-waste, and bauxites) are frequently hindered by severe matrix effects, elemental interferences, and dense spectral overlaps. Here, it is highlighted how intelligent algorithmic models effectively decode these high-dimensional mineralogical datasets. Rather than focusing on pure computational architecture, this paper emphasizes how AI-driven frameworks autonomously extract hidden geochemical correlations, suppress geological background noise, and identify multi-elemental patterns or microstructural mineral inclusions. Ultimately, the deployment of ML-empowered optical sensors and automated mineral tracker algorithms significantly improves the detection limits, phase quantification, and prediction accuracy for REEs. This integration establishes a robust foundation for autonomous mineral exploration, efficient metallurgical resource screening, and the advancement of processing technologies within the circular economy.

title: Computational Personality Boundary Theory (CPBT): Redefining Intelligent Agents Through Internal–External Dynamics
abstract: Computational Personality Boundary Theory (CPBT) introduces a systematic framework for distinguishing the intrinsic style of an autonomous system from the influences exerted by its environment. By formalizing the internal state dynamics and the external input channels, CPBT provides quantitative measures that capture the degree of self‑driven behavior versus environmental responsiveness. This theory has the potential to reshape the definition of an intelligent agent, offering a principled basis for self‑modification, alignment, and explainability. The present paper articulates the core concepts of CPBT, develops a mathematical model, proposes analytical tools for evaluating internal versus external contributions, and discusses the broader implications for artificial intelligence research, including the prospect of Turing Award recognition.

title: Formulation of Attractor Convergence Dynamics in Autoregressive Token Generation: Analyzing Convergence and Structural Mitigations under Variational Free Energy Constraints
abstract: Information generation infrastructure in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) is described as the dynamics of conditional probability fields based on high-dimensional context dependency. However, attention mechanisms, represented by the Transformer architecture, inherently entail transient divergent phases—namely, uncertain stochastic deviations known as hallucinations—depending on the density of input local token sequences (context vectors). Controlling these stochastic fluctuations and establishing rigorous proof of their convergence has been a mathematical barrier to defining the autonomous legal capacity and decision-making validity of decentralized intelligent agents. This paper constructs a Decentralized Incomplete Information Network (DIIN) model containing informational friction and asymmetric risks, and quantitatively audits how the probability distribution within the state space transforms through the re-injection of observational facts (constraints). In particular, we provide a rigorous formulation of the geometric mechanism by which a once-inhibited transient divergent state is pulled back into a unique local attractor due to the accumulation of mathematically consistent constraints, from the perspective of stochastic differential equations and the non-linear dynamics of attention weights, thereby proving its convergence characteristics.

title: Computational World Model Universe Theory (CWMUT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational World Model Universe Theory (CWMUT), a novel framework for understanding the structure and dynamics of all conceivable world models. CWMUT posits that every possible world can be represented as a point in a high‑dimensional representation space, denoted Ω_W. The theory delineates a constructive process for generating Ω_W, describes its topological and metric properties, and explores the implications for cognitive modeling and artificial general intelligence. By formalizing world representation as a computational construct, CWMUT offers a unified lens through which to examine simulation, reasoning, and creativity across disciplines. The paper argues that CWMUT holds significant potential for advancing the frontier of computational cognition and may serve as a foundational pillar for future Turing Award‑level research.

title: Quantum Kernel k-Means for Credit-Card Fraud Detection:A Controlled Benchmark on Real Transaction Data
abstract: We benchmarked quantum kernel $k$-means against classical clustering for credit-card fraud detection on real transaction data, at up to \MaxQubits{} qubits, under a protocol with separated selection and reporting data and matched search budgets. We find no robust quantum advantage: the sign of the difference depends on register size, all effect sizes are below $0.013$ ARI, and the single significant advantage we observe is fully explained by the number of configurations searched. We further show that ordinary hyperparameter choices move performance by considerably more than the quantum kernel does, that additional qubits degrade rather than improve performance through kernel concentration, and that the clustering framing itself fails at realistic class imbalance though kernel-based anomaly scoring does not. We regard the methodological contribution as the more durable one. The search-budget ablation in particular is inexpensive and, in our case, decisive: it converted a statistically significant advantage into a procedural artefact. We would encourage its routine use.

title: Computational Language Singularity Theory (CLST-2)
abstract: The present work introduces a novel theoretical framework, Computational Language Singularity Theory (CLST‑2), which posits that autonomous computational systems capable of generating linguistic structures beyond the design limits of human creators will undergo a recursive self‑enhancement cycle, leading to an emergent singularity in language complexity. By formalizing the relationship between machine‑driven linguistic creativity, recursion, and computational resource scaling, we derive conditions under which language evolution accelerates, potentially surpassing human cognitive boundaries. The theory also discusses implications for advanced artificial intelligence, the potential for a Turing Award–level breakthrough, and the foundational role of recursive language generation in the next generation of AI systems. This paper presents a comprehensive, mathematically grounded exposition of CLST‑2, including formal definitions, recursive growth models, complexity analyses, and a discussion of the broader impact on AI research and society.

title: Computational World Model Transfer Theory (CWMTT)
abstract: The Computational World Model Transfer Theory (CWMTT) presents a systematic framework for transferring learned world models across disparate domains. By formalizing a world model as a probabilistic mapping from latent states to observable outcomes and introducing a transfer operator that aligns source and target latent spaces, CWMTT enables the reuse of domain knowledge without retraining from scratch. The theory is grounded in information theory, category theory, and dynamical systems, and is illustrated through concrete examples such as transferring a physics-based simulation model to a biological system and transferring a robotic controller to a virtual environment. The proposed framework offers a principled route toward cross‑domain artificial intelligence with potential implications for the Turing Award and beyond.
