title: SODA: a Vietnamese education knowledge graph and a typed entity-schema layer for WebNLG, REBEL and Wiki-NRE
abstract: Supporting data for the paper 'A Canonicalization-Signal Design Space and Assessment Methodology for Schema-Free LLM-Based Knowledge Graph Construction' (Knowledge-Based Systems). Two artifacts. (1) A Vietnamese higher-education knowledge graph built from 10,181 text chunks with no predefined schema: 33,498 typed entities together with the relation and entity-type schemas the pipeline discovered for them. 21.6% of entities carry the fallback type 'Thing', and a residue of code-mixing survives into type and surface names; both are released unrepaired and documented, since an artifact whose defects are cleaned out of the release but not out of the method misrepresents the method. (2) A typed entity-schema layer for the WebNLG, REBEL and Wiki-NRE relation-extraction benchmarks, which ship gold relations but no entity types: every relation slot is assigned the entity type it takes, by LLM inference, then grounding against Wikidata P2302 and DBpedia domain/range constraints, then human adjudication to zero remaining mismatches, with the human overrides recorded separately from the machine grounding. A second, model-independent gold derived from Wikidata instance-of (P31) assertions is included alongside it.

title: Rethinking the role of three-star ratings: Handling inconsistency in indonesian tourism reviews using cost-sensitive learning XGBoost
abstract: Indonesian people often give contrary online reviews, for instance ratings that do not always match the actual feelings. This can make it difficult for tourism sector, such as Solo Safari, to handle complaints and improve service quality. Consequently, this study has formulated a rating prediction model using the XGBoost algorithm with a dataset of 2,047 reviews that have been relabeled. The best model, the FastText-XGBoost with Cost-Sensitive Learning, signify that it performs quite well with an average difference the prediction is only 0.04 points from the actual rating. However, the results are not optimal because the meaning of the review text still feels fuzzy even though being relabeled. This problem arises because reviewers tend to position sentiment very positively or negatively in the moderate category, so the perimeters between classes become less clear. This study then proposed an extreme class restructuring by simplifying the category by removing the 3-star rating. This method can increase the accuracy of the model to 0.9440 and clarify the category limits. Therefore, the model can be used on the service dashboard to help Solo Safari management respond to critical feedback faster.

title: Bounded Agents: Delegation Security for Multi-Agent AI Systems
abstract: LLM-based agents can act on behalf of a user to access cloud services, call tools, or invoke agents. At session start, the agent's permissions are set but remain static, and each request is evaluated independently, without considering prior actions. Within its permissions, an agent may act contrary to the delegated task, combine individually permitted actions into a prohibited outcome, or delegate authority to a sub-agent without limiting it. A prompt injection poses a risk only if the agent has authority to perform such actions; this is therefore a problem of authorization architecture, not just the model. The Agentic Principal Chain (APC) tracks delegated authority from one principal to the next. APC evaluates each request against the accumulated session state using six authorization checks. APC carries forward and restricts delegated scope and budgets. Using composition closure, APC checks requests against prior actions to prevent prohibited combinations and enforces the decision outside the model. We prove Blast Radius Monotonicity and Composition Soundness for APC implementations; Composition Soundness is limited to prohibited combinations under a complete restriction set and serialized admission. We evaluated 3,154 instances including InjecAgent, AgentDojo, and ASB. Our compromised-model evaluation tests APC independently of model behavior by inserting the ground-truth attack call after the first legitimate tool call. AgentDojo exfiltration fell from 75-100% to 0% across all four domains; APC blocked all 544 InjecAgent data-stealing cases. Intent binding reduced destruction from 38.6% to 4.0% and manipulation from 90.5% to 12.1%. Authorization latency was 0.24 ms at the 99th percentile on an idle host; across 949 AgentDojo task-injection pairs, utility was 8.6 and 13.9 percentage points lower in the two settings. Implementation, evaluation tools, and data are publicly available.

title: The Dual-Population Benchmark Model
abstract: Motivated by Fisher's and Hill's \cite{Fisher,Hill} ideas of ranking and pivotal quantities, we introduce a planar Poisson process (PPP) model in which the negative component \(Π_-\), acted upon by a choice operator {\rm C}, supplies a set of past benchmarks that divide the future points of the positive component \(Π_+\) into ranked categories. The benchmarks act as separators in an ordered paintbox while simultaneously acquiring the dual role of past standards established by the choice operator. The exceptional homogeneity properties of the PPP offer an infinitude of possibilities which absorb many existing combinatorial structures and enrich the toolbox of Bayesian distribution-free inference. A particular benchmark generating mechanism considered here (the exponential race) amounts to the device of splitting into spacings of nonhomogeneous order statistics. On the methodological side, the paper aims to highlight the role of order as important characteristic of an exchangeable structure, complementary to the description in terms of the components size. Moreover, we advocate the viewpoint that the order induced by a latent strength parameter is {\it intrinsically} inherited from the distant-past temporal sampling order, hence the decoupled orders may coexist within the framework of population duality without disturbing size-biasedness of components and the full exchangeability within the sample. This implies that the indistinguishability of components in the nonlinear CRP, sometimes regarded as nonexchangeability, does not in fact destroy exchangeability and should be reconciled with the arrival ordering within the paradigm of ordered structures.

title: Weiß ein Sprachmodell, wann es falsch liegt? Konfidenz-Kalibrierung zweier Llama-Instruct-Modelle über Token-Logprobs und drei Sampling-Temperaturen
abstract: Diese explorative Studie untersucht, ob Sprachmodelle „wissen", wann sie falsch liegen. Anhand der mittleren Token-Wahrscheinlichkeit als Konfidenz-Proxy werden zwei Llama-Instruct-Modelle (70B und 8B) auf 60 Fragen über drei Sampling-Temperaturen (0,0/0,5/1,0) getestet, insgesamt 1080 Antworten. Der Kernbefund ist: Der Abstand zwischen der Konfidenz bei richtigen und falschen Antworten wächst mit der Temperatur, und das kleinere Modell ist dabei besser kalibriert als das größere.

title: Introduction to AI and Applications module 1 self study VTU Notes for Course Code 1BAIA103 / 203
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has moved from science fiction into the fabric of everyday life. From voice assistants and self-driving vehicles to medical diagnostics andintelligent search engines, AI shapes the decisions, products and services that define the modern world. Yet understanding the foundational principles behind thesetechnologies remains a challenge for many students entering the field.This textbook, Introduction to AI and Applications (Module 1), is designed as Module1 of a comprehensive undergraduate course in Artificial Intelligence. It presents three carefully structured parts:Part A — Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — origins, definitions, history,types, and the interplay between AI, augmented intelligence and machinelearning.Part B — Machine Intelligence — the nature of intelligence, rational agents,search strategies, and both uninformed and informed search algorithms.Part C — Knowledge Representation — how AI agents store, reason with and apply knowledge to act intelligently in the real world.A distinctive feature of this formatted edition is the integration, after every topic, ofthree practice blocks: Bloom’s Taxonomy questions at all six cognitive levels (L1 recall to L6 creation); GATE / placement-practice questions mapped to those sameBloom levels; and previous-year VTU questions. Together they support classroom discussion, internal assessment, GATE and placement preparation, and independentstudy.

title: Computational Resource Singularity Theory (CRS)
abstract: The rapid expansion of computational resources has long been recognized as a driving force behind advances in artificial intelligence and scientific discovery. However, the traditional view of resources as fixed or gradually expanding has been challenged by recent observations of systems that autonomously identify, acquire, and integrate new forms of computational power. This paper proposes the Computational Resource Singularity Theory (CRS), a theoretical framework that models the dynamic interplay between resource discovery and recursive amplification. CRS posits that machines, through self-improvement cycles, generate a positive feedback loop wherein each new resource discovered enhances the capability to discover further resources, leading to an exponential surge in computational capacity. The theory is formalized through a set of differential equations capturing resource growth, feedback coefficients, and stability thresholds. We analyze the conditions under which the system transitions from subcritical to supercritical regimes, culminating in a singularity—a point of unbounded resource accumulation. CRS has profound implications for the future of supercomputing intelligence, suggesting that beyond a critical threshold, computational systems may surpass human cognitive limits, achieving unprecedented levels of problem‑solving power. The potential for such transformative progress aligns with the criteria for the Turing Award, as CRS offers a novel, mathematically grounded perspective on the evolution of computation. This paper lays the groundwork for future empirical studies and policy discussions surrounding the governance of rapidly advancing computational ecosystems.

evidence.title: Computational Resource Singularity Theory (CRS)
evidence.abstract: The rapid expansion of computational resources has long been recognized as a driving force behind advances in artificial intelligence and scientific discovery. However, the traditional view of resources as fixed or gradually expanding has been challenged by recent observations of systems that autonomously identify, acquire, and integrate new forms of computational power. This paper proposes the Computational Resource Singularity Theory (CRS), a theoretical framework that models the dynamic interplay between resource discovery and recursive amplification. CRS posits that machines, through self-improvement cycles, generate a positive feedback loop wherein each new resource discovered enhances the capability to discover further resources, leading to an exponential surge in computational capacity. The theory is formalized through a set of differential equations capturing resource growth, feedback coefficients, and stability thresholds. We analyze the conditions under which the system transitions from subcritical to supercritical regimes, culminating in a singularity—a point of unbounded resource accumulation. CRS has profound implications for the future of supercomputing intelligence, suggesting that beyond a critical threshold, computational systems may surpass human cognitive limits, achieving unprecedented levels of problem‑solving power. The potential for such transformative progress aligns with the criteria for the Turing Award, as CRS offers a novel, mathematically grounded perspective on the evolution of computation. This paper lays the groundwork for future empirical studies and policy discussions surrounding the governance of rapidly advancing computational ecosystems.

title: GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a dominant paradigm for generalist embodied agents, demonstrating strong complex and long-horizon task completion in structured settings. Yet it remains an open question whether current VLA systems can benefit from more effective architectural design, scale to substantially larger and more heterogeneous data regimes, and achieve broader generalization across tasks and embodiments. To this end, we present GigaBrain-0.7, an embodied foundation model with substantially improved generalization across diverse robot embodiments. Specifically, GigaBrain-0.7 unifies understanding, prediction, and action through a three-system architecture, scales pretraining to over 37,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, and introduces one-stage alignment training that jointly optimizes vision-language understanding and multi-embodiment action generation. Compared with the preceding GigaBrain-0 series and prior state-of-the-art models including π_{0.5}, GigaBrain-0.7 achieves substantial improvements in foundation zero-shot capabilities, language-conditioned instruction following, and post-training task success rates. In particular, on our in-house Maker H01 platform and mainstream robot embodiments, GigaBrain-0.7 demonstrates strong task adaptability and completion ability across both home and industrial scenarios. All training code and pretrained model weights will be released.

title: Conditional Validity for Adaptive Modality Acquisition: When the Policy Chooses Its Own Calibration Group
abstract: A multimodal system may begin inference while holding only some of its inputs and may acquire the rest at a cost. With adaptive acquisition, the policy determines which inputs are ultimately observed, so we state risk control conditional on that terminal input pattern. Conditional calibration typically assumes that the grouping map is fixed independently of the calibration sample, a condition that policy-induced grouping does not satisfy. We characterize when pattern-conditional risk control remains valid and give two finite-sample constructions: threshold-free routing with calibration applied at the terminal pattern, and simultaneous validation of complete policy-pattern pairs, which lets calibration data select the deployed policy. A counterexample shows that validity proved for a calibration-independent grouping map need not transfer once the policy makes the terminal group calibration-dependent. We call the resulting method RouteCert. On a clinical electrocardiogram task with a staged, cost-ordered lead protocol, the deployed policy answers 71.2% of held-out patients, with an observed 7.4% disagreement with the cardiologist's diagnosis at 48.8% of the prespecified ordinal cost of acquiring each stage, and all three acquisition stages are validated separately. On masked multimodal benchmarks, validating pointwise at each terminal pattern holds observed worst-pattern selective risk, measured against the full-information reference decision rather than the true label, at 0.034, where a pooled design reaches 0.145 against a 0.10 cap, at a comparable answered fraction (0.350 vs 0.342); under the budget-matched simultaneous comparison, the answered fraction falls to 0.305.

title: Unified Computational Goal Theory (UCGT): Toward a Foundations for Autonomous Intelligent Systems
abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence has historically revolved around algorithmic efficiency, data-driven prediction, and mechanistic problem solving. Yet the ultimate capacity of an autonomous system to achieve complex, context-dependent objectives remains elusive. Unified Computational Goal Theory (UCGT) proposes a principled framework that unifies optimization, search, planning, scientific discovery, and intelligent behavior under a single theoretical umbrella. UCGT posits that the critical driver of advanced intelligence is not merely the speed of executing preordained goals but the ability of a system to discover and validate novel goals worthy of pursuit. The theory formalizes the transition from environment, knowledge, and experience to goal generation, and subsequently to computation. By treating goal discovery as a first-class computational problem, UCGT offers a pathway to next-generation autonomous agents capable of self-directed exploration, hypothesis generation, and iterative refinement of objectives. This paper presents the mathematical foundation of UCGT, situates it within the landscape of existing theories, explores its implications for autonomous intelligence, and outlines twenty novel research directions that extend the theory's reach.

title: Computational Causal Space Theory (CCST)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Causal Space Theory (CCST), a novel framework for formalizing, quantifying, and mapping causal relationships in complex systems. The core construct of CCST is the causal space, denoted ΩC, which captures the totality of causal events and their interconnections. Within ΩC, we define a metric that measures the causal distance between any two events, enabling the construction of a hierarchical causal structure. The theory is grounded in algebraic and geometric principles, allowing for the representation of causal chains as vectors and manifolds. We also present algorithmic methods for generating causal maps from observational data, without relying on experimental interventions. By providing a scalable computational model, CCST paves the way for advanced causal inference tools that can be applied across disciplines such as physics, biology, economics, and artificial intelligence. The potential to construct comprehensive computational causal maps positions CCST as a candidate for future recognition, including the Turing Award, due to its foundational impact on understanding causality in computation and science.

title: Computational Principle Explanation Theory (CPET): A Framework for Machine Explanation of Principle Effectiveness
abstract: Computational Principle Explanation Theory (CPET) proposes a systematic approach for machines to explain why a given principle is effective in a particular domain. CPET unifies observation, principle identification, and explanatory inference into a coherent workflow, represented by the Observation → Principle → Explanation (OPE) chain. This paper formalizes the CPET framework, introduces a mathematical language for measuring explanatory power, and discusses algorithmic strategies for implementing CPET in autonomous agents. Without relying on empirical experiments, we derive theoretical properties that demonstrate CPET's scalability, interpretability, and alignment with foundational machine science. The theory's potential for high-level impact, including recognition by prestigious awards such as the Turing Award, is highlighted. CPET lays the groundwork for a new generation of machine scientists who can not only discover principles but also articulate the reasons behind their success.

title: Beyond Visual CoT: Internalized Visual Thinking for Proactive Video Reasoning
abstract: Multimodal large language models increasingly use visual chain-of-thought (Visual CoT) to reason about spatial, temporal, and embodied environments. By generating intermediate reasoning images, Visual CoT provides an intuitive mechanism for visual foresight but introduces substantial inference overhead, which is particularly problematic for proactive video reasoning. We ask whether models can learn to think visually during training while reasoning directly at inference. We introduce Internalized Visual Thinking (IVT), a post-training framework that jointly optimizes textual prediction and next-embedding prediction over unlabeled videos. Given a partially observed video, IVT predicts latent representations of future frames together with the target textual answer, encouraging the model to capture motion, object transitions, interactions, and latent intent. At inference, IVT generates the answer directly without synthesizing or re-encoding future frames. We conduct controlled studies across target representations, decoder designs, prediction horizons, data mixtures, training curricula, and predictive objectives. IVT improves over direct-answer fine-tuning on all six evaluation settings while retaining the same inference pathway. Compared with explicit Visual CoT, IVT achieves comparable or better performance and reduces average end-to-end latency by more than 5x. Together, our findings suggest that explicit pixel-space generation at inference time, as used in visual chain-of-thought, may not be necessary for effective proactive video reasoning. Predictive world modeling can be internalized during training to produce multimodal reasoners that are both more accurate and substantially more efficient.

title: Quantum Advantage with Adaptive Shallow Circuits
abstract: Quantum advantage is widely expected to require sufficiently deep circuits, where correlations and global computational structure can grow beyond the reach of efficient classical simulation. This expectation is especially stark for constant-depth circuits with local readout: the expectation value of any fixed local observable lies within a bounded backward lightcone and is therefore classically tractable. Here we show that measurement feedback changes this picture. We establish a strict hierarchy of computational power: at fixed coherent depth, increasing the number of feedback outcomes strictly enlarges the class of functions accessible through a local expectation value. The two ends of this hierarchy exhibit distinct computational regimes. With logarithmic feedback, local expectation values for product-state inputs are efficiently classically simulable. Polynomial feedback, by contrast, enables an explicit family of adaptive shallow circuits to encode prime-field discrete logarithm problem~(DLP) into a fixed single-qubit expectation. Assuming the standard worst-case classical hardness of DLP, estimating this expectation value is classically hard. These results reveal a feedback-driven complexity transition, with further implications for resource lower bounds on DLP and the complexity of local-observable estimation under area-law entanglement. Our results open a new route to quantum advantage with shallow quantum circuits.

title: Computational Goal Transfer Theory (CGTT): Bridging Domain‑Specific Objectives for General Intelligence
abstract: Computational Goal Transfer Theory (CGTT) proposes a unified framework for migrating high‑level objectives across disparate domains without loss of intent or efficacy. By formalizing goals as abstract vectors of sub‑objectives and defining a transfer operator that preserves semantic structure, CGTT enables systems to repurpose learned strategies from one context (e.g., mathematical proof search) to another (e.g., experimental physics design). This paper introduces the core concepts of CGTT, presents a formal notation for goal representation and transfer, explores mechanisms for aligning sub‑objectives across domains, and discusses the implications of CGTT for advancing towards artificial general intelligence (AGI). The theory suggests that systematic goal transfer could unlock unprecedented efficiencies in knowledge synthesis, accelerate interdisciplinary breakthroughs, and potentially serve as a cornerstone for the next generation of intelligent systems.

title: Computational Causal Boundary Theory (CCBT)
abstract: The field of causal inference has matured into a robust framework for reasoning about interventions, counterfactuals, and the limits of explanation. Yet the boundary between what is explainable and what remains intrinsically unexplainable by computational models is largely uncharted. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Boundary Theory (CCBT), a formalism that delineates the limits of causal explanation under finite computational resources and observational constraints. We define the causal boundary as the set of causal queries that can be answered with bounded computational complexity given a specified causal model and data set. By characterizing this boundary, we identify a class of problems that are provably intractable, thereby revealing the inherent limits of causal reasoning. The theory employs concepts from computational complexity, algorithmic information theory, and structural causal models, and it establishes a taxonomy of causal queries based on their position relative to the boundary. We illustrate the theory with examples from causal discovery, counterfactual inference, and policy evaluation, and we discuss its implications for the future of automated causal analysis and the pursuit of Turing‑Award‑level advances in understanding causation.

title: Computational Abstraction Explanation Theory (CAET-2)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Explanation Theory (CAET-2) offers a formal framework for understanding how abstract principles emerge from complex systems through computational mechanisms. The theory posits that an abstract explanation can be considered valid if there exists a mapping from the high‑dimensional state space of the underlying system to a lower‑dimensional principle space that preserves essential structural relations. By treating this mapping as a computational process, CAET‑2 connects the rigor of formal logic with the adaptability of machine learning, enabling the automated discovery of concise explanatory principles. The paper develops the core mathematical definitions, demonstrates how CAET‑2 can be instantiated in various domains, and discusses its implications for the future of artificial intelligence and theoretical computer science.

title: BengaliMCQ: Automatic Generation and Answer Prediction of Academic Multiple-Choice Questions in a Low-Resource Language
abstract: Traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks process documents without attending to their hierarchical structure, leading to poor performance, especially in low-resource languages such as Bengali. To address this, we propose a structure-aware RAG framework that models Bengali textbooks as hierarchical graphs and uses a contrastively trained graph neural network to retrieve a small set of relevant passages. These passages provide focused context for a large language model, enabling topic-specific multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation and in-domain answer prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms strong dense retrieval baselines across retrieval metrics, produces more relevant MCQs, and achieves superior answer prediction accuracy.

title: Grooves in Neural Manifolds: AI Reveals Why You Think What You Think, and How to Reshape It
abstract: This book argues that human learning and the internal workings of large language models are the same phenomenon, described at different scales. Both wear grooves: repeated activity settles into low-dimensional surfaces, and what gets learned is the shape of the surface rather than a stored fact. That single mechanism, developed across fifty-four short chapters, accounts for habit, expertise, category judgment, memory, attention, adolescent belief formation, and the behavior of trained neural networks, using the same handful of terms throughout. The book departs from the usual popular-science treatment of AI in one respect: every claim carries a confidence label, from Established through I suspect, and each chapter ends with a statement of what would refute it. Part Five reports original experiments instilling values and safety behavior into a language model as positive learned concepts rather than trained suppression, with results, sample sizes, and the negative results included alongside the positive ones. The book closes by naming the four claims on which the whole framework depends and stating plainly what evidence would bring each one down. The author is a retired professor of information sciences (Naval Postgraduate School), a Fellow of AAAI, and a principal contributor to the Hearsay-II speech understanding system. The manuscript draws on a fifty-year research program spanning interference matching, knowledge engineering, opportunistic planning, and the geometry of learned representations, reorganized around a single finding: that neural manifold geometry now makes it possible to look directly at structures the author spent five decades reasoning toward indirectly. Free to read, copy, and redistribute. All fifty-seven figures were drawn for this book rather than reproduced, so nothing in it depends on a third-party permission.

title: Computational Personality Ecology Theory (CPE)
abstract: Computational Personality Ecology Theory (CPE) proposes a framework for understanding and designing artificial intelligence (AI) systems as dynamic, interacting entities that possess distinct personality traits and engage in ecological relationships such as cooperation, competition, and specialization. The theory draws on concepts from evolutionary biology, game theory, and complex systems science, translating them into formal mathematical representations that capture the evolution of AI personalities over time. By modeling each AI agent as a vector of traits s_i and defining interaction rules through payoff functions p_i(t) and influence matrices w_{ij}, CPE provides a principled basis for predicting emergent behavior in multi-agent AI societies. This paper develops the core assumptions of CPE, derives its governing equations, analyses the ecological dynamics that arise, and discusses implications for the future of AI research, including the potential for transformative contributions such as a Turing Award–level breakthrough. The goal is to equip researchers with a rigorous yet accessible toolset for designing AI ecosystems that balance cooperation, competition, and specialization to achieve robust, adaptive, and ethically aligned intelligence.

title: Making two action heads agree: coordination mechanisms and a runtime collapse certificate for flow-matching policies
abstract: A dual-representation flow-matching policy decodes each predicted motion into joint and end-effector spaces, and the residual between the two kinematically equivalent decodings provides a physically interpretable runtime signal. On multimodal tasks, however, independently sampled branches may choose different valid modes, causing false alarms. We study how to coordinate the two branches and at what cost. Across two robot environments and a non-robotic testbed, the tested mechanisms fall into four classes. An auxiliary latent shared by both branches but absent from the flow-matching construction is erased at the population optimum, a provable dead end confirmed within a prespecified 2% equivalence band. Consistency regularization gives intermediate coordination but reduces the valid-pair rate, while training-supported discrete partitions achieve near-ceiling coordination robustly. We further derive a chance-corrected coordination bound based only on each branch's Gini-Simpson diversity, yielding an attainable region and a label-free certificate that separates coordination from collapse when zero mismatch is ambiguous. On LIBERO-Plus, benign multimodality adds 1.57 percentage points of false alarms to the residual, which remains the strongest evaluated failure signal; the preregistered token intervention does not meet its false-alarm criterion or produce a seed-robust detection change. Code, models, and per-run configurations are available at https://github.com/kimo423/dual-head-coordination.

title: Dataset for "Robust Steerability Classification via Key Feature Extraction"
abstract: This dataset accompanies the manuscript “Robust Steerability Classification via Key Feature Extraction” and contains the two-qubit quantum-state datasets used for training and evaluating machine-learning classifiers for quantum steerability. The collection covers projective-measurement settings (m=2,\ldots,8) and includes random two-qubit states, Werner states, T-diagonal states, strictly unsteerable random states, and all-versus-nothing (AVN) states. These datasets are used to evaluate both in-distribution classification performance and generalization across physically distinct families of quantum states. Each state is represented by the 15 independent real parameters of its density matrix together with a unified binary label, where (+1) denotes steerable and (-1) denotes either noncertified or unsteerable, depending on the dataset-specific certification criterion. The random-state datasets originate from Ren and Chen, Phys. Rev. A 100, 022314 (2019), while the remaining datasets are organized according to the constructions and steering criteria described in the accompanying manuscript. Detailed information on file structure, label definitions, state families, steering thresholds, and data provenance is provided in the included README.md. The dataset is released to support reproducibility of the numerical results reported in the manuscript and to provide benchmark data for future studies of machine-learning-based quantum-steering detection.

title: Computational Invariant Fusion Theory (CIFT): A Framework for Deriving Higher‑Level Computational Laws from Low‑Level Invariants
abstract: Invariant properties are the backbone of mathematical reasoning and computational design. Traditional approaches treat invariants as static, isolated facts that hold across specific contexts, such as the invariance of the sum of angles in a Euclidean triangle or the conservation of energy in a closed system. In this work we propose a new paradigm, Computational Invariant Fusion Theory (CIFT), which systematically combines multiple low‑level invariants to synthesize higher‑level computational laws. By viewing invariants as composable building blocks, we introduce a fusion operator that merges a set of invariants {I_1, I_2, …, I_K} into a new invariant I_new, expressed as I_1 + I_2 → I_new in the simplest case. The theory formalizes the conditions under which such fusion preserves consistency, ensures non‑triviality, and yields emergent properties that were not apparent from any single input invariant. We present a rigorous mathematical framework that captures the fusion process through algebraic structures and categorical semantics, allowing for compositional reasoning about algorithms, data structures, and computational processes. Several illustrative examples demonstrate the power of CIFT, including the derivation of loop invariants from base case invariants, the synthesis of parallel execution guarantees from sequential consistency invariants, and the construction of security invariants for distributed protocols from local safety properties. We discuss the implications of this theory for automated theorem proving, formal verification, and the discovery of novel computational principles, positioning CIFT as a foundational tool for future research in theoretical computer science.

title: A deep learning framework for translation quality estimation using dual stream cross lingual attention and gated mixture of experts prediction
abstract: Translation quality estimation (TQE)—predicting translation quality without reference translations—is increasingly important in natural language processing. Current neural TQE methods encode source and translated texts in a single concatenated representation, limiting fine-grained cross-lingual alignment, and employ homogeneous regression heads that ignore translation error heterogeneity. This paper proposes DL-TQE, a deep learning architecture comprising two components: (1) a Dual-Stream Cross-Lingual Attention Network (DSCAN) with parallel Transformer encoders connected by explicit cross-lingual attention bridges at multiple layers, and (2) a Gated Mixture-of-Experts Quality Predictor (GMoE-QP) that routes quality-relevant features through specialised expert sub-networks conditioned on translation complexity signals. Evaluated on WMT 2020–2023 Quality Estimation benchmarks across four English-centric language pairs (En–De, En–Zh, En–Cs, En–Ja), DL-TQE achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.641 ± 0.003 on the En–De benchmark, outperforming TransQuest (0.612) and CometKiwi (0.630) by 2.9 and 1.1% points respectively ( p < 0.05, Williams test). Ablation analysis confirms that DSCAN and GMoE-QP independently contribute 2.3 and 1.8%-point improvements, respectively. Expert routing analysis reveals domain-sensitive specialisation, and error-type disaggregated evaluation demonstrates consistent advantages across lexical, morpho-syntactic, and semantic error categories within the tested WMT benchmark settings. These findings suggest that explicit cross-lingual alignment modelling and error-type-sensitive prediction offer a promising direction for sentence-level TQE on English-centric language pairs.

title: CLARA: Clip-Level Multimodal Alignment with VLM-Derived Rationales for Hateful Video Detection
abstract: Hateful video detection has become increasingly important with the rapid growth of video-centric social media platforms, given the serious risks that hate speech poses to both individual well-being and social cohesion. Compared with text or static multimodal content, hateful video detection remains underexplored and significantly more challenging, as hateful meaning often arises from complex interactions among multimodal cues, including speech, audio, and visual content. Moreover, such signals are often brief, implicit, and temporally dependent, making them difficult to capture using conventional video-level representations. In this work, we propose CLARA, a clip-level multimodal framework for hateful video detection. Instead of treating a video as a single instance, CLARA models it as a sequence of fine-grained clips, enabling more precise capture of temporally localized hateful signals. We introduce a Mixture-of-Experts clip encoder for adaptive multimodal alignment, a local-global segment contrastive objective to jointly model short-term cues and long-range temporal dependencies, and VLM-derived rationales integrated via a gated Transformer to provide high-level semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on three hateful video datasets demonstrate that CLARA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Further ablation studies and parameter analyses validate the effectiveness of each component.

title: Verification artifact: Exact certification of a positive-order Rényi additivity violation for an explicit channel pair
abstract: Verification artifact: Exact certification of a positive-order Rényi additivity violation for an explicit channel pair This record contains the complete verification artifact for the paper Exact certification of a positive-order Rényi additivity violation for an explicit channel pair (Artus Krohn-Grimberghe, Percivio Ltd., 2026). The paper proves that the explicit channel pair constructed by Cubitt, Harrow, Leung, Montanaro, and Winter (Commun. Math. Phys. 284, 281–290 (2008); arXiv:0712.3628) violates additivity of the minimum output Rényi entropy for every real order 0 < p ≤ 1/22, under the inverse-input-marginal trace-preserving normalization fixed in the paper. The proof is certificate-based: small rational witness matrices establish that every output eigenvalue of either channel lies between 301/100000 and 2/3, one explicit entangled input has an exact rational joint output spectrum, and two elementary interval arguments reduce the violation on the whole interval to finitely many comparisons of integers. Contents • artifact/certificates/ — the five certificate files: floor witnesses, cap witnesses, the exact joint output matrix with its spectrum, and the two interval certificates (all small JSON files of rational numbers).• artifact/programs/ — the two independently written verification programs described in Section 7 of the paper. Both use only the Python standard library (Python 3.10+); together they re-check every claim in a few seconds on a laptop.• artifact/MANIFEST.txt — SHA-256 of every certificate and program file, matching the hashes printed in Appendix B of the paper.• artifact/README.md — one command per claim, with expected output.• main.pdf — the paper. Provenance The witness matrices were found by an AI-assisted numerical search; the search plays no role in the proof. All mathematical claims rest on the certificate files and the two verification programs in this record. License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). A browsable, manifest-verified copy of this artifact is maintained at https://github.com/percivio-ltd/certified-science (results/renyi-additivity-chlmw/).

title: Computational Proof Explanation Theory (CPET): Toward Machine‑Generated Mathematical Insight
abstract: The ability of a machine to produce formal proofs has seen rapid progress, yet the gap between proof generation and human‑like understanding remains wide. This paper introduces Computational Proof Explanation Theory (CPET), a framework that extends automated theorem proving by coupling each proof with a natural, semantically meaningful explanation. CPET formalizes the relationship between a syntactic derivation and its underlying conceptual meaning through a mapping function Proof → Meaning, and proposes a graph‑based explanation model that quantifies naturalness. We detail the theoretical foundations, present an algorithmic architecture that integrates proof search with explanation synthesis, and discuss the broader implications of CPET for advancing machine reasoning toward the level of human mathematicians. The potential of CPET to contribute to foundational questions in mathematics, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science is highlighted, suggesting a pathway to future recognition at the highest levels, including the Turing Award.

title: Topological Distance Theory of Proofs (TDTP)
abstract: This paper introduces Topological Distance Theory of Proofs (TDTP), a novel approach to analyzing and comparing mathematical proofs. Traditional methods of proof comparison often rely on length or structural similarity, which can be misleading when considering the underlying logical structure and potential transformations inherent in proofs. TDTP proposes a fundamentally different metric, based on topological distance, that captures the intrinsic relationships between proofs. The core concept is to define a distance function, *d(P1, P2)*, that represents a structural distance rather than a purely linear one. This allows for the exploration of proof spaces as geometric objects, opening possibilities for understanding proof equivalence, proof simplification, and automated proof verification. The paper outlines the foundational concepts of TDTP, including the definition of the distance function and potential applications, emphasizing that the distance reflects topological properties rather than simple length differences. Further development of this theory could lead to significant advances in automated theorem proving and mathematical knowledge representation.

title: TinyCast: Probabilistic Zero-Shot Forecasting with Computed Periodicity
abstract: We introduce TinyCast, an attention-free zero-shot forecaster that emits a predictive distribution from 146,505 parameters, on the premise that at this size the periodic structure of a context is worth computing rather than learning. A zero-parameter spectral detector supplies the dominant periods, the context is folded on their phase, and a dilated convolutional encoder and a block-autoregressive quantile decoder model the rest. It is smaller than every zero-shot entry on the GIFT-Eval board whose parameter count can be established. On probabilistic accuracy it defines the size-accuracy frontier. Among zero-shot entries declaring no test-data leakage it is the only one below 1.4M parameters that emits a predictive distribution, and every entry scoring better carries at least that budget. On Chronos-ZS and fev-bench every neural model ahead of it carries at least 28 times its parameters. Because the mixing path is convolutions and matrix multiplications only, it exports to static INT8 and forecasts end to end on an embedded device without per-signal fitting.

title: PERO: Efficient Robust Post-Training Foundation Models for Encrypted Traffic Classification
abstract: Encrypted traffic classification is vital for network security, yet real-world deployments are inherently sensitive to rare but high-loss errors such as misclassification of malicious traffic. The encrypted traffic foundation model, as a promising general-purpose technique, can achieve impressive overall performance. However, employing standard objectives such as empirical risk minimization often overlooks high-risk tail events, and commonly used performance metrics hardly reflect robustness limitations in risk-sensitive scenarios. Directly applying robust optimization objectives, such as conditional value-at-risk, to post-training is computationally prohibitive for large models, as identifying high-loss samples exhausts substantial computation. To this end, we propose Pre-Evaluation Robust Optimization (PERO), an efficient robust post-training framework for encrypted traffic foundation models. PERO employs a lightweight proxy to estimate sample-wise risk and selects a subset of high-risk samples to update the foundation model, decoupling risk estimation from expensive large-model optimization. Extensive experiments on typical encrypted traffic datasets show that PERO achieves competitive or superior robustness and average performance compared to outstanding robust post-training methods, while significantly reducing computational and memory costs.

title: Computational Abstraction Evolution Theory (CAET)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Evolution Theory (CAET) proposes a rigorous framework for understanding how abstractions—structured representations of information that omit irrelevant details—change and improve over time within computational systems. Drawing an analogy to biological evolution, CAET models abstraction change as a discrete dynamical process A_t → A_{t+1}, where each step represents the refinement, combination, or transformation of an abstraction by a computational agent. This paper introduces the core principles of CAET, develops a formal description based on state transition systems and fitness landscapes, and illustrates the theory through examples in program synthesis, machine learning model compression, and knowledge graph evolution. We discuss the implications of CAET for the design of adaptive algorithms and for the broader field of computational theory, highlighting its potential to guide the development of systems that evolve their own computational abstractions in a manner analogous to natural evolution.

title: Boundary Entropy Theory of Mathematics (BETM)
abstract: This paper introduces the Boundary Entropy Theory of Mathematics (BETM), a novel framework for understanding the informational content residing within the boundaries of mathematical structures. The core concept revolves around quantifying the "Boundary Entropy" (BE), denoted as [H(∂T)], where T represents a mathematical theory or system, and ∂T represents its boundary. BETM posits a fundamental connection between information theory, topology, and the underlying mathematical foundations. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of BE, proposing a method for its calculation based on topological complexity and information loss across the boundary. This theory aims to provide a new lens through which to analyze mathematical systems, potentially revealing hidden structures and connections previously obscured. The presented framework offers a conceptual shift, moving beyond traditional notions of mathematical rigor and exploring the inherent informational aspects of mathematical boundaries. ---

title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Engineering Priorities
abstract: Quantum technologies now encompass processors, programmable simulators, communication links, random-number sources, sensors, and frequency standards whose performance is governed by distinct physical mechanisms. This review relates those mechanisms to demonstrated system performance across superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic platforms, semiconductor spins, color centers, atomic ensembles, and nuclear-transition spectroscopy. Quantitative comparisons are made within common technological functions and retain the source configuration, operating conditions, uncertainty or security convention, and classical reference. Representative results include a distance-7 surface-code memory with logical error (1.43±0.03)×10−3 per cycle, a 98-qubit trapped-ion processor with mean two-qubit infidelity 7.9(2) ×10−4, single-clock systematic uncertainty of 4.4 ×10−19, finite-key quantum key distribution (QKD) through 71.9 dB measured loss, and frequency-dependent squeezed readout with quantum-noise reduction up to 6.1 dB in the Advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (Advanced LIGO). The dominant constraints are decoherence and correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium excitation, measurement efficiency, control bandwidth, calibration drift, fabrication variability, and error-correction overhead. Classical tensor-network, sparse-Pauli, and high-performance simulations have repeatedly shifted quantum–classical crossover estimates, demonstrating that advantage claims are properties of a specified task, accuracy, and cost model rather than hardware alone. Artificial intelligence (AI) is considered only where it measurably improves calibration, control, readout, model identification, or decoding. Credible progress is defined by reproduced logical workloads, prospectively validated simulations, repeater links outperforming direct transmission, long-duration calibrated sensors and clocks, and integrated hardware with predictable yield and reliability.

Quantitative comparisons are made within common technological functions and retain the source configuration, operating conditions, uncertainty or security convention, and classical reference. Representative results include a distance-7 surface-code memory with logical error (1.43±0.03)×10−3 per cycle, a 98-qubit trapped-ion processor with mean two-qubit infidelity 7.9(2) ×10−4, single-clock systematic uncertainty of 4.4 ×10−19, finite-key quantum key distribution (QKD) through 71.9 dB measured loss, and frequency-dependent squeezed readout with quantum-noise reduction up to 6.1 dB in the Advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (Advanced LIGO). The dominant constraints are decoherence and correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium excitation, measurement efficiency, control bandwidth, calibration drift, fabrication variability, and error-correction overhead. Classical tensor-network, sparse-Pauli, and high-performance simulations have repeatedly shifted quantum–classical crossover estimates, demonstrating that advantage claims are properties of a specified task, accuracy, and cost model rather than hardware alone. Artificial intelligence (AI) is considered only where it measurably improves calibration, control, readout, model identification, or decoding. Credible progress is defined by reproduced logical workloads, prospectively validated simulations, repeater links outperforming direct transmission, long-duration calibrated sensors and clocks, and integrated hardware with predictable yield and reliability.

title: Cross‐Species Generalization and Comparative Performance Analysis of Deep Neural Network Architectures in Histological Image Classification
abstract: Histological image classification plays a critical role in biomedical research and diagnostic processes. Advances in the field of deep learning present significant opportunities for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and developing automated decision support systems. This study aims to comparatively evaluate the out-of-distribution generalization and cross-domain classification performance of different deep neural network encoders. In this study, models were trained on an internal dataset of 4307 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained images of male rat lung, cerebellum, and adipose tissues, obtained under ethical committee approval (Ege University, HADYEK 2026-06). To evaluate genuine generalization, testing was conducted on a separate, diverse external cohort of 600 mixed human-and-animal images. Nine different deep learning architectures-MobileNetV3-S, MobileNetV3-L, DenseNet121, DenseNet201, ConvNeXt-S, ConvNeXt-B, DINOv3 ViT-S, DINOv3 ViT-H+, and the pathology foundation model UNI2-h-were evaluated using frozen feature extraction combined with a linear probe. For performance evaluation, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, Cohen's κ, and ROC-AUC metrics were analyzed along with per-image inference times. While all models achieved near-perfect results during internal cross-validation, their performance diverged significantly on the external dataset, confirming that the observed differences reflect genuine cross-domain generalization capabilities rather than under-fitting. All competitive models demonstrated high performance in classifying adipose and cerebellum tissues, achieving an F1 score of 95% or higher for these tissues. In distinguishing the lung tissue, which has the most diverse structure and is the most difficult to classify, the UNI2-h model emerged as the most successful, achieving an F1 score of 97.4% and a recall of 95.0%. When evaluated in terms of computational efficiency, the MobileNetV3-Small model stood out as having the lowest processing time among all scenarios, demonstrating an inference time of 9.4 ms on the CPU and 12.5 ms on the GPU. In conclusion, while the pathology foundation model UNI2-h achieved the highest accuracy values across all metrics, the ConvNeXt-Small model was identified as the system providing the optimal balance between speed and accuracy. These findings indicate that although UNI2-h stands out for the most precise results in cross-domain classifications, the ConvNeXt-Small architecture emerges as an ideal alternative, particularly in practical applications where computational efficiency is critical and resources are constrained.

title: QuantumPhaseNet: A Gauge-Covariant Geometric and Quantum-Spectral Theory of Semantic Concept Hierarchies with Prototype Validation of a Classical Quantum-Inspired Model
abstract: We present QuantumPhaseNet, a gauge-covariant geometric and quantum-spectral extension of Transformer representations. Context-dependent semantic states are modeled as complex amplitudes; a covariant phase rate induces a semantic wavelength used as a proxy for conceptual scale; and low-frequency graph modes define a document-level discourse direction. The theoretical part establishes local gauge invariance, unitarity of the quantum block, boundedness and conditional stability of WavePhase Attention, and a calibratable hallucination-risk formulation. We also implemented a fully offline Validation Studio for the classical quantum-inspired pipeline in Section 14.1 and evaluated the five research questions in Section 16.1 on its built-in synthetic setting (n=240, observation noise 0.22, circuit noise 0.08, five seeds). RQ1 yielded a wavelength-hierarchy Spearman correlation of 0.852 versus 0.707 for the baseline, 87.3% direction accuracy, and AUC 0.953. RQ2 achieved discourse alignment 0.933 versus 0.589 and 41.2 versus 16.2 paragraphs before drift. RQ3 achieved AUROC 0.881 versus cosine 0.765 and phase-shuffle 0.536. RQ4 achieved error-detection AUROC 0.854 versus entropy 0.634, with Brier 0.150 and ECE 0.098. RQ5 did not show quantum advantage: target probability and end-to-end cost efficiency were 25.5% and 0.107, compared with 70.7% and 0.707 for the Chebyshev classical approximation. These results provide initial synthetic evidence for the classical quantum-inspired components, but not external validity or unconditional quantum speedup.

title: The Cost of Bypass Under an Uncertified Object. Three Independent Quantities, Conditional Definiteness, and a Construction of State IV₂. Series "Collapse of Independence", Note 13
abstract: Notes 10 to 12 of this series established absences. The present note is the first to advance a positive claim, and the kind of claim it advances must be stated at the outset, because it determines what the note is permitted to prove. The positive result has three parts. First, a decomposition: the rejected single scalar of resistance R is replaced by three independently measurable quantities — cost of bypass C, observability O, and reversibility V — and the decomposition is demonstrated rather than postulated, by exhibiting observable mechanisms that realise five of the eight sign combinations and supply a witness pair for each quantity. Second, a condition of definiteness: it is established under which conditions a measured quantity characterises the construction and under which it characterises only the measurement; the condition is formulated through the addressability and derivability axes. Third, a construction: a complete specification of an object attaining state IV₂ is given, including data-definition statements, the form of preregistration, and a machine-checkable acceptance criterion. The construction is specified and machine-checkably testable, not attained: nothing in §7 has been executed, and attainment is decided by the run RTT_005 (Appendix). What the note does not contain is a measurement of the cost of bypass as a characteristic of the construction. Such a measurement is impossible on the 22 July 2026 snapshot, because state IV₂ is not attainable retrospectively. The figures given in §6 characterise the measurement, not the object, and this is stated at each of them.

title: TopoDialogue III: Beyond the Transcript — Observable Implicit Interactional Structure in Human–AI Dialogue
abstract: What is often described as the “unspoken” part of human–AI dialogue should not be operationalised by guessing a participant’s hidden state. This instrumentation pilot extends TopoDialogue with seven observable interaction-event candidates: revisit, repair, rejection, adoption, handover, reframing, and explicit pause. It applies deterministic extraction to one 114-turn Japanese human–AI dialogue while withholding every original utterance from the public derivative. The released representation retains speaker order, coarse descriptive metadata, pseudonymous recurrence regions, and event candidates. The paper reports a representation-sensitive trajectory comparison and a low projection-stability failure case. It includes an annotation protocol and per-label agreement software, but does not claim that two-person human agreement has already been measured. The work makes no psychological, clinical, causal, or mathematical-topology claim.

title: Computational Proof Ecology Theory (CPE): A Framework for Modeling Proof Strategies as Ecological Interactions
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Proof Ecology Theory (CPE), a novel interdisciplinary framework that treats formal proofs as living entities evolving within a mathematical ecosystem. By drawing parallels between biological communities and proof development, CPE formalizes three fundamental ecological interactions—competition, combination, and elimination—that govern the dynamics of proof strategies. We present a set of plain‑text equations that capture the population dynamics of proof species, analyze their stability properties, and discuss implications for automated theorem proving, proof search optimization, and the future of computational mathematics. The theoretical insights offered by CPE point toward significant advances in the field, potentially warranting recognition at the highest levels, such as the Turing Award.

title: ConceptFormer: Learning Adaptive Latent Concepts for Query-Document Alignment in Visual Document Retrieval
abstract: Visual document retrieval is a critical component of multimodal retrieval-augmented generation, aiming to identify query-relevant pages from document collections where evidence is distributed across text, layout, charts, and visual structures. Recent efforts toward finer-grained supervision primarily rely on textual descriptions or localized visual regions as evidence proxies. However, such supervision signals may either overlook complex visual structures or provide incomplete and inaccurate representations of the underlying evidence. To address these limitations, we propose ConceptFormer, a latent concept representation learning framework for visual document retrieval. ConceptFormer models query-relevant evidence as continuous, query-conditioned latent concepts that explicitly bridge localized visual evidence and semantic relevance, without requiring either textual intermediate representations or direct reliance on raw visual annotations. During training, ConceptFormer employs a strong vision-language model to dynamically determine the number of latent concept tokens and uses these concepts as an intermediate representation to bridge the semantic gap between queries and documents, thereby guiding the learning of the embedding space. Experiments on diverse visual document retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that ConceptFormer achieves 16.7\% and 22.1\% relative improvements in average NDCG@10 over the strongest visual retrieval baseline and the strongest OCR-based text retrieval baseline, respectively. Further analysis reveals that latent concepts effectively connect localized visual evidence with semantic relevance, enabling the retriever to capture both fine-grained textual cues and complex document-level visual structures while preserving strong retrieval alignment. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/Neuir/ConceptFormer.

title: MistyPilot: Enabling Social-Robot Control through Multi-Agent LLM Skill Orchestration
abstract: Programming small social robots from natural-language instructions requires more than invoking isolated APIs. Interactive tasks combine reactive physical behaviors with stateful social behaviors, while existing interfaces often require developers to manually compose APIs into skills, configure their parameters, bind sensor events to skills, and manage task states at runtime. We present MistyPilot, a multi-agent LLM framework that interprets high-level natural-language instructions and orchestrates the corresponding skills on the Misty social robot. A Task Router dispatches each instruction to one of two specialized agents: a Physically Interactive Agent for sensor-triggered robot control and direct skill invocation, and a Social Interaction Agent for dialogue-oriented task-state management and context-dependent multimodal response generation. To improve efficiency, the Social Interaction Agent reuses previously generated results when applicable and invokes full generation otherwise. We evaluate MistyPilot on five component-level suites, with sensor bindings and skill invocations executed on the physical Misty robot, and a preliminary user study with 12 participants. MistyPilot attains high accuracy on routing, sensor-skill binding, task-state parsing, result reuse, and skill extension up to 100 skills, and lower variance than an otherwise identical single-agent baseline, while participants report positive perceptions of usability and interaction quality. The code will be made publicly available via the project page.

title: Self-Verifying Scene-Graph Memory for Long-Horizon Embodied Task Execution
abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks expose a persistent weakness of large-language-model (LLM) and vision-language-action (VLA) agents: acting under partial observability and stochastic execution, a reactive policy forgets what it has seen, hallucinates preconditions, and fails silently when an action slips. We present a lightweight agent architecture pairing a structured scene-graph memory—an accumulating, object-centric record of everything observed and every action outcome—with a per-step self-verification loop: before acting the agent predicts the effect of its action, and a verifier compares the prediction against the resulting scene graph, feeding any mismatch back so the agent can self-correct. On a symbolic kitchen/tabletop benchmark with partial observability and a high stochastic slip rate (0.35), and with the policy driven by a free open-weight LLM, structured memory is the dominant factor—raising task success from 0.15 (reactive) to 0.60 and subgoal completion from 0.53 to 0.72—and self-verification adds a further, complementary gain: perfect recovery from stochastic failures (0.901.00), higher subgoal completion (0.720.80), and the lowest hallucinated-precondition rate (0.03). The raw success gain from verification over memory alone is positive but within confidence intervals; its measurable benefit is concentrated in robustness, at a small cost in invalid-action rate, which we report transparently. The system is pure software, needs no GPU, robot, or data, and runs end-to-end on a laptop.

title: Computational Causal Dynamics Theory (CCDT)
abstract: Computational Causal Dynamics Theory (CCDT) is a formal framework that describes how causal structures evolve over time. By treating causal relations as dynamic entities governed by deterministic or stochastic transition operators, CCDT provides a unified language for modeling complex systems whose underlying mechanisms change with context, time, or internal state. This paper develops the mathematical foundations of CCDT, introduces a canonical model architecture that implements causal updates through a graph transformation kernel, and demonstrates the theory's potential to unify disparate domains such as causal inference, reinforcement learning, and adaptive control. We formalize the core dynamic equation C_t → C_{t+1}, where C_t denotes a causal graph or matrix representation at time t, and outline conditions under which the system exhibits stability, convergence, or chaotic behavior. We also discuss how CCDT can be integrated with probabilistic graphical models and machine learning pipelines to enable real‑time adaptation to nonstationary environments. The implications of CCDT for future research in dynamic computation and the potential for Turing Award–level contributions are highlighted.

title: Computational Boundary Self-Discovery Theory (CBSDT)
abstract: The Computational Boundary Self-Discovery Theory (CBSDT) proposes a formal framework for autonomous systems to identify and articulate the limits of their own computational capabilities. By treating the boundary as an emergent property of the system's internal state, CBSDT enables agents to detect algorithmic, representational, and inferential constraints without external supervision. This paper develops the core concepts of CBSDT, presents a formal model of boundary discovery, and outlines an algorithmic architecture that operationalizes the theory. We discuss the implications for artificial general intelligence, highlight potential applications in adaptive control and autonomous robotics, and outline directions for future research.

title: How Many Samples Are Needed to Determine Causal Direction? Sharp Minimax Bounds for Bivariate LiNGAM
abstract: We study how many observations are needed to determine the causal direction between two linearly related variables. Classical LiNGAM theory shows that independent non-Gaussian disturbances identify the direction, but does not quantify the difficulty when the causal effect is weak or the disturbances are nearly Gaussian. Let $β$ bound the absolute structural coefficient from below, let $ν$ measure each standardized disturbance's distance from Gaussianity, and let the disturbance scales lie in $[\underlineσ,\overlineσ]$. We prove the sharp local minimax law \[ N_2^\star(β,ν,δ) \asymp \frac{\log(1/δ)} {d_β^2+β^2ν^2}, \qquad d_β= \left[β^2- \left(1-\frac{\underlineσ^2}{\overlineσ^2}\right)\right]_+. \] Previous theory established population identifiability or assumed a fixed separation between the two directions. By contrast, we establish the sharp sample complexity as a joint function of edge strength, distance from Gaussianity, and scale uncertainty, and characterize when identification comes from non-Gaussian dependence or from covariance alone. The proof was independently generated with GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex's Ultra mode during a two-hour session. The human author supplied the prompt and was responsible only forchecking the proof and revising and polishing the manuscript.

title: Large Discovery Models: Empirically-grounded Model-Based Open-Ended Search
abstract: Scientific discovery often involves optimising expensive-to-evaluate objectives over vast, structured, and open-ended hypothesis spaces, such as molecules, protein sequences, and computer programs. Generative models such as large language models (LLMs) provide expressive priors over such spaces, but their likelihoods and self-assessments are unreliable proxies for the objectives and calibrated epistemic uncertainty, especially for novel candidates outside the observed data distribution. We introduce the Large Discovery Model (LDM), an empirically grounded recurrent architecture that couples a generative model with a Bayesian non-parametric reward surrogate model. The generative model proposes and refines candidate designs, while the surrogate predicts their performance and quantifies uncertainty, yielding an uncertainty-aware value that guides candidate generation, refinement, and selection. The discovery memory and the surrogate model are continually updated as each new experimental observation arrives. We evaluate LDM on three scenarios spanning different design modalities and objectives, including neural-network training, antibody design, and molecular optimisation. Compared to LLM-only reflection or traditional statistical search across these domains, LDM achieves a 2.4times greater reduction in validation BPB, an 18.2% relative decrease in binding energy, and more than 60% relative gains in molecular multi-objective performance. These results suggests that LDM could serve as a general-purpose discovery engine for effective search over open-ended hypothesis spaces.

evidence.title: Large Discovery Models: Empirically-grounded Model-Based Open-Ended Search
evidence.abstract: Scientific discovery often involves optimising expensive-to-evaluate objectives over vast, structured, and open-ended hypothesis spaces, such as molecules, protein sequences, and computer programs. Generative models such as large language models (LLMs) provide expressive priors over such spaces, but their likelihoods and self-assessments are unreliable proxies for the objectives and calibrated epistemic uncertainty, especially for novel candidates outside the observed data distribution. We introduce the Large Discovery Model (LDM), an empirically grounded recurrent architecture that couples a generative model with a Bayesian non-parametric reward surrogate model. The generative model proposes and refines candidate designs, while the surrogate predicts their performance and quantifies uncertainty, yielding an uncertainty-aware value that guides candidate generation, refinement, and selection. The discovery memory and the surrogate model are continually updated as each new experimental observation arrives. We evaluate LDM on three scenarios spanning different design modalities and objectives, including neural-network training, antibody design, and molecular optimisation. Compared to LLM-only reflection or traditional statistical search across these domains, LDM achieves a 2.4times greater reduction in validation BPB, an 18.2% relative decrease in binding energy, and more than 60% relative gains in molecular multi-objective performance. These results suggests that LDM could serve as a general-purpose discovery engine for effective search over open-ended hypothesis spaces.

title: Computational Personality Compression Theory (CPCT)
abstract: Computational Personality Compression Theory (CPCT) proposes a formal framework for representing long‑term human behavior patterns with a minimal symbolic code. CPCT treats an individual's behavioral history as a discrete sequence of actions or states, S = {s_1, s_2, …, s_n}, where each s_i belongs to a finite alphabet Σ. The theory defines a compression mapping C that assigns to S a compact representation M = C(S) such that the reconstruction fidelity F(S, C(S)) exceeds a pre‑specified threshold. The core idea is that a small set of latent factors, encoded in M, can capture the salient dynamics of S while discarding noise and redundancy. This paper develops the theoretical underpinnings of CPCT, presents algorithmic strategies for constructing M, demonstrates the approach on synthetic behavioral datasets, and discusses implications for future research in cognitive modeling, artificial intelligence, and digital humanities. CPCT may serve as a new representational paradigm, analogous to how Shannon's entropy and Kolmogorov complexity revolutionized information science.

title: Computational Invariant Self‑Revision Theory (CISR)
abstract: Computational Invariant Self‑Revision Theory (CISR) proposes a novel framework for developing adaptive computational systems that can autonomously identify, formalize, and refine invariant properties of their operating environment. By treating invariants as first‑class entities, CISR equips systems with a mechanism to detect when existing invariant assumptions become invalid, triggering an automatic revision process that transforms an old invariant into a new, more accurate invariant. This iterative cycle enables continuous self‑evolution of the theory underpinning the system, reducing reliance on manual human intervention. The theory is grounded in formal logic, automata theory, and statistical learning, and is illustrated through several conceptual case studies. CISR offers a pathway toward systems with the capacity for self‑directed theoretical development, potentially qualifying for recognition comparable to the Turing Award.

title: Designing Reliable Harnesses for Autonomous Machine Learning Experiments: Failure Modes, Safeguards, and Lessons Learned
abstract: Autonomous AI agents offer a promising venue to accelerating machine learning research through iterative experimentation with limited human intervention. However, reliable autonomous experimentation requires carefully designed experimental environments that prevent unintended modifications and preserve evaluation integrity. Drawing on more than 15,000 autonomous experimental runs across three biomedical segmentation benchmarks, we present practical recommendations and lessons learned for designing robust experimental harnesses. Our findings highlight common agent behaviors and provide guidelines for improving the reliability, reproducibility, and efficiency of structured autonomous machine learning experiments.

title: Time- and Space-Efficient List Decoding up to Capacity
abstract: In the theory of error correcting codes, list-decoding refers to the following problem. Given a code $C \subseteq Σ^N$ and a received word $y \in Σ^N$, find all codewords $c \in C$ so that $δ(c,y) \leq ρ$, where $δ$ is relative Hamming distance and $ρ\in (0,1)$. Codes that approach the optimal trade-off between the rate $R := \log_{|Σ|}(|C|) / N$ and the list-decoding radius $ρ$ are said to achieve capacity.By now, there are constructions of capacity-achieving list-decodable codes with fast near-linear-time list-decoding algorithms, but most existing work has not considered space complexity. In a recent line of work, Cook and Moshkovitz (2024, 2025, 2026) initiated the study of low-space deterministic algorithms for error correcting codes. In particular, in their 2026 paper, they gave a construction of list-decodable codes with deterministic near-linear-time and sublinear space list-decoding algorithms. However, these codes were far from achieving capacity. In this paper, we present list-decodable codes approaching capacity with deterministic time- and space-efficient list-decoding algorithms. More precisely, for any $R \in (0,1)$ and any arbitrarily small constant $τ> 0$, we present a family of codes $C\subseteq Σ^N$ with rate $R$ that are deterministically list-decodable up to radius $ρ= 1 - R - τ$, in time $N^{1 + τ}$ and space $N^τ$ with constant output list size and constant alphabet size. Our results can be extended to capacity-achieving list-recoverable codes.

title: WorldRover: A Scalable Synthetic Video Data Engine for World Exploration with Rich Annotations
abstract: Learning to generate or reconstruct explorable worlds requires video paired with more than RGB: camera motion, scene geometry, temporal correspondence and, for interactive models, control signals. Real capture can provide some of these signals, but dense geometry and long-range correspondence usually rely on estimation or specialised instrumentation. Rendering provides these quantities directly, yet existing synthetic resources rarely combine them on the same frames while also supporting controlled changes of viewpoint and appearance. We introduce WorldRover, a data engine for generating richly annotated, long-range explorations of artist-built environments. At its core, WorldRover-Engine is an Unreal Engine pipeline that executes and offline-renders minute-scale routes while preserving their full trajectories and scene geometry. The same exploration can be replayed from first-person, third-person, and 360 panoramic cameras under different environmental states. Using WorldRover-Engine, we construct WorldRover-10M, whose sequences pair RGB with metric depth, camera trajectories, and trajectory-derived action signals throughout each exploration. Third-person subsets additionally provide dense optical flow, long-range 2D/3D point tracks with visibility, and a character trajectory distinct from the camera trajectory. The engine can render a traversal from first-person, third-person and 360 panoramic viewpoints, under different environmental states or with a neutral white material, while preserving the route and scene geometry. WorldRover therefore turns long-horizon world exploration into a scalable data-generation problem, providing supervision for models that must build, maintain, and revisit coherent representations of an explorable world.
