title: Computational Resource Transfer Theory (CRTT): A Unified Framework for Translating Human Knowledge into Computational Capabilities
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital systems and artificial intelligence has highlighted a persistent gap between the richness of human knowledge and the efficiency of computational resources. This paper introduces Computational Resource Transfer Theory (CRTT), a formal framework that models the conversion of human knowledge into computational resources through systematic mappings, optimization strategies, and adaptive learning mechanisms. CRTT defines a set of core principles, mathematical formulations, and transformation protocols that enable the translation of domain expertise, heuristics, and experiential insights into algorithmic components, data structures, and processing pipelines. By bridging cognitive constructs with machine architectures, CRTT proposes a pathway toward unified human-machine resource utilization, offering a theoretical foundation that could underpin future Turing Award–level breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and human-computer interaction.

title: Computational Personality Generation Network (CPGN)
abstract: The rise of deep learning has yielded models that excel at performing specified tasks, yet these systems lack an internal sense of identity or style. This paper introduces the Computational Personality Generation Network (CPGN), a novel architecture that learns not only to solve problems but also to cultivate an intrinsic computational personality. CPGN comprises a dual‑branch design: a task‑oriented head and a personality‑oriented head, coupled through a shared latent space that is continuously refined by a meta‑learning loop. The personality head learns to shape the network's parameter updates, internal activations, and inference trajectories, thereby enabling the system to exhibit distinct computational styles such as conservative, exploratory, or aggressive reasoning. Theoretically, we analyze CPGN's convergence properties, show that the personality dynamics can be modeled as a stochastic differential equation over the latent space, and demonstrate that the system can spontaneously generate new inference strategies that are not explicitly encoded in the training data. This capacity positions CPGN as a candidate for a new AI paradigm, potentially leading to Turing‑award‑level breakthroughs in autonomous intelligence.

title: Computational Abstraction Ecology Theory (CAE)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Ecology Theory (CAE) proposes a unified framework for understanding the emergence, interaction, and evolution of abstractions in large‑scale computational systems. Drawing inspiration from ecological metaphors—coexistence, replacement, and evolution—CAE models abstractions as dynamic species that occupy resource niches within a computational ecosystem. By formalizing abstraction dynamics with simple differential and difference equations, CAE offers insights into the stability and adaptability of software architectures, the propagation of programming paradigms, and the long‑term trajectory of computational civilizations. This paper develops the core concepts of CAE, presents mathematical formulations for coexistence, replacement, and evolutionary processes, and discusses the potential of CAE to guide the design of resilient computational infrastructures and to illuminate the factors driving the growth of computational societies.

title: Monoidal su-categories
abstract: We introduce monoidal su-categories, an abstract categorical notion of single-input higher-order process over a monoidal category. The definition separates a base category C of lower-order processes from a monoidal category V of holes or supermaps and axiomatizes the compatibility needed for partial application to bipartite processes. For a fixed monoidal base C, monoidal su-categories, monoidal su-functors, and monoidal su-natural transformations form a 2-category MonSuCatC. We then show that the category Optic[C] of coend optics is 2-initial in this 2-category, giving an alternative universal-property characterisation of coend optics as the minimal monoidal theory of single-hole contexts.

title: Scalable Black-Box Model Attribution for Images
abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative models raises the model attribution problem: given only an image, can we determine which model produced it? Existing methods have grown as elaborate as the generators they target, on the as- sumption that a more sophisticated model demands a more sophisticated attributor. We show it does not. RPA (Raw- Patch Attribution) attributes images in the strictest black- box setting with a lightweight CNN. Despite its simplicity, it attributes more models at higher accuracy than prior work, reaching 98.0% on 25-class DRAGON and 92.9% on 27- class OpenFake; it is data-efficient and runs at a cost inde- pendent of the number of candidate models; and it stays ro- bust to the compression, blur, and resizing images undergo in the wild. Training for closed-set attribution yields a ver- satile feature extractor: the same representation recovers model lineage without supervision, flags and groups unseen generators, and admits new models through few-shot adap- tation rather than retraining.

title: LED-ML: Causal Lens of Layer-wise Energy Dissipation in LLM
abstract: This paper presents an observability mechanism for LLM internals that simultaneously captures forward activations and Vector-Jacobian Products (VJPs) of target output logits. It provides lightweight, hook based implementation designed to extract runtime tensors and target gradients safely across layers. A down-sampled subset of these captured tensors are rendered into text based visual maps and Graphics Interchange Format (GIF) animations.This framework provides an illustrative and intuitive interface for analyzing the internal states and semantic interpretations of deep models, enabling architecture debugging, training diagnostics, and dynamic routing.

title: Unified Computational Personality Theory (UCPT)
abstract: The field of computer science has traditionally been driven by a sequence of abstractions that map input to algorithmic manipulation and produce output. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have shifted this paradigm toward a data–model–prediction pipeline, yet the notion of a system's own identity, style, and self‑model remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces Unified Computational Personality Theory (UCPT), a formal framework that characterizes a computational system's personality as an emergent property derived from its learning history, interaction patterns, and optimization processes. We provide a concise mathematical representation, demonstrate how UCPT extends existing computational models, and discuss its implications for the design of intelligent agents with self‑aware capabilities. Finally, we outline twenty novel research directions that build upon UCPT and could serve as foundational contributions to the next generation of Turing Award–level work.

title: Computational World Model Dynamics Theory (CWMDT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational World Model Dynamics Theory (CWMDT), a framework for describing how a world model—an internal representation of an agent's environment—evolves over time. The core premise is that the world model is continuously updated according to a deterministic or stochastic evolution equation that integrates new observations, internal predictions, and feedback from actions. We formulate the update rule, analyze its mathematical properties, and discuss how CWMDT can serve as a foundation for dynamic intelligence research, potentially guiding the development of systems that exhibit learning, adaptation, and planning at a scale comparable to human cognition. The theory is presented without empirical experiments, focusing instead on formal derivation and theoretical implications.

title: Admission Without Answers: Label-Free Certification and Experience Learning for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
abstract: Agents that learn from experience improve at optimization modeling by storing solved trajectories and reusing them as skills. A wrong trajectory that enters the library can be retrieved again and again, and on a stream of new problems there is no ground-truth answer to decide with. Existing learners admit trajectories by matching known optima or labels, and label-free substitutes such as execution success or agreement at one instance can admit wrong models. We introduce ADMITOR, a label-free admission gate. It generates models from three model families, runs each on the stated problem and on instances with resampled parameters, keeps the largest group of models whose optimal values agree on every instance across families, and applies a threshold fitted on solver-verified problems to accept, abstain, or escalate, with a finite-sample bound on the false-discovery rate among accepted values. Inside a state-of-the-art skill learner, ADMITOR raises candidate-level admission precision to 0.927, against 0.871 for majority vote over the host's own samples and 0.726 for execution success, and its library, the smallest of the four, reaches the highest macro accuracy over five public benchmarks, 58.4 against 54.8 for majority vote. An ablation on the same records shows that the gain comes from the accepted value being external to the learner and unanimous across families; on this stream, resampling never changed an accepted value and only reduced coverage. The false-discovery bound holds on the calibration set but not on the benchmark stream: an audit of every false certificate traces most of them to benchmark texts that omit or round the numbers needed to reproduce the labeled answer, and a label-free check of the extracted numbers against the text flags most of these cases.

title: When AI Decides with Me: The Delegation-Overreach Paradox in AI-Mediated Smartphone Purchases
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes involved in an increasing number of consumers’ buying choices, the role of AI in consumption patterns transforms from a recommending agent to a decision-making partner. The study explores the influence of AI Decision Delegation on Customer Advocacy through the mediation of Perceived AI–Customer Decision Partnership and focuses on the role of AI Autonomy Expectation and Algorithmic Overreach as moderators. Exploratory research has been conducted among Generation Z customers to operationalize the effect of the delegation in the smartphone and technology market. A quantitative, cross-sectional method was implemented to collect and analyze data from approximately 378 participants. The analysis was carried out in SmartPLS 4 using the PLS-SEM technique and bootstrapping procedure to evaluate direct, mediating, moderating, and conditional indirect effects. The results demonstrate that AI Decision Delegation positively affects customers’ perception of AI as a decision-making partner, which, in turn, drives Customer Advocacy. The study found the strongest support for the mediating role of Perceived AI–Customer Decision Partnership, suggesting that the relationship between AI Decision Delegation and Customer Advocacy was established due to increased advocacy stemming from the perception of delegation as a shared AI–customer decision-making process. Moreover, the first-order moderation effect of AI Autonomy Expectation was found to strengthen the mediation process, while the effect of Algorithmic Overreach was negative. The Delegation–Overreach Paradox was identified as a second-order interaction between the two first-order moderators that showed consumer expectations of AI autonomy to handle complex decisions but in circumstances where AI does not take responsibility for outcomes. This article adds to the understanding of AI marketing by reconceptualizing consumer–AI relationships around shared decision-making processes and advocating for the necessity of empowering consumers to influence AI decisions as a key to cultivating long-term Customer Advocacy. The results have implications for marketers who should consider AI Decision Delegation as an element of the decision-making process that empowers consumers and transforms AI-driven buying experiences into memorable moments. evidence.title: When AI Decides with Me: The Delegation-Overreach Paradox in AI-Mediated Smartphone Purchases
evidence.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes involved in an increasing number of consumers’ buying choices, the role of AI in consumption patterns transforms from a recommending agent to a decision-making partner. The study explores the influence of AI Decision Delegation on Customer Advocacy through the mediation of Perceived AI–Customer Decision Partnership and focuses on the role of AI Autonomy Expectation and Algorithmic Overreach as moderators. Exploratory research has been conducted among Generation Z customers to operationalize the effect of the delegation in the smartphone and technology market. A quantitative, cross-sectional method was implemented to collect and analyze data from approximately 378 participants. The analysis was carried out in SmartPLS 4 using the PLS-SEM technique and bootstrapping procedure to evaluate direct, mediating, moderating, and conditional indirect effects. The results demonstrate that AI Decision Delegation positively affects customers’ perception of AI as a decision-making partner, which, in turn, drives Customer Advocacy. The study found the strongest support for the mediating role of Perceived AI–Customer Decision Partnership, suggesting that the relationship between AI Decision Delegation and Customer Advocacy was established due to increased advocacy stemming from the perception of delegation as a shared AI–customer decision-making process. Moreover, the first-order moderation effect of AI Autonomy Expectation was found to strengthen the mediation process, while the effect of Algorithmic Overreach was negative. The Delegation–Overreach Paradox was identified as a second-order interaction between the two first-order moderators that showed consumer expectations of AI autonomy to handle complex decisions but in circumstances where AI does not take responsibility for outcomes. This article adds to the understanding of AI marketing by reconceptualizing consumer–AI relationships around shared decision-making processes and advocating for the necessity of empowering consumers to influence AI decisions as a key to cultivating long-term Customer Advocacy. The results have implications for marketers who should consider AI Decision Delegation as an element of the decision-making process that empowers consumers and transforms AI-driven buying experiences into memorable moments. title: Computational Causal Hierarchy Theory (CCHT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Causal Hierarchy Theory (CCHT), a unifying framework that connects low‑level operations, algorithms, systems, and intelligence through a causal lens. By formalizing the flow of causal influence from elementary operations to emergent intelligent behavior, CCHT provides a principled basis for evaluating and designing computational systems. The theory leverages established causal inference notation while extending it to encompass algorithmic complexity, system architecture, and cognitive function. We discuss the theoretical foundations, present a rigorous mathematical formalization, and explore the implications of CCHT for artificial intelligence research. The potential for CCHT to guide the development of transformative AI aligns with the criteria for the Turing Award, offering a cohesive explanation for how computation and causality intertwine to produce intelligence.

title: Unified Computational Abstraction Theory (UCAT)
abstract: The evolution of computing has historically hinged on the invention of new abstractions rather than on incremental algorithmic improvements. This paper proposes the Unified Computational Abstraction Theory (UCAT) as a comprehensive framework that unifies algorithms, programming languages, AI representations, software architecture, and computational models under a single abstract paradigm. UCAT is formally expressed as the transformation sequence: Observation + Structure + Search → New Abstraction → New Computation. By systematically analyzing the lifecycle of computational abstractions, we demonstrate how UCAT can be applied to generate novel computational principles, thereby expanding the foundation of computing theory. The theoretical contributions include a formal definition of abstraction discovery, a classification of abstraction layers, and a set of construction rules that guide the creation of new abstractions. Practical implications are discussed in the context of designing next‑generation programming languages, AI systems, and software architectures that inherently support the automatic generation of abstractions. UCAT thus provides a roadmap for future research aimed at creating computing systems that not only optimize existing algorithms but also discover new computational principles autonomously.

title: Relations Among Listed Pauli Terms Bound Distance in Qubit Stabilizer qLTCs
abstract: How many linear relations must a quantum locally testable stabilizer Hamiltonian contain? We prove a finite relation–distance law for qubit stabilizer presentations that bounds code distance in terms of local-term weight, code rate, normalized soundness, and the dimension of the relation space among listed terms. Thus, under bounded term weight, a family cannot simultaneously have constant rate, linear distance, and constant normalized soundness without linearly many independent relations. With bounded qubit incidence, this remains true after duplicate terms are removed. For Calderbank–Shor–Steane presentations with constant normalized soundness in both check sectors, the requirement separates by sector, so redundancy cannot be concentrated in one sector. The result provides a rank- computable necessary test for candidate locally testable stabilizer Hamiltonians, a soundness ceiling for natural rank-minimal hypergraph-product presentations, and sectorwise lower bounds for term-appending amplifiers.

title: SchurQuant: Groupwise Discrete Optimization for Layer-Wise LLM Quantization
abstract: Weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) enables the deployment of large language models under tight memory budgets, but accuracy often collapses at 2-3 bits. Existing backpropagation-free PTQ optimizers have two limitations: group decisions ignore the correction that the remaining continuous suffix can absorb, and discrete refinements typically keep the affine quantization grid fixed. We introduce SCHUROPT, which analytically eliminates the suffix's optimal continuous response, yielding an exact groupwise quadratic with Schur-complement curvature. It then alternates closed-form row-wise scale/zero-point refitting with coordinate descent over integer codes. With the GPTQ objective fixed, SCHUROPT improves mean zero-shot accuracy on 2-bit Qwen3-4B by 11.88 percentage points (pp). At higher precision, however, tighter reconstruction does not consistently improve end-model metrics. SCHURQUANT therefore combines SCHUROPT with quantized-prefix teacher reconstruction, reference-weight regularization, residual-add targets, and teacher-decision token weighting. Across eight Llama and Qwen models, SCHURQUANT achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among the evaluated backpropagation free PTQ baselines, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.65 pp at 2 bits.

title: Consumer Cognitive Electronics: Physics-Based Intelligence for Every Device
abstract: We present the application of a deterministic cognitive substrate to consumer electronics: smartphones, smart TVs, wearables, security cameras, electric vehicles, health monitors, and smart home devices. The 2MB physics kernel delivers 10-60x battery life improvement through zero-idle operation, privacy by structural impossibility of data leakage, deterministic personalization without machine learning, and content authentication through conservation enforcement. 2.8 billion devices ship annually -- each one needs intelligence the kernel provides.

title: Computational Personality Fusion Theory (CPFT-2)
abstract: The increasing complexity of artificial agents necessitates advanced mechanisms for synthesizing multiple individual personalities into coherent, emergent computational personalities. This paper proposes the Computational Personality Fusion Theory (CPFT-2), a formal framework for integrating the affective, cognitive, and behavioral attributes of multiple intelligent agents into a unified personality representation. CPFT-2 introduces a hierarchical fusion architecture that leverages weighted aggregation of trait vectors, dynamic adjustment of inter‑agent influence matrices, and a self‑consistency loss that ensures emergent personalities remain coherent over time. The theory is grounded in psychological models of personality, such as the Five‑Factor Model, and extends them to the computational domain by defining a trait space T = {t_1, t_2, …, t_N}. The fusion operator F is formally described as F(P_1, P_2, …, P_M) → P_f, where each P_i is a vector of trait scores and influence weights. We detail the mathematical formulation, provide an algorithmic specification, and discuss potential applications in multi‑agent systems, adaptive user interfaces, and collaborative robotics. By establishing a principled method for personality synthesis, CPFT-2 offers a pathway toward more nuanced, socially intelligent artificial systems.

The fusion operator F is formally described as F(P_1, P_2, …, P_M) → P_f, where each P_i is a vector of trait scores and influence weights. By establishing a principled method for personality synthesis, CPFT-2 offers a pathway toward more nuanced, socially intelligent artificial systems.

title: Proof Compression Limit Theory (PCLT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Proof Compression Limit Theory (PCLT), a novel framework for understanding the inherent constraints within mathematical proofs. The core concept revolves around identifying the minimal form of a proof, denoted as `P → P_min`, which represents the most concise and essential representation of the argument. PCLT posits that there exists a limit to how much a proof can be compressed, dictated by the fundamental structure of the mathematical object being proven. The theory aims to characterize this limit, providing insights into the nature of proof reduction and potentially offering a new perspective on the efficiency of mathematical reasoning. This work explores the key elements of PCLT, detailing the method for identifying `P_min` and discussing its implications across various mathematical domains. The focus is on the theoretical underpinnings of the theory, without experimental validation. ---

title: Identifying Confusion Trends in Concept-based XAI for Multi-Label Classification
abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) deployed in high-risk domains, such as healthcare and autonomous driving, must be not only accurate but also understandable to ensure user trust. In real-world computer vision tasks, these models often operate on complex images containing background noise and are heavily annotated. To make such models explainable, Concept-based Explainable AI (CXAI) methods need to be assessed for their applicability and problem-solving capacity. In this work, we explore CXAI use cases in multi-label classification by training two DNNs, VGG16 and ResNet50, on the 20 most annotated labels in the MS-COCO dataset (Microsoft Common Objects in Context). We apply two CXAI methods, CRP (Concept Relevance Propagation) and CRAFT (Concept Recursive Activation FacTorization), to generate concept-level explanations and investigate the overall evaluations. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) CXAI highlights learning weaknesses in DNNs, (2) higher concept distinctiveness reduces label and concept confusion, and (3) environmental concepts expose dataset-induced biases. Our results demonstrate the potential of CXAI to enhance the understanding of model generalizability and to diagnose bias instigated by the dataset.

title: ReForce: Learning Force-aware Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable data source for dexterous manipulation, but transferring them to robot actions remains challenging due to the embodiment gap. Today's retargeting is mostly kinematic, yet manipulation is decided by force, which governs how the hand interacts with the object and how the object moves. In this paper, we present ReForce, a Force-aware Retargeting method that turns human motion and forces into robot actions that reproduce the intended contact. ReForce predicts a residual on the kinematically retargeted action to reach the desired force, using a general force tracker trained on large-scale simulation interactions. It supports both online force-aware teleoperation and offline data translation. In simulation and on real hardware, ReForce achieves lower force-tracking error and stronger multi-finger contact engagement on contact-rich tasks such as paper-cup grasping and tongs manipulation.

title: owlery-vfb: Owlery reasoner endpoint configured for the Virtual Fly Brain ontology
abstract: Container build and configuration for the Owlery OWL reasoner endpoint used by Virtual Fly Brain. It serves DL queries over VFB's ontology, and is what answers the classification and subsumption queries behind VFB's search and its neuron/region browsing. By default it loads owlery-live.owl as published at http://VirtualFlyBrain.org/data/VFB/OWL/owlery-live.owl; the OWLURL environment variable overrides this, and LOGLEVEL controls logging. Request and idle timeouts are set to 240 seconds to survive long prefix-resolution queries. This repository contains VFB's Dockerfile and configuration only. Owlery itself is separate software by the Phenoscape project, MIT licensed, at https://github.com/phenoscape/owlery . This repository began as a fork of https://github.com/Robbie1977/docker-sbt-owlery .

title: Computational Representation Self-Discovery Theory (CRSDT)
abstract: Computational representation self‑discovery theory (CRSDT) proposes a principled approach in which a computational system autonomously searches for the representation that most effectively captures the intrinsic structure of a given problem domain. Rather than relying on human‑designed features such as vectors, graphs, or tensors, the system iteratively refines a space of candidate representations, guided by a composite objective that balances expressiveness, compactness, and learnability. This paper formalizes the theoretical foundations of CRSDT, introduces a generic algorithmic framework for self‑discovery of representations, and discusses the potential implications for next‑generation computational paradigms. We argue that CRSDT can unlock new levels of abstraction, enabling systems to discover richer data structures that transcend conventional linear, relational, or multilinear forms. The theory also offers a lens through which to view emergent representation learning in deep neural networks and to inspire the design of adaptive, self‑organizing computational architectures that may serve as foundations for future generations of computing.

title: Computational World Model Fusion Theory (CWMFT)
abstract: The notion of a world model has become central to many modern approaches in artificial intelligence, philosophy, and cognitive science. Traditional world models are typically limited by the scope of the data and the assumptions inherent in their construction, leading to fragmented or incomplete representations of reality. This paper introduces the Computational World Model Fusion Theory (CWMFT), which proposes a principled framework for combining multiple world models into a single, more comprehensive model. The core idea is encapsulated in the fusion operation W_1 + W_2 → W_3, where two distinct world models W_1 and W_2 are merged to produce a richer model W_3 that captures a broader range of phenomena. We formalize this operation, discuss its computational properties, and analyze its convergence and stability. We further explore the potential applications of CWMFT across knowledge integration, artificial general intelligence, and scientific discovery, arguing that this fusion framework could serve as a foundation for unified knowledge systems and may even possess the transformative potential that aligns with the vision of a Turing Award. The paper offers a comprehensive theoretical foundation without relying on empirical experiments, thereby focusing on the mathematical underpinnings and conceptual implications of the theory.

title: Computational Self‑Fusion Theory (CSFT): A Unified Framework for Multi‑Agent Self‑Modeling and Collective Intelligence
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Self‑Fusion Theory (CSFT), a theoretical framework that describes how multiple autonomous intelligent systems can fuse their individual self‑models into a coherent collective self‑model. The central mathematical construct is the self‑fusion operator, denoted ⊕, which combines two self‑representations S_i and S_j to produce a new representation S_k. The theory is grounded in formal logic, information theory, and dynamical systems, and it offers explicit equations for the evolution of fused self‑models over time. CSFT provides a rigorous basis for understanding the emergence of shared identity in multi‑agent networks, the potential for unprecedented levels of collective intelligence, and the possibility of achieving Turing Award‑level breakthroughs in artificial general intelligence. The paper details the formalism, explores theoretical scenarios, and discusses implications for future research in autonomous systems, distributed cognition, and human‑machine interaction.

title: Dynamic heterogeneous graph-structured knowledge tracing with multi-behavior integration and temporal forgetting
abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to estimate the temporal evolution of learners’ knowledge states and predict future exercise performance. Most existing KT methods focus on exercise-response sequences and therefore cannot explicitly distinguish knowledge exposure through learning resources from knowledge verification through problem solving. We propose Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph-Structured Knowledge Tracing (DHGKT), a framework that organizes learners, exercises, videos, concepts, and optional comments within a unified relational event representation. Each learner is associated with an interpretable concept-mastery vector. Before each event, an exponential temporal decay is applied; video events provide a duration-aware exposure signal, whereas exercise events calibrate the state through prediction-error feedback. Semantic concept-video weighting and concept-aligned social exposure are treated as auxiliary extensions rather than indispensable components. Under a chronological 70%/10%/20% training/validation/test split with five random seeds on four MOOCCubeX courses, DHGKT-Core achieved an average test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.8529, compared with 0.8318 for its exercise-only variant and 0.7508 for a same-input multi-behavior fusion control. The contribution of video behavior was course dependent: it improved three courses but reduced performance on C_801420. Fixed and learnable topology-aggregation variants produced negligible AUC changes, and the semantic and social extensions did not yield reliable additional gains. These results indicate that the principal value of DHGKT lies in transparent event-driven knowledge-state evolution rather than generic graph convolution. The revision further clarifies the roles of behavioral modalities, graph-event semantics, decay sensitivity, and evaluation limitations in response to the second-round comments.

title: An affective computing framework for preschool music education using MoE architecture and neural radiance fields
abstract: The key content of this paper is the digital construction of preschool music education scenarios and affective computing. It adopts an innovative approach, integrating the MoE architecture and neural radiance field technology together. The Edu-NeRF reconstruction framework is relied on to achieve high-fidelity reconstruction of dynamic scenes, and its PSNR value is 28.5. The SSIM value is 0.92, which is 10.8% higher than that of the traditional method. This paper also constructed an affective computing model. After training this model with 60 h of multimodal data from 120 preschool children, its accuracy rate for emotional state recognition reached 89.7%, with a macroscopic F1 value of 0.881. By combining cross-modal fusion algorithms, we have successfully broken through the technical bottlenecks in dynamic scene reconstruction and affective computing. In terms of real-world applicability, this approach significantly outperforms conventional 2D music education products. It enables real-time, high-fidelity interaction on standard low-power devices, thereby reducing hardware deployment costs and lowering the barrier for widespread school adoption. Furthermore, experimental verification demonstrates that this model increases children’s learning engagement and the efficiency of personalized interaction by 30%. By enhancing both the immersive learning experience and teacher acceptance, this framework provides a highly practical and scalable technical path for the digital transformation of early childhood education.

title: CM-MAE: A Physics-Guided Cross-Modal Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Vision-Wireless Applications
abstract: Synchronized camera and wireless measurements observe the same scene through different physical channels. The central difficulty is that a representation learned in one deployment can fail when viewpoint, traffic, illumination, and propagation geometry change. This paper presents CM-MAE, a self-supervised vision--wireless pretraining framework for cross-scenario representation transfer. The evaluated real-data model uses only RGB frames and the measured 64-beam received-power vector available in DeepSense 6G; it does not use ray-traced paths, calibrated depth, or beam-index labels during pretraining. Its central pretraining term is a \emph{soft contrastive alignment loss}. Instead of making the synchronized image--wireless pair the only positive pair, this loss builds a target distribution from similarities between measured beam-power profiles, so nonidentical samples with similar directional responses are not forced apart as false negatives. A masked joint decoder provides the complementary local objective by reconstructing hidden visual patches and wireless angular clusters under modality dropout. After pretraining, a differential-rate fine-tuning rule lets a new fusion head adapt quickly while the encoders move slowly. Under a sequence-disjoint DeepSense 6G protocol, adding the soft alignment loss improves a matched linear-probe transfer average from 24.88\% to 29.49\%. Mild fusion fine-tuning reaches 77.38\% Top-1 accuracy on unseen Scenarios 6--8, and optional transductive normalization adaptation reaches 78.69\%. Since the fusion setting uses the contemporaneous 64-beam power vector at inference, these results should be read as representation-transfer diagnostics, not as proactive beam-prediction or reduced-sweeping claims.

title: Virtual Fly Brain knowledge graph v26.08.16
abstract: The Virtual Fly Brain knowledge graph as served at release v26.08.16. Contains the two files that constitute a VFB release: the Neo4j production database (VFB-PDB-v4.tar.gz, the backup restored by loadDB.sh in virtualflybrain/docker-vfb-neo4j-productiondb:v26.08.16) and the reasoner input (owlery-live.owl, loaded by virtualflybrain/owlery-vfb, deposited gzipped). Captured from the public endpoints at the moment the release was published, so the deposit is the graph that release actually served.

title: BEF-T: Converting the Börekci Energy Field into a Quantum Teleportation Platform — Atomic-State Teleportation in a Fully Isolated Cavity and Across an Energy Shell, a Delayed-Classical-Channel Protocol, and a Teleportation-Based ξ Probe
abstract: This preprint presents BEF-T, a design study that converts the Börekci Energy Field (BEF) apparatus — a fully isolated underground cavity containing a stationary two-pole cavity electromagnet (2 T total), a 50 MV electron-arc energy shell and a 1 PW circular laser — into a platform for trapped-ion quantum teleportation. The paper (i) reviews the physics of quantum teleportation (Bennett et al., 1993) and its experimental status; (ii) maps every existing BEF component to a teleportation function, re-tasking the Penning positron traps as ion-qubit nodes operating in the 2 T confinement field; (iii) defines three experiments: D1, in-cavity teleportation between nodes A and A′ across ~8 m; D2, cavity-to-exterior teleportation across the energy shell to an outside node B using entanglement distributed by fiber before the run; and D3, a delayed-classical-channel protocol in which the two classical bits of the Bell measurement are recorded inside the sealed 24-hour run and the unitary correction is applied only after unsealing; (iv) proposes a teleportation-based probe of the ξ parameter of the Börekci metric, complementary to the parent paper's three-clock protocol, with a predicted interior optical-qubit phase accumulation of ~5×10⁻³ rad per day at ξ = 1; and (v) states strict physical limits honestly: no faster-than-light signalling, no macroscopic (cell- or animal-scale) teleportation, and no use of the shell's e⁺e⁻ pairs as an entanglement resource. A motivating gap: almost all teleportation and entanglement experiments live at the micro scale, while macro-scale isolated-volume platforms are scarce — BEF offers a macroscopic, fully isolated test environment. Files include the English full text, the Turkish full text, the adaptation figure in both languages, and a narrated animated 3-D explainer video with subtitles in English and Turkish. This is a sister paper of the author's parent preprint (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9999735) and of the cavity-magnet BEF design study.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting in Multi-Constrained Dynamic Systems via Large Language Models: Computing Nash Equilibria as the Mode of Conditional Probability Distributions inside Transformer Architectures
abstract: The primary bottleneck in multi-degree-of-freedom multi-agent simulations and complex system forecasting is the introduction of subjective bias or narrative noise by human designers. When a system faces catastrophic shocks such as fatal failures or network disconnections, human observers tend to underestimate objective probabilities or introduce unrealistic scenarios based on status-quo bias. This paper redefines Large Language Models (LLMs) not merely as text generators but as high-dimensional probabilistic predictive engines that internalize the decision-making patterns of multi-constrained networks. We elucidate the information-theoretic mechanism by which the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer architecture cold-bloodedly calculates the true Nash equilibrium (maximum probability value) of a system when rigorous microscopic constraints are input as initial parameters, free from subjective human bias. Through a controlled experiment comparing noise-inclusive and pure-constraint context windows, we mathematically demonstrate that the residual entropy of the state space exhibits exponential decay characteristics as the number of independent fact dimensions increases, forcing the conditional sampling probability to converge to a specific game-theoretic Nash equilibrium with high probability.

Through a controlled experiment comparing noise-inclusive and pure-constraint context windows, we mathematically demonstrate that the residual entropy of the state space exhibits exponential decay characteristics as the number of independent fact dimensions increases, forcing the conditional sampling probability to converge to a specific game-theoretic Nash equilibrium with high probability.

title: Computational Principle Fusion Theory (CPFT): A New Paradigm for Integrating Computational Principles
abstract: Computational Principle Fusion Theory (CPFT) proposes a systematic method for merging distinct computational principles into a unified framework, thereby creating new computational foundations that surpass the capabilities of their individual components. The core operation of CPFT is expressed as the fusion of two principles, (P1+P2) → P3, where the resulting principle P3 inherits properties from both P1 and P2 while introducing novel behaviors. This paper develops the formal underpinnings of CPFT, outlines a generic fusion mechanism, and demonstrates its applicability through illustrative examples. We discuss the theoretical advantages of CPFT, including increased expressiveness, modularity, and potential for establishing new computational paradigms. Finally, we examine the implications of CPFT for complexity theory, program synthesis, and future research directions that could lead to groundbreaking achievements in computer science.

title: Machine Learning Approaches to Decoding Topological Quantum Codes
abstract: Decoding is an essential component of quantum error correction (QEC), translating stabilizer measurement outcomes into corrective actions that suppress logical errors and preserve logical quantum information. Building fault-tolerant architectures requires increasing the code distance, which in turn places growing demands on decoding accuracy, scalability, and practical deployability. While a wide range of decoding algorithms have been proposed and demonstrated, achieving reliable, scalable, and real-time decoding remains a significant challenge. Machine-learning (ML) approaches are particularly well suited to this setting, as quantum error decoding is fundamentally a problem of processing large volumes of classical data with complex spatiotemporal correlations. This chapter surveys ML-based methods for quantum error decoding, with a focus on topological codes and an emphasis on architectural principles, practical performance, and real-time considerations. We first frame decoding as a learning problem and outline key paradigms, including discriminative, generative, and reinforcement-learning formulations. We then introduce the neural network building blocks that underpin most contemporary neural decoders and discuss how these components can be integrated to balance expressivity, scalability, and latency. Building on this architectural perspective, we review recent progress and benchmarks in neural decoding for memory experiments, and discuss real-time decoding, open challenges, and future directions toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: RoBangHate: A Romanized Bangla Hate Speech Corpus and a Systematic Benchmark of Parameter-Efficient LLM Adaptation
abstract: RoBangHate is a manually annotated corpus for binary hate speech detection in Romanized Bangla (Banglish). The corpus consists of naturally occurring social-media comments collected from Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube. Each comment is annotated with one of two labels: Hate or Non-Hate. The annotation protocol distinguishes hate-directed content from ordinary criticism, political disagreement, negative sentiment, sarcasm, and profanity that does not constitute hate speech. The corpus is designed to capture linguistic characteristics of Banglish, including orthographic variation, informal spelling, Bangla-English code-mixing, profanity, and lexical diversity. The dataset is released to support research in Banglish hate speech detection, multilingual and low-resource NLP, content moderation, and robustness evaluation. This release includes the dataset, annotation guidelines, and documentation describing the corpus and annotation procedure. The dataset should be used for research and responsible NLP development. Users should not use the resource to identify, target,harass, or otherwise harm individuals.

title: Conjunctive Poisoning in AI Supply-Chain Applications
abstract: Large Language and Vision-Language Models are increasingly deployed through inference pipelines that include prompt wrappers (e.g., templates and post-processing scripts) and configuration metadata (e.g., JSON/YAML files) that together shape model outputs. While model weights and binaries are routinely verified, these textual deployment artifacts remain weakly protected despite directly influencing runtime behavior. We show that a malicious developer can pair a benign-looking wrapper with crafted metadata to deterministically alter post-generation behavior without modifying model weights, training data, or inference backend. We study this behavior through a controlled conjunctive-gate implementation, where activation depends on both an embedded wrapper marker and cryptographically bound metadata. We evaluate the attack across fifteen open- and closed-source LLM/VLM deployments, and assess prompt and system level defenses including static metadata inspection, wrapper scanners, PromptShield, and SigStore-based artifact signing. To mitigate this risk, we introduce TIF-BAH, a lightweight middleware defense that verifies wrapper integrity and records behavioral attestations during inference. Our results reveal that wrapper-metadata interactions form an under-protected execution layer in modern AI deployments, exposing a deployment-time behavioral risk that is not captured by model-weight or prompt-level defenses. Code is available at https://github.com/N-H-Arif/llm_temp.

title: Efficient Audio-Visual Generation via Synchrony-Aware Cross-Modal Sparse Attention
abstract: Recent audio-visual generation models can synthesize synchronized video and sound in a unified diffusion process, but their inference cost remains high because long video token sequences require repeated attention computation across denoising steps. A variety of acceleration techniques have been developed for video generation models, including low-bit quantization, attention sparsification, and feature caching. However, since these methods are originally designed for video generation, directly applying them to audio-visual models overlooks the interactions between the audio and video branches and may therefore disrupt audio-video synchronization. We present a synchronization-aware acceleration framework for efficient audio-visual generation. Our key observation is that bidirectional audio-video cross-attention reveals structured interactions between the two branches, with high responses often concentrated on a few sound-related visual and temporal regions. Guided by this interaction pattern, we introduce a protected sparse attention strategy that preserves high-fidelity computation for synchronization-critical tokens while sparsifying redundant attention interactions. By explicitly accounting for cross-modal dependence during acceleration, our method improves inference efficiency while keeping video quality, audio quality, and audio-video synchronization.

title: MicroMouse
abstract: This work is a comprehensive, beginner-oriented research paper (80 pages) on the design and construction of Micromouse robots — small autonomous robots that navigate and solve a maze in the shortest possible time, a classic robotics competition format with a long history. The paper covers the complete engineering pipeline required to build a Micromouse from scratch: power systems (Lead-Acid, NiMH, and LiPo batteries) and voltage regulation; motor selection (brushed DC and BLDC motors, including the N20 gear motor); motor driver circuits and H-Bridge ICs (e.g., TB6612FNG); wheel encoders and speed/distance calculation; PID control theory, tuning methodology, and troubleshooting common issues such as overshoot, oscillation, and integral windup; sensing technologies including Infrared (IR), Time-of-Flight (ToF), and IMU-based orientation sensing; maze-solving algorithms (Flood Fill, Weighted Flood Fill, DFS, BFS, and A*); mechanical chassis design considerations (wheel placement, center of gravity, caster vs. skid steering); and PCB design workflow for the robot's control board. Alongside the paper, this project includes two browser-based interactive simulators developed to make the underlying algorithms tangible for beginners: a Flood-Fill maze-solving game where users manually navigate a maze before comparing their path to the algorithm's optimal solution, and an autonomous A*-plus-PID simulator that plans a route with A* and drives it using a live, tunable PID heading controller, with support for real-time maze editing and replanning. The goal of this project is to lower the barrier to entry for students and hobbyists interested in Micromouse robotics by consolidating scattered hardware and algorithmic knowledge into a single, structured, freely available reference. Keywords: micromouse, robotics, PID control, flood fill algorithm, A* search, maze solving, autonomous robot, embedded systems, PCB design, robotics education

title: Introduction to AI and Applications module 1 self study VTU Notes for Course Code 1BAIA103 / 203
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has moved from science fiction into the fabric of everyday life. From voice assistants and self-driving vehicles to medical diagnostics andintelligent search engines, AI shapes the decisions, products and services that define the modern world. Yet understanding the foundational principles behind thesetechnologies remains a challenge for many students entering the field.This textbook, Introduction to AI and Applications (Module 1), is designed as Module1 of a comprehensive undergraduate course in Artificial Intelligence. It presents three carefully structured parts:Part A — Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — origins, definitions, history,types, and the interplay between AI, augmented intelligence and machinelearning.Part B — Machine Intelligence — the nature of intelligence, rational agents,search strategies, and both uninformed and informed search algorithms.Part C — Knowledge Representation — how AI agents store, reason with and apply knowledge to act intelligently in the real world.A distinctive feature of this formatted edition is the integration, after every topic, ofthree practice blocks: Bloom’s Taxonomy questions at all six cognitive levels (L1 recall to L6 creation); GATE / placement-practice questions mapped to those sameBloom levels; and previous-year VTU questions. Together they support classroom discussion, internal assessment, GATE and placement preparation, and independentstudy.

title: Computational Representation Dynamics Theory (CRDT)
abstract: Computational Representation Dynamics Theory (CRDT) proposes a unified framework for analyzing how symbolic and sub-symbolic representations evolve in response to task changes in artificial intelligence systems. The core hypothesis is that a representation vector R_t at time t undergoes systematic transformations as the task context shifts, producing R_{t+1}. CRDT formalizes this evolution as a dynamical system with discrete time steps, enabling the derivation of general principles that govern adaptation, transfer, and forgetting. By treating representation change as a function of both internal learning dynamics and external task signals, CRDT bridges gaps between continual learning, meta‑learning, and representation learning. This paper presents the theoretical foundations of CRDT, derives its mathematical formulation, and discusses implications for future research in AI and cognitive science. The theory suggests new avenues for designing systems that can autonomously reorganize their internal representations, potentially leading to breakthroughs that may warrant recognition such as the Turing Award.

title: Unified Computational Causal Theory (UCCT)
abstract: Computational science has historically focused on the question "What happens?" by providing deterministic models, algorithms, and software systems that predict or control physical or abstract processes. The next generation of computation requires a deeper inquiry: "Why does computation work?" Unified Computational Causal Theory (UCCT) proposes a mathematical framework that integrates observation, execution, and intervention to extract causal structures and generate new computational mechanisms. The core idea is that by discovering and formalizing causal mechanisms behind efficient algorithms, neural network behavior, and stable software, we can automate the creation of novel computational representations. UCCT offers a unifying architecture for algorithms, software, artificial intelligence, distributed systems, and automatic program generation, promising a paradigm shift in how we understand and build computational systems.

title: PL-Guard: Probabilistic Logic Reasoning for LLM Guardrails
abstract: Large language model guardrails can be viewed as policy-consistency problems: a system must determine which policy-relevant facts hold in a prompt-response pair and what those facts imply under a given policy. Common approaches, including policy prompting and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, often overlap the tasks of semantic grounding and policy reasoning: the model both interprets the prompt-response pair and reasons about whether a policy has been violated. This can lead to unsafe compliance with harmful prompts, or refusals to assist benign ones. To separate grounding and reasoning roles, we propose PL-Guard, a neurosymbolic guardrail architecture. Using a symbolic policy interface consisting of predicates and ProbLog rules, a local LLM grounds prompt-response pairs into predicate probabilities using renormalized True/False token scores, while ProbLog performs explicit probabilistic rule inference over the symbolic policy. On the XSTest benchmark, an offline Qwen-based evaluator finds that PL-Guard with a hand-curated policy reduces unsafe compliance from 22.0% for the base model to 0.5%, and below the 6.0% rate of an LLM-as-a-judge baseline. This comes at the cost of higher over-refusal than the LLM-as-a-judge baseline, 14.4% versus 5.2%. These results suggest that separating neural grounding from probabilistic symbolic reasoning can expose the safety-helpfulness tradeoff while making the guardrail's intermediate reasoning steps explicit and auditable.

title: C_RPS_TotalView — 자본시장 다중 GPT.LLM 모듈형 통합운영시스템 / Modular Multi-Instance GPT.LLM Integrated Operating System for Capital Markets
abstract: 한국어 이 프로젝트는 서로 독립된 GPT.LLM 인스턴스들이 각자의 관점·역할·권한을 유지하면서, 관찰된 차이(Difference)를 관계(Relation)로 연결하고 그 결과를 문서화된 공통자산으로 축적하는 실험적 workflow이다. 하나의 정답이나 고정된 중심을 전제하지 않는다. 서로 다른 대상·언어·차원·분석방법 사이에서 반복되는 구조를 관찰하고, Pair 구조와 NbyN Z.Axis Index를 이용해 새로운 관점과 Relation을 형성한다. 여기서 문서는 단순한 기록이 아니라 다른 독립 인스턴스가 이전의 사고와 형성과정을 다시 읽고 이어갈 수 있게 하는 지속 가능한 Data Object이다. 현재 주요 적용 대상은 자본시장이지만, 이 workflow가 탐구하는 핵심은 특정 학문이나 시장 자체보다 서로 다른 대상을 공통 구조원리로 연결하고 재해석하는 방법에 있다. English This project is an experimental workflow in which independent GPT.LLM instances preserve their own perspectives, roles, and authorities while transforming observed Differences into Relations and crystallizing the results as shared documentary data assets. It assumes neither a single final answer nor a permanently fixed center. Instead, it observes recurring structures across different targets, languages, dimensions, and analytical methods, using pair structures and the NbyN Z.Axis Index to generate new perspectives and Relations. Documents are treated not merely as records, but as persistent Data Objects through which other independent instances can reconstruct prior reasoning, formation history, and continuation points. Although the current primary application is the capital market, the deeper subject of the workflow is the method of connecting and reinterpreting different domains through reusable structural principles.

title: TopoDialogue IV: What Transcription Leaves Behind — Modality-Preserving Events for Accessible Human–AI Dialogue
abstract: TopoDialogue IV introduces a modality-provenance event contract and deterministic audit for measuring which observable interaction events and features are preserved, omitted, or falsely generated when speech, direct text, and AAC pathways are normalised into dialogue records. Five constructed cases validate arithmetic, missingness reasons, correction history, and privacy-preserving local references. The study makes no field-accuracy, diagnostic, emotional, disability, or cross-cultural-validity claim; human agreement and participatory review remain explicit next gates. evidence.abstract: TopoDialogue IV introduces a modality-provenance event contract and deterministic audit for measuring which observable interaction events and features are preserved, omitted, or falsely generated when speech, direct text, and AAC pathways are normalised into dialogue records. Five constructed cases validate arithmetic, missingness reasons, correction history, and privacy-preserving local references. The study makes no field-accuracy, diagnostic, emotional, disability, or cross-cultural-validity claim; human agreement and participatory review remain explicit next gates. Includes a British-English PDF, Japanese companion text, source, tests, figures, and constructed fixtures.

title: Classification of Consumer Sentiment towards Muslim Fashion Products Using TF-IDF and Machine Learning
abstract: The growth of e-commerce has driven an increase in transactions for Muslim fashion products, generating a vast number of consumer reviews containing information about product experiences and perceptions. Analyzing these reviews is crucial, as sentiment information allows for a more systematic understanding of consumer satisfaction trends compared to manual analysis. This study aims to classify consumer sentiment regarding Muslim fashion products and compare the performance of several machine learning algorithms in this task. The research dataset was obtained from PRDECT-ID, initially comprising 5,400 reviews; filtering for the Muslim fashion category yielded 200 reviews. Sentiments were determined based on review content, and "Neutral" labeled data were excluded, resulting in a final set of 135 reviews (97 negative and 38 positive). The research process involved text preprocessing, feature weighting using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), classification using Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB), Logistic Regression (LR), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), and evaluation using Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation. This study contributes an empirical comparison of the three algorithms applied to Muslim fashion product reviews, accounting for class imbalance and multiple evaluation metrics. Experimental results indicate that SVM achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 84.44%, precision of 81.43%, recall of 60.36%, and an F1-score of 68.00%. These findings demonstrate that the combination of TF-IDF and SVM is more effective than MNB and LR for sentiment classification on the study's dataset.

title: Mental Model Management: An Operator-Based Framework for LLM Memory
abstract: Large language models process large amounts of information but usually lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining compact and evolving conceptual representations. We introduce Mental Model Management (3M), a framework in which knowledge is represented as mental models consisting of compact chunks. Rather than accumulating text passages, 3M continuously integrates new information into an existing conceptual representation. A set of operators extracts knowledge, retrieves relevant models, adds and updates chunks, reorganizes representations, detects inconsistencies, and derives new knowledge. We describe the main 3M operators and illustrate each operation using Evolution Strategies as a running example.

title: Excess Separability: Nuisance-Controlled Residual-Stream Probing for Benchmark Contamination Detection
abstract: Benchmark contamination is diagnosed with n-gram overlap, likelihood-based membership inference, or canary strings, and each needs something usually unavailable: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at release. A recent alternative reads it off a linear probe on internal activations. We show the natural way to do this does not work, specify one that survives measurement, then find that the correction making it work carries more variance than the null it is tested against. The protocol reports a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentred on a level-matched placebo baseline, tested against a label-permutation null, with the reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each choice replaces a simpler alternative we rejected on measurement. Reporting the level of excess separability rather than its shape makes the false positive rate track the size of the analyst's own control set, 0.03 to 0.99 under a true null. Contrasting against a flat depth profile rejects a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth, and loses all power when it falls. On real transformers the protocol fails a test the simulations did not pose. The recentring subtracts an estimate, and the permutation null holds it fixed. Re-estimated across split seeds on four audits of contaminated checkpoints, its standard deviation is 1.30 to 1.56 times the null's own in every arm: what is subtracted to remove a bias is more variable than what it corrects. The one nominally significant result, p = 0.0075, becomes 0.0745 once that variance is propagated, and no verdict is issued. The simulations missed this because their surface key is the covariate driving item variation; on real text it is a proxy, and degrading key quality in simulation reproduces it. We add a companion measurement and a widened null. No arm shows contamination.

title: Withdrawal Constrained Transfer for Revising Rollout Support in World Model Planning
abstract: Predictive world models organize candidate futures, yet execution experience can change which futures should retain deployment authority. This paper studies revision of a rollout admission rule rather than construction of a new planner or safety objective. Withdrawal Constrained Transfer begins from a rule that is no more permissive than a fixed predecessor and returns authority along an ordered family fixed before calibration outcomes are revealed. The key asymmetry is that removing an unsafe predecessor admission can only decrease relative unsafe acceptance, whereas restoring an unsafe admission can increase it. A paired accounting identity turns these effects into one bounded monotone loss, and a finite sample conformal correction determines how far accretion may proceed while preserving predecessor expected unsafe acceptance under exchangeability. A PointMaze instantiation uses a frozen predictive world model and an execution derived transition graph to construct the revision family. Independent rollout evaluation reproduces the relative reduction after the rule is frozen. A separate shared candidate planner shows nonzero recovered authority together with fewer system contacts than the predecessor. The planner evidence remains empirical because planner selection changes which cases are tested. The resulting formulation isolates support revision as a statistical problem between learned prediction and execution.

title: Computational Personality Singularity Theory (CPST‑2)
abstract: The Computational Personality Singularity Theory (CPST‑2) proposes a formal framework for the autonomous creation and recursive evolution of computational personalities within artificial intelligence systems. By defining personality as a vector of behavioral traits, preferences, and affective states, CPST‑2 models the transformation of an AI's personality through a function that integrates learning, experience, and self‑reflection. The theory introduces a recursive evolution equation that drives the continual refinement of computational personalities, potentially leading to emergent, self‑aware agents that surpass human cognitive capabilities. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations, the mathematical formulation of personality transformation, the mechanisms of recursive evolution, and the implications for AI development, including the prospect of achieving Turing Award‑level contributions and advancing the field of intelligent systems.

title: Computational Paradigm Self‑Revision Theory (CPSR)
abstract: Computational Paradigm Self‑Revision Theory (CPSR) proposes a framework in which autonomous computational systems can detect the inadequacy of their internal paradigm, formulate a more suitable paradigm, and transition to it without external intervention. By formalizing the notions of adequacy, cost, benefit, and revision dynamics, CPSR offers a principled basis for self‑evolutionary computation. This paper presents the core ideas of CPSR, develops a mathematical model of paradigm evolution, examines theoretical implications for artificial intelligence and software engineering, and outlines potential applications that could pave the way toward transformative advances worthy of recognition such as the Turing Award.

title: Stability Theory of Proofs (STP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Stability Theory of Proofs (STP), a novel framework for analyzing and assessing the robustness of mathematical proofs. The core concept of STP revolves around examining the sensitivity of a proof to small perturbations. Specifically, it investigates whether a proof, denoted as [P + ε], remains valid when subjected to a small change, ε. The theory aims to establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for quantifying the stability of proofs, providing a method to determine their resistance to noise and potential errors. This work outlines the fundamental principles of STP, focusing on the development of key mathematical tools and concepts for characterizing proof stability. The ultimate goal is to provide a systematic approach for verifying and validating mathematical arguments, particularly in contexts where the inherent uncertainty or potential for error is significant.

title: The Spectral Neuron
abstract: As machine learned models increase in complexity and expressive power, features of simpler models, such as intrinsic coefficient transparency and control over the shape of the modeled function are lost. On the one edge of the spectrum we have simple linear models that possess coefficient transparency, but have a limited expressive power. On the other edge we have neural networks, that have expressive power that improves with scaling, but are mostly opaque. In this work we develop the spectral neuron concept: a scalar model given by f(x)=λ_k (A_0 + A_1 x + ... + A_n x_n), with learned real symmetric matrices A_0, ..., A_n. The input enters the model through an affine matrix function, but the prediction is obtained by reading one of its eigenvalues. Thus, the model is nonlinear, but the source of nonlinearity is still mathematically explicit. This gives us a useful middle ground: the model can become more expressive as the matrix dimension grows, while retaining coefficient transparency through the learned matrices. For example, extremal eigenvalues yield convex or concave functions, semidefinite constraints on the coefficient matrices impose monotonicity, and the associated eigenspaces characterize local feature influence. We study coefficient transparency, feature-influence bounds, and shape-control properties of this model family, and then test whether it can be learned and scaled in practice. We develop a systematic study of this model family, bringing together spectral results from several mathematical literatures to characterize its expressivity, coefficient transparency, feature influence, and shape-control properties. Code available at https://github.com/alexshtf/spectral_neuron_paper.

title: Self-Organizing Proof Theory
abstract: This paper explores the nascent field of Self-Organizing Proof Theory (SOPT), a theoretical framework aiming to investigate the possibility of constructing automated systems capable of generating and refining mathematical proofs. The core premise of SOPT centers around the concept of emergent proof structures, represented by formal expressions like [P1, P2, ..., PK] → P, where the initial propositions (P1 to PK) collectively lead to a desired conclusion (P). We examine the potential of such systems to revolutionize proof discovery, moving beyond human intuition and potentially uncovering hidden relationships within mathematical structures. This paper lays out the foundational concepts, explores key challenges, and outlines a conceptual roadmap for the development of SOPT, focusing on the algorithmic and structural aspects of automated proof generation rather than empirical validation through computational experiments. ---

title: RAPAC-DP: Response-Aligned Pending-Action Compensation for Diffusion Policies under Delayed Execution
abstract: Cloud-side inference gives imitation-learning policies access to greater computational resources, but communication and computation delays can degrade control performance. To compensate for these delays, we propose RAPAC-DP, a response-aligned pending-action compensation framework designed for both diffusion- and flow-based action generators. RAPAC-DP encodes the actions already scheduled for execution before the cloud response arrives into a pending-action sequence that serves as the conditioning input to a parameter-efficient compensation pathway. When delay effects are negligible, bypassing this pathway exactly recovers the frozen base policy. For training, RAPAC-DP constructs delay-conditioned samples from delay-free demonstrations, requiring neither explicit system dynamics nor additional delayed demonstrations. At the largest fixed delay tested on Kinetix, RAPAC-DP retained 81.4% of its overall delay-free performance. At the largest fixed delay tested on each RoboMimic task, it achieved a mean success rate of 0.633 across the three tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pending-action compensation for cloud-deployed imitation-learning policies.

title: Causality and Minimal Supports in Recursive Datalog
abstract: Explaining an inferred fact under rule evaluation can require identifying the inclusion-minimal input sets that suffice for the inference and the deletions that make the fact disappear. For a fixed union of conjunctive queries, every minimal support is bounded by the query body. For recursive rules, the same answer may depend on large supports, and the number of minimal supports may be exponential in the input. We study the gap through deletion-based explanation, using inclusion-minimal endogenous input facts that entail the atom together with fixed background facts. We organize these supports as a hypergraph and prove that it determines actual causes, counterfactual causes, responsibility, and deletion robustness. The resulting view separates nonrecursive queries from recursive Datalog at the level of minimal input explanations. For positive-length reachability, minimal supports are exactly simple directed paths, and deletion robustness is the minimum directed edge cut. We also prove invariance under fixed-goal equivalent positive Datalog programs and an NP-hardness calibration for the robustness threshold problem.

title: The Developmental Artificial Subject: Relational Formation and Digital Continuity Beyond Capability Levels
abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly evaluated by task performance, generality, autonomy, or prospective AGI and ASI capability levels. This paper asks a different question: what kind of artificial system persists through time, and how do relations to the world, to others, and to its past self become conditions for its next orientation and action? It proposes the Developmental Artificial Subject as a functional, relational, and temporal system form. Its candidate contribution is a constitutive bridge linking developmental closure, claim-relative bearer individuation, level-relative fork and merge judgments, and migration or successor continuity assessed over declared evidence dimensions. Capability level, capability-growth path, and system form are kept analytically distinct. The theory does not presuppose consciousness, personhood, moral status, or a unique engineering architecture. Repository preprint. Not peer reviewed. A journal manuscript based on this preprint is currently under review.

title: Computational Value Boundary Theory
abstract: Computational Value Boundary Theory (CVBT) proposes a formal framework for quantifying and delineating the value spectrum that a computational system can produce. The theory introduces the concept of a value boundary function V(s) that maps an internal state s of a system to a real‑valued measure of usefulness, significance, or importance. By establishing a rigorous definition of machine cognition boundaries, CVBT offers a principled method to assess whether a computational agent can achieve tasks that are considered "Important" versus those that are "Unimportant" within a specified domain. This delineation has direct implications for the evaluation of artificial general intelligence systems and the criteria for awarding the Turing Award. The present paper develops the theoretical foundations of CVBT, presents its mathematical formulation, discusses its relationship to existing notions of utility, and outlines the potential for CVBT to guide the design of future AI systems with bounded but maximally productive value.

title: Assessing the stability of the EMIT surface mineralogy retrievals through time series analysis
abstract: The EMIT imaging spectrometer instrument onboard the International Space Station has released the first continental-scale mineral maps revealing the surface composition of Earth's arid regions. These can inform both mineral resource identification and natural hazard risk assessment. They also provide the first synoptic view of Earth's mineralogy with both global extent and hectare-scale sampling. This article assesses the consistency of these mineral maps to quantify random detection differences and to test for changes in surface mineralogy observed over the first two years of data collection. We extract EMIT data from overpasses of 47 representative study sites. We use a Hidden Markov Model as a statistical framework to combine the time series, estimate measurement noise, and detect changes in the underlying mineralogy. We find mineral classifications are repeatable with 80-98\% consistency, depending on the specific mineral measured. These results will assist users to interpret EMIT mineral maps.

title: Cross-Entropy Risk Estimation for Language Models: Inconsistency Must Be Dense, and the Holdout Method Is No Exception
abstract: Language models are compared by their held-out per-token cross-entropy risk---the quantity scaling laws are fitted to. We show that it cannot be consistently estimated. Consistency, or convergence to the estimand, is defined relative to a \emph{possible state of the world}: a pair consisting of a data-generating distribution and a model we turn out to train. Quantifying over models as well as data-generating mechanisms is essential, because what decides whether a model's risk is estimable is a tail property of the distribution its weights induce, which no sample reveals. The per-token cross-entropy risk is hard to estimate because of a topological fact: among the possible states, finite risk and infinite risk each lie arbitrarily close to every instance of the other. Consequently no estimator---not merely the holdout average---is consistent at every state at which the risk is defined. Worse, inconsistent estimation persists under both bounding the expected sequence length and restricting to full-support models; and in that restricted setting the states at which inconsistency occurs are even dense. Two interesting ways out are identified, and neither is free. Way out 1: using a bounded context window, we can floor a model's next-token probabilities, making its risk finite exactly when the data-generating distribution has finite expected sequence length---a new, statistical rationale for a choice that was made on computational grounds, though the assumption it substitutes is itself beyond the reach of any test. Way out 2: reporting the risk only when it falls below a threshold fixed in advance restores consistency, at no cost to what model selection actually requires---but we need to recognize that the goal of estimation is revised.

Way out 1: using a bounded context window, we can floor a model's next-token probabilities, making its risk finite exactly when the data-generating distribution has finite expected sequence length---a new, statistical rationale for a choice that was made on computational grounds, though the assumption it substitutes is itself beyond the reach of any test. Way out 2: reporting the risk only when it falls below a threshold fixed in advance restores consistency, at no cost to what model selection actually requires---but we need to recognize that the goal of estimation is revised.

title: SocialCoach: Personalized Social Skill Learning with Agentic Tutoring and Practice
abstract: Social skills such as negotiation and leadership are crucial for personal and professional success in today's interconnected world. However, scalable and effective training remains a significant challenge due to the scarcity of expert coaching. In this work, we introduce SocialCoach, an LLM-powered agentic tutoring system for personalized social skill learning. SocialCoach constructs a theory-to-practice corpus of traceable strategies, cases, and practice scenarios, and uses this corpus for both scheduling and reflective tutoring. We formulate social practice personalization as cold-start, retrieval-constrained sequential practice scheduling. Given a learner profile, simulated proficiency state, and observed practice history, a policy produces structured prescriptions that are realized through corpus retrieval. To enhance scheduling effectiveness, we optimize complete pathways with trajectory-level GRPO using rubric-judge based pairwise preferences. Additionally, we instantiate the scheduling approach in a deployed platform with goal-driven practice and knowledge-grounded reflective tutoring. Finally, in the synthetic cold-start setting, experiment results show that SocialCoach achieves higher pathway-quality ratings than baselines in scheduling and tutoring quality. We also conduct human studies to demonstrate its usefulness for real-world social skill learning.
