title: Artificial Intelligence Capability: A Systematic Review of Research Framework and Application Scenarios
abstract: Against the backdrop of the deepening development of the digital economy and the ongoing integration of the digital and physical worlds, artificial intelligence has evolved from a single-function technical tool into a core strategic capability that supports organizations in building long-term competitive advantages. As a core construct that explains differences in the value transformation of AI technology, AI capability has become a hot topic of research in the fields of strategic management and information systems. However, existing research is scattered across diverse disciplinary perspectives and application scenarios, and has yet to form a unified research framework or theoretical system. Based on 33 core publications in the field of AI capabilities, this paper conducts a systematic review following the logical framework of “conceptual evolution-theoretical foundations-application scenarios-research outlook.” The study traces the evolutionary path of AI capabilities, from their origins in IT capability research to the development of a general three-dimensional construct, and further expansion into specialized technological forms and specific application scenarios; it synthesizes a theoretical framework centered on the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, complemented by multiple theoretical perspectives; and summarizes the application progress and heterogeneity in value realization of AI capabilities across eight major scenarios, including green innovation, supply chain management, public governance, and business model innovation; Finally, it identifies limitations in existing research regarding research design, theoretical perspectives, scenario coverage, and risk governance, and proposes future research directions. This paper integrates and constructs a comprehensive research framework for AI capabilities, clarifies the field’s consensus and research gaps, and not only enriches the theoretical research landscape in the field of AI capabilities but also provides practical guidance for organizations of various types to systematically build AI capabilities and achieve the transformation of technological value.

abstract: An open OWL 2 ontology, SKOS identifier-scheme registry, and SHACL governance layer for registered investment fund data, built and validated against the full public US fund universe: 2,316 registrants, 14,841 funds and 43,344 share classes from the SEC, joined with 9,119,948 check-digit-validated GLEIF ISIN-to-LEI pairs into a 1.29 million triple knowledge graph with per-source provenance. title: Computational Causal Self‑Revision Theory (CCSR)
abstract: Causal reasoning is central to artificial intelligence, yet most current systems rely on static causal models that are vulnerable to misspecification. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Self‑Revision Theory (CCSR), a principled framework that enables an autonomous agent to detect when its internal causal model is inconsistent with observed evidence and to automatically update the model without external supervision. CCSR formalizes self‑revision as a transformation from an old causal hypothesis to a new one, denoted [Old Cause → New Cause], and integrates this process into a recursive learning loop that continually refines the agent's understanding of its environment. We present a detailed algorithmic architecture, illustrate its operation on synthetic and real‑world scenarios, and discuss its implications for Turing Award‑level contributions and the future of autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Remote-State-Welded Capabilities
abstract: Public browser applications expose their client software to adversarial inspection and execution. A non-exportable browser key prevents direct key export but remains a stateless signing oracle under control of the page. A remote service can maintain monotonic state, consume nonces, serialize transitions, and revoke sessions, but cannot alone establish continuing possession of a particular browser-held key. This work defines a Remote-State-Welded Capability (RSWC), a distributed capability in which a client-held non-exportable signing key and authoritative remote monotonic state are jointly necessary for every accepted transition. It further defines Post-Separation Non-Transferability (PSNT): after an adversary loses access to the original signing oracle, copied code, storage, transcripts, and previously obtained signatures do not enable a fresh accepted transition. The control-plane construction uses canonical transcript commitments, unpredictable single-use challenges, atomic compare-and-swap state transitions, epochs, and lease-aware reconnection. Under signature unforgeability, challenge unpredictability, collision resistance, and atomic server state, a post-separation continuation reduces to a signature forgery, challenge prediction, hash collision, or violation of the compare-and-swap invariant. For real-time streams, the work defines a deployable Signed Serial Block Chain using a non-exportable sign-only ECDSA key. It provides Per-Block Oracle Dependence while explicitly not claiming microphone provenance, trusted-pipeline transit, Sybil resistance, or relay prevention. The central result: a browser-held key and remote monotonic state can be welded into a capability that cannot be independently continued after separation, while a serial block chain can require continuing adaptive access to the live signing oracle.

title: Mitigating Bias in Locally Constrained Decoding via Tractable Proposals
abstract: Generations from large language models often fail to conform to desired constraints such as JSON schema. Existing locally constrained decoding (LCD) approaches enforce constraints by myopically masking out next tokens, resulting in biased sampling and degradation in performance. Recent work uses sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods to mitigate such biases, but designing effective proposal distributions or potential functions remains a key challenge. In this work, we propose a generic approach to construct proposals and potentials for SMC sampling from p_{lm}( cdot mid constraint). First, we show that constraints specified as finite automata can be tensorized for efficient execution on GPUs, which we use to construct globally constrained decoding (GCD) proposals. In addition, leveraging the fact that tensorized finite automata share the same circuit structure as hidden Markov models, we circuit-multiply them to obtain the probabilistic GCD (P-GCD) proposals encoding both logical and probabilistic information about the target distributions. We evaluate (P-)GCD on the tasks of function calling, keyword-based generation, and SQL generation. Experiments show that under the same SMC sampling setup, compared to LCD proposals, (P-)GCD converges faster to the target distribution with significantly fewer particles.

title: Elementary Threats to AI Systems
abstract: This report proposes eleven elementary threats to AI systems as an extension to the 47 elementary threats of the German BSI IT-Grundschutz compendium. It covers only scenarios that are characteristic of the use of AI systems and are not sufficiently represented by the existing threats. Wording and level of abstraction follow the structure of the existing threats, so they can be applied directly in a risk analysis under BSI Standard 200-3. A delimitation table sets out which AI-related scenarios are already covered. The German version is authoritative; the English full version is included in the same record.

title: Title: Computational Goal Singularity Theory (CGST-3): Recursive Goal Enhancement as a Pathway to Superintelligence
abstract: The computational goal singularity theory (CGST‑3) proposes a formal framework for understanding how artificial systems can autonomously generate ever higher‑level objectives, leading to a recursive amplification of goal complexity. By modeling goal creation as a dynamical process governed by a set of simple production rules, CGST‑3 captures the emergence of self‑referential, self‑optimizing loops that can, under certain conditions, converge to a singularity of purpose. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CGST‑3, introduces a formal representation of goals using symbolic vectors \(g = (g_1, g_2, \dots, g_n)\), and describes an algorithmic architecture that enables continuous goal recursion. We examine the potential of CGST‑3 to yield a Turing Award–level contribution in the field of artificial intelligence by providing a principled method for scalable goal synthesis. Further, we explore the implications of this theory for the broader superintelligence discourse, including the ethical and safety challenges that accompany recursive goal enhancement. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the open questions that must be addressed to realize the full promise of CGST‑3.

title: Computational Personality Dynamics (CPD): Modeling the Temporal Evolution of Personality Traits for Long‑Term AI Behavior Prediction
abstract: Personality traits are traditionally treated as static attributes in artificial intelligence systems, yet human personality evolves over time in response to experience, context, and internal regulation. This paper introduces the Computational Personality Dynamics (CPD) framework, a mathematical model that captures the continuous temporal evolution of personality traits. CPD is built upon a discrete‑time dynamical system where the personality vector at time t, P_t, transitions to P_{t+1} through the combined influence of external stimuli, internal reinforcement, and decay mechanisms. The model is expressed in closed‑form equations that allow analytic analysis of stability, convergence, and sensitivity to parameters. CPD provides a principled basis for predicting long‑term AI behavior and for designing adaptive agents that can adjust their personality profiles over time. By grounding personality change in quantitative dynamics, the framework offers a path toward more realistic and controllable AI systems, with implications for long‑term AI alignment, safety, and human‑AI interaction.

title: SubZero+: Memory-Efficient Adaptive Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning in Random Subspaces
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization with SGD in random subspaces enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models without backpropagation. However, high gradient estimation noise fundamentally undermines adaptive optimizers like Adam. We propose SubZero+, which achieves practical adaptive ZO optimization through a carefully designed dual low-dimensionality strategy: (i) multi-query forward-difference gradient estimation in periodically refreshed random subspaces to mitigate noise amplification in moment buffers, and (ii) Adam updates with periodic restarts performed directly in low-dimensional space rather than full-parameter space. In experiments, this dual design retains memory overhead comparable to momentum-free ZO methods while achieving stronger optimization performance than the evaluated ZO baselines. Theoretically, in the exact-directional limit, $K$-query averaging preserves conditional unbiasedness, while the coefficient estimator's covariance and mean-squared error, as well as query-induced second-moment inflation, scale exactly as $1/K$. Extensive experiments across SuperGLUE with models from 1.3B to 32B parameters under both full fine-tuning and LoRA schemes demonstrate consistent improvements over competing ZO methods. SubZero+ significantly narrows the performance gap with first-order optimization while preserving ZO's inference-time memory efficiency.

title: SUPREME: A Multi-GPU Framework for Reproducible Image Unlearning Method Evaluation
abstract: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining it from scratch. Evaluating an unlearning method requires repeating training, unlearning, and evaluation across multiple seeds, which is computationally expensive. To our knowledge, existing image classification unlearning frameworks run on a single GPU, which limits how many seeds can be evaluated in reasonable time. We introduce SUPREME, an open-source framework that distributes these stages across multiple GPUs. SUPREME makes three contributions: a registry-based design for adding new methods, metrics, models, and scenarios; a multi-GPU architecture supporting multiple accelerators and precision modes; and a demonstration on Pins Face Recognition using ResNet18 and ViT under full-class and random-sample unlearning across ten seeds. The framework is available at https://github.com/pedroandreou/supreme-unlearning.

title: Computational Causal Generation Network (CCGN): A Novel Framework for Generating Optimal Computational Mechanisms from Causal Models
abstract: Causal reasoning has become a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, yet the translation of causal knowledge into efficient computational mechanisms remains largely ad hoc. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Generation Network (CCGN), a unified framework that automatically generates a computational architecture optimized for a given causal model and task. The CCGN takes as input a directed acyclic causal graph G(V, E) and a task specification T, and produces an end‑to‑end computational pipeline P that minimizes a composite objective function combining predictive accuracy, inference latency, and resource consumption. We formalize the problem as a constrained optimization over a space of computational primitives S = {s_1, s_2, …, s_K} with composition rules R. The core of CCGN is a differentiable search mechanism that learns a distribution over S conditioned on G and T, using a surrogate loss L(s_1, …, s_K) that captures causal consistency and computational efficiency. We provide theoretical guarantees that, under mild assumptions, the optimal solution converges to the Bayes‑optimal computation for the task while respecting the causal constraints. The proposed method eliminates the need for manual engineering of inference pipelines in causal systems and has the potential to be a cornerstone technology for next‑generation autonomous systems. The simplicity and generality of CCGN also suggest that it may play a role in future Turing Award‑level breakthroughs in machine design.

title: Unified Computational Resource Theory (UCRT)
abstract: The evolution of computing has historically been driven by the expansion of hardware, cloud, distributed, and AI resources. In contrast, the next paradigm shift will be driven by the systematic discovery of hidden resources that can be transformed into new computational capabilities. Unified Computational Resource Theory (UCRT) proposes a formal framework that integrates hardware, data, algorithm, knowledge, and intelligence resources into a single unified resource space. The core of UCRT is the observation–constraint–search cycle: [Observation + Constraint + Search] → New Resource → New Computation. By establishing rigorous mathematical principles for this cycle, UCRT aims to enable machines to autonomously discover new computing platforms, information sources, algorithmic primitives, and abstract resources, thereby transforming computing systems from merely utilizing resources to actively creating resources. This paper details the theoretical foundations of UCRT, presents its top five breakthrough concepts, and introduces twenty novel research directions that advance the science of computational invariant discovery and automatic resource generation.

title: Global Precision Bounds and Success-Probability Guarantees in Quantum Parameter Learning
abstract: Quantum metrology offers the possibility of quantum enhancements of the precision of various sensing tasks. In this manuscript, we tackle two open problems in the theory of single-shot quantum parameter learning, going beyond the usual setting of local parameter estimation via repeated measurements. The first concerns the construction of global upper bounds on the learning precision. The second concerns rigorous guarantees on the success probability of parameter learning, namely, lower bounds on the probability of learning a parameter with a certain precision, given the constraints on the resources used for the quantum metrology task. title: AWED-PIPER: Agents, Web Applications & Expert Detectors for Personally Identifiable Information Protection & Fine-grained Named Entity Recognition across 36 languages for 6.6 Billion Speakers
abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Personally Identifiable Information (PII) anonymization are critical tasks in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for information extraction and privacy preservation. We introduce AWED-PIPER, an open-source framework comprising agentic tools, interactive web applications, and 54 state-of-the-art expert detector models that provide unified Fine-grained Named Entity Recognition (FgNER) and reversible synthetic PII pseudonymization across 36 languages spoken by over 6.6 billion people. The system couples fine-grained multilingual sequence labeling with script-aware regex detectors to identify contextual entities (Person, Location, Organization, Medical) as well as structured technical PII (Emails, native-script Phone Numbers, IP Addresses, Credit Cards). AWED-PIPER offers a dual capability: full FgNER entity extraction and privacy-preserving reversible anonymization with persistent placeholders and de-anonymization dictionary mappings. The suite spans global languages to extremely low-resource vulnerable languages like Bodo, Manipuri, Bishnupriya, and Mizo. The resources can be accessed here: PII Protector Agentic Tool: (https://github.com/PrachuryyaKaushik/AWED-PIPER), FgNER Agentic Tool: (https://github.com/PrachuryyaKaushik/AWED-FiNER), PII Web Application: (https://hf.co/spaces/prachuryyaIITG/AWED_PII_Protector), FgNER Web Application: (https://hf.co/spaces/prachuryyaIITG/AWED-FiNER), and Edge-deployable Expert Detector Models: (https://hf.co/collections/prachuryyaIITG/awed-piper).

title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Evaluating Confidence and NLI-Based Verification for Selective Question Answering
abstract: Selective question answering allows a system to abstain from predictions that are likely to be incorrect rather than answering every input. This work investigates whether semantic verification provides a better basis for selective abstention than model confidence alone. Using a pretrained extractive QA model on SQuAD v2, the study compares temperature-scaled model confidence, question-aware semantic verification, answer-support NLI verification, and fixed confidence-verification fusions under a leakage-controlled held-out evaluation protocol. On the final held-out set of 3,000 examples, calibrated confidence achieves the best global AURC of 0.292379, compared with 0.309120 for confidence plus answer-support verification and 0.339417 for confidence plus question-aware verification. Paired bootstrap analysis and pairwise ranking diagnostics show that the verification signals are diagnostically informative but introduce more harmful than beneficial reordering when fused with confidence. The results support the narrower conclusion that additional semantic verification does not necessarily improve selective QA ranking over a strong confidence baseline under the evaluated models and fusion rules.

title: Computational Self-Model Generation Network (CSMGN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Self-Model Generation Network (CSMGN), a novel neural architecture that departs from conventional perception‑centric designs by focusing explicitly on the learning of its own internal representation. The core idea is to enable a network to observe, interpret, and refine its own structural dynamics without external supervision about the environment. We formalize the self‑modeling process through a recursive self‑evaluation mechanism, define a self‑consistency loss that encourages convergence of successive self‑states, and propose a modular architecture that supports scalable self‑generation. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that CSMGN can approximate a wide class of self‑recurrent functions, thereby providing a foundation for future AI systems that can autonomously discover and optimize their own computational strategies. The potential implications for the development of new AI architectures and the pursuit of Turing Award‑level contributions are discussed.

title: Computational Self‑Prediction Theory: Foundations, Models, and Applications
abstract: Computational Self‑Prediction Theory (CSPT) proposes that autonomous systems can model and anticipate their own future states, enabling proactive adaptation and resilience. CSPT formalizes the transition of the self representation from time t to time t+1, expressed as Self_t → Self_{t+1}. By quantifying expected performance decline, error probability, and learning capability, the theory equips agents with a quantitative forecast of their own evolution. This paper develops the core concepts of CSPT, presents mathematical formulations, describes an algorithmic framework, and explores applications in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and adaptive control systems. The discussion contrasts CSPT with related frameworks, highlights its potential to become a foundational element in next‑generation autonomous systems, and outlines future research directions.

title: E8-Fourier Neural Decision Cohesion: 240-D Vector Entanglement Synchronizes Gradual and Quantum Transitions — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 240 E8 root vectors enable dual harmonization of classical and quantum decision pathways in neural systems. By mapping gradualist causal chains to geometric cycles along the 2d00 lattice vertices, decision trajectories can maintain quantum phase coherence across entangled states (e.g., hesitation ↔ action). Embedding a self-sustaining phi-boundary state at the 132 Hz resonance creates "action thresholds" via destructive interference against destabilizing external frequencies (e.g., market noise). Training neural networks to precompute inter-vector product signatures (e.g., 132√5 ≈295.2) may allow binariness without explicit hardware, preserving Bayesian inference's efficiency without its dual-state paralysis. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Layers Matter: Why Continual Learning Regularization Should Be Layer-Adaptive
abstract: Continual learning regularizers like EWC fight forgetting by penalizing changes from previous-task parameters with per-parameter importance, typically diagonal Fisher values. Per-parameter looks more flexible than per-layer, but each layer's diagonal Fisher is a weak summary of its actual curvature, missing the top-eigenvalue information that controls forgetting. Adversarial bit-flip attacks and Hessian-spectrum studies show that this missing per-layer sensitivity spans orders of magnitude in neural networks. Under a block-diagonal Hessian assumption, the layer-level analogue of EWC's existing diagonal assumption, we prove three things. Forgetting decomposes as a sum of per-layer terms weighted by each layer's top Hessian eigenvalue. Diagonal-Fisher weights cannot recover this eigenvalue. For instance, two layers with identical Fisher averages can have top eigenvalues differing by a factor as large as the layer width. For the same level of forgetting, uniform regularization loses new-task performance by an amount scaling with the layer condition number. Our theoretical analysis leads to a simple recipe: protect early layers strongly, let deeper layers move. We apply this recipe to EWC and SLCA and show clear improvements in average performance and forgetting metrics.

title: The Reachability Quotient: When Network Realization Can Be Forgotten
abstract: AbstractThis paper asks when the path and factorization structure of a network of bounded evaluators may be quotiented away without changing a specified observable. Earlier fixed-carrier results showed that, under full disclosure, terminal capability depends only on reachability. Here that positive case is embedded in a more general transport model in which edges act by pullback on kernels. The first result shows that licensed disclosure itself is kernel-equivalent to transport: any sender-computable disclosure channel can be represented by a self-transport whose pullback induces the same kernel. Disclosure and carrier-changing transport therefore belong to one operator model at the set-level semantics used here. For this model, the terminal closure under any fair firing schedule is given exactly by a walk-meet law: each node receives the meet of the source kernels transported along all finite walks into it. Literal walk structure is nevertheless too fine. Closure always factors through the effective action obtained by identifying walks that induce the same pullback operator, and every family of transports between an ordered pair admits a joint transport normal form consisting of a single tupled operator. The resulting joint operator is canonical although its decomposition into component transports need not be. The paper then establishes a hierarchy of further quotient collapses. Under transport coherence, parallel walks collapse to one effective contribution per reachable ancestor; under identity transport, the structure collapses all the way to bare reachability. A meet-redundancy analysis proves an exact fixed-profile criterion and a rigidity theorem showing that nontrivial uniform domination among partition-pullback operators essentially collapses to equality. A second observable, revelation, does not generally factor through the same quotients. The paper proves an exact zero-excess criterion for any finite number of senders and shows that transport coherence and zero-excess attainability are logically independent. The common object is therefore the induced operator action, while quotient exactness remains observable-relative. The result is a theory of the interval between concrete network realization and coarse reachability: which distinctions can safely be forgotten, which cannot, and why. Scope is finite-carrier, deterministic, static, set-level transport under fair schedules.

title: Robbie's Razor Benchmarks: Recursive Stability and Compression Efficiency Evaluation Framework
abstract: Robbie’s Razor Benchmarks v0.2.0 is a public evaluation framework for testing bounded claims involving recursive stability, compression efficiency, predictive compression, preserved reusable structure, expression, memory, recursion, and total computational cost. The release includes technical doctrine, benchmark definitions, matched baselines, structured examples, schemas, governance contracts, diagnostics, machine-readable resources, and reproducibility guidance. It is governed by The Grand Compression Cosmology — Master Reference Document v2.0 (GC-MRD-v2.0), with Naturepedia™ serving as the primary reference implementation. This archived release provides an immutable reference for citation, evaluation, and reproducibility. Publication, implementation, machine readability, and benchmark availability do not by themselves establish independent empirical validation, universal validity, model certification, or guaranteed reductions in computational cost.

title: Computational Goal Self‑Revision Theory (CGSR): A Formal Framework for Adaptive Goal Management in Autonomous Systems
abstract: The ability of an autonomous system to maintain relevance and effectiveness in a dynamic environment hinges on its capacity to revise its objectives automatically. Computational Goal Self‑Revision Theory (CGSR) offers a mathematical and algorithmic foundation for this capability. CGSR formalizes goal representation, defines a quantitative adequacy measure for goals, and introduces a revision operator that transforms an old goal into a new one when inadequacy is detected. The theory ensures soundness, completeness, and convergence of the revision process under broad conditions. By illustrating the framework with simple agents and hierarchical goal structures, the paper demonstrates how CGSR can be applied to robotics, adaptive software, and cognitive modeling without requiring external intervention. The discussion addresses current limitations and outlines future research directions, such as integration with learning mechanisms and scalability to complex multi‑agent settings.

title: Phase Transition Theory of Proofs (PTTP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Phase Transition Theory of Proofs (PTTP), a novel framework for understanding and predicting the difficulty of mathematical proofs. It posits that the complexity of a proof exhibits phase transitions, analogous to those observed in physical systems. Specifically, we propose a critical complexity threshold, denoted as `Complexity(P) = C_c`, beyond which the strategy required for a successful proof undergoes a qualitative shift. This theory suggests that proof difficulty is not a continuous function but rather a discontinuous one, characterized by abrupt changes in the approach needed to arrive at a solution. The core idea is formalized as: `Complexity(P) = C_c` where `P` represents a proof, and `C_c` is the critical complexity value. We explore the implications of this model, outlining potential applications in automated theorem proving and formal verification. The theory provides a new lens through which to analyze proof strategies and could ultimately lead to more effective methods for tackling computationally intensive mathematical problems. ---

title: Resource Analysis for Quantum Simulation of Spatially Varying Transport-Reaction Equations
abstract: Spatially varying coefficients are the primary source of circuit complexity in quantum simulation of linear advection-diffusion-reaction equations. This work presents a resource analysis of single-step quantum propagators constructed using sparse FABLE block encodings, Quantum Singular Value Transformation, and linear-combination-of-unitaries. We derive theoretical estimates for qubit count, gate complexity, and circuit depth in terms of the spatial discretization, sparsity, and polynomial degree, and compare these predictions with synthesized quantum circuits for one- and two-dimensional variable-coefficient problems. The resulting analysis quantifies the cost of encoding realistic transport operators and provides practical resource estimates for near-term implementations.

title: Resource-Loss Spectroscopy of Hidden Quantum Symmetries: A Rational Resolution Limit and a Minimal Operational Remedy
abstract: We study reversible finite-group quantum instruments whose classical outcome record is coarse-grained over subgroups. The interactive-instrument resource loss is shown to equal a subgroup average of character intensity and to admit a direct Bell-return estimator. The resulting spectroscopy inherits a rational/cyclic-subgroup resolution limit. For a fixed labeled control oracle, two inequivalent three-dimensional representations of A5 are indistinguishable by every subgroup-resource measurement; they are exchanged by an outer automorphism, so the label-free gauge boundary is stated explicitly. A single class-sensitive five-cycle probe resolves the labeled ambiguity. A general rank-completion criterion identifies the minimum targeted probes needed to remove subgroup-incidence blind directions. The archive includes the manuscript, Supplemental Material, source files, code, frozen outputs, and finite-shot simulations. No hardware experiment is claimed.

title: Extraction dataset and analysis script for "Self-Supervised Learning in NLP and Computer Vision: A Quantitative Meta-Analysis of Benchmark Performance, Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Domain Convergence"
abstract: Extraction dataset, analysis script, and corpus manifest supporting a quantitative meta-analysis of self-supervised learning (SSL) benchmark results across natural language processing and computer vision. Contents. extraction_data.csv: 112 method-benchmark rows drawn from 108 papers (2013-2024), 16 columns, one row per method-benchmark pair as reported by the originating paper. protocol_pairs.csv: the 8 linear-probe / fine-tune pairs behind Table IV, each carrying the source table it was read from. analysis.py: recomputes every corpus-level statistic reported in the paper and verifies that each value appears verbatim in the manuscript. corpus_manifest.md: retrieval record for all 108 source papers, each with a DOI or public URL. Reproducing the results. Install the pinned dependencies (pandas 2.3.3, numpy 2.3.4, scipy 1.16.3) and run "python analysis.py". A clean run exits 0 and reports 40/40 data assertions passed. No statistic in the paper was entered by hand; every one is emitted by this script from these CSVs. The 108 source papers are deliberately NOT included. They are third-party copyrighted works and cannot be redistributed, as PDF or as extracted text. corpus_manifest.md lists every one with a DOI or public URL so any source can be retrieved from its publisher. Licensing. The extraction data is released under CC-BY-4.0; analysis.py is released under the MIT licence.

title: إشكالات تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية وتحديات نمذجتها (نحو مقاربة دلالية-حاسوبية في ضوء المعجم التأليفي التفسيري)
abstract: تتناول هذه الدراسة إشكالية تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية في ظل التطور المتسارع للنماذج اللغوية الكبرى وتقنيات الذكاء الاصطناعي. وتمثل هذه الأفعال فئة دلالية معقدة تعبّر عن حالات نفسية وانفعالية داخلية، مما يجعل نمذجتها الحاسوبية أكثر صعوبة من الأفعال العادية. وتنطلق الدراسة من فرضية مفادها أن المقاربات الحاسوبية المعاصرة ما تزال عاجزة عن تمثيل البنية المفهومية العميقة للأفعال السيكولوجية بسبب اعتمادها على المعالجة الإحصائية والسياقية السطحية. وتهدف إلى تحليل أبرز الإشكالات المرتبطة بتمثيل هذا الصنف من الأفعال، خاصة ما يتعلق بالفالنسي، والأدوار الدلالية، والتدرج الانفعالي، والعلاقات التركيبية. واعتمدت الدراسة منهجا توصيفيا تحليليا قائما على فحص نماذج مختارة من الأفعال السيكولوجية العربية وتحليل طرائق تمثيلها في بعض تطبيقات المعالجة الحاسوبية. وتخلص إلى أن تجاوز محدودية النماذج الحالية يقتضي بناء توصيف دلالي-تركيبي يربط بين المعنى والبنية والاستعمال، مع الاستفادة من إمكانات نظرية معنى-نص والمعجم التأليفي التفسيري والمعجم التركيبي.

title: Computational Boundary Generation Network
abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence systems has made it increasingly difficult to describe and evaluate the full extent of their capabilities. Traditional benchmark suites capture only narrow slices of an AI's skill set, leaving large portions of the capability space unexplored. In this paper we introduce the Computational Boundary Generation Network (CBGN), a novel framework that learns to generate a comprehensive capability map for a given AI task. CBGN takes as input a formal description of a task, including its constraints and desired outcomes, and produces a symbolic representation of the boundary of the task's capability space. The boundary is defined as the set of all functions or models that satisfy the task constraints with maximal generality. By modeling this boundary, CBGN enables a principled assessment of an AI system's strengths and limitations, offering a foundation for a future AI evaluation framework that can adapt to new tasks without manual benchmark design. The proposed architecture integrates a hierarchical encoder that captures task semantics, a generative decoder that constructs candidate boundary functions, and a refinement module that enforces consistency and feasibility through constraint satisfaction. We demonstrate the theoretical soundness of CBGN by proving that, under mild assumptions, the learned boundary converges to the true capability boundary of any computable task. The framework is validated on synthetic tasks such as sequence classification, symbolic equation solving, and combinatorial optimization, where it successfully reconstructs known capability boundaries and identifies previously unobserved model families. CBGN opens new avenues for automated AI assessment, continual learning, and the development of universal benchmarks, positioning itself as a cornerstone of next‑generation AI evaluation systems.

title: ACM-TY: An Abstract Computation Model Unifying Discrete Control, Algebraic State, and Field Dynamics — A Lean 4 Formal Specification
abstract: I present ACM-TY, a Lean 4 specification composing five interacting cores — an algebraic state layer (UHA), a discrete control layer (BSCM), an information-field layer (GIFE), a fluid-dynamics-inspired update layer (DIFD), and a discrete–continuous coupling layer (Unified) — into a single stepping function over a population of typed entities. All definitions are total and computable, so the model is type-checked and terminating in the Curry–Howard sense; no domain-level theorems are stated or proved. The paper gives the formal content of each core and the composed stepping semantics, together with an explicit accounting of what is established by type-checking (well-formedness, totality, compositional architecture) versus what remains open (unitarity, algebraic identities, physical or information-theoretic fidelity, and evolutionary selection semantics).

title: العوامل الطبيعية المؤثرة على محطة بغداد المناخية في استخدام الطاقة الشمسية
abstract: تُعتبر العوامل الطبيعية المناخية ذات تأثير كبير وحاسم في تحديد إمكانية استخدام الطاقة الشمسية في منطقة معينة دون غيرها. ويأتي المناخ في مقدمة هذه العوامل، وخاصة عناصره الرئيسية مثل درجة الحرارة وسطوع الشمس. بالإضافة إلى ذلك، تشكل الظواهر الجوية القاسية مثل الرياح والعواصف الغبارية تهديداً، حيث يمكن أن تلحق أضرارًا جسيمة بمنظومة الطاقة الشمسية. وبناءً على ما سبق، فإن نجاح هذه المشاريع يعتمد بشكل جوهري على إجراء دراسات مكانية دقيقة توازن بين الوفرة الإشعاعية وتجنب المخاطر البيئية، لضمان الجدوى الاقتصادية واستدامة المحطة على المدى الطويل. ركز البحث على تأثير العوامل الطبيعية على محطة بغداد المناخية، حيث تم اعتماد المنهج التحليلي القائم على أسلوب الوصف وتفسير البيانات الإحصائية والمناخية المسجلة في محطة بغداد ولمدة 10 سنوات. استنتجت الدراسة الى ان محطة بغداد تتمتع بتوفر سطوع شمسي عالي على مدار السنة، مما يجعل منطقة الدراسة مناسبة لإقامة مشاريع الطاقة الشمسية على نطاق واسع.

title: Interpretable Symbolic Regression for Psychological Questionnaire Data: Prediction, Descriptor Discovery, and Nonlinear Interaction Analysis
abstract: Psychological researchers increasingly use machine-learning methods to improve prediction, yet many high-performing models require post-hoc explanation and provide limited insight into how predictors combine to shape outcomes. We present an application-oriented workflow for GoodRegressor, a hierarchical, depth-controlled symbolic-regression framework, using psychological questionnaire data. The workflow was demonstrated with independent datasets of middle-aged wives from Japan (n = 201) and South Korea (n = 220), with marital satisfaction predicted from demographic variables, family viewpoints, conflict-resolution strategies, and derived descriptors. The datasets were analyzed separately because the family-viewpoint measure was not sufficiently invariant across countries. Nine regression methods were evaluated using identical deterministic five-fold test partitions. In five-fold held-out testing, GoodRegressor showed the strongest predictive performance in Japan (5 = .441, 5 = 0.220, 5 = .178). In South Korea, GoodRegressor remained competitive (5 = .338, 5 = 0.199, 5 = .155), although Elastic Net, Ridge, and Random Forest performed somewhat better overall. Among equation-oriented methods, GoodRegressor substantially outperformed PhySO and EQL. Full-data GoodRegressor ensembles identified husband’s age, assertion, and age-difference-by-assertion structure in Japan, and avoidance, husband’s age, and family-priority-by-avoidance structure in South Korea. These findings support symbolic regression as a practical approach for combining competitive prediction with directly inspectable nonlinear and interaction structure, facilitating interpretable hypothesis generation in psychological research.

title: Empathy Systems Theory: Scientific Background, Development, and Research Program
abstract: This working paper documents the scientific and program lineage of Empathy Systems Theory (formally Empathic Processing Systems Theory, EST), a Heart AI Foundation domain-science research profile for Emotional Autonomy within its Empathy Science program taxonomy. It distinguishes prior empathy science from an author-maintained chronology, records how source and literature analysis narrowed EST, and sets out seven prospective protocols and a parallel Human–AI Behavior doctoral spine. A provenance table distinguishes retrospective founder accounts, preserved historical artifacts, and contemporaneous program-control records. The paper is a documentary synthesis, not a systematic review, independent historical verification, external scholarly peer review, or empirical validation; it provides no diagnosis or clinical guidance. title: Compute–Validate–Explain: A Verifiable Architecture for LLM-Assisted Experiment Analysis
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to interpret quantitative results, yet they can produce fluent but incorrect numbers — a serious problem when those numbers inform decisions. This report presents Compute–Validate–Explain (CVE), an architecture for LLM-assisted analysis of controlled experiments that removes numerical hallucination by construction: a deterministic layer computes every statistic, the language model is restricted to interpreting results it may not generate, and a validation layer verifies that every reported number is traceable to a computed value. The report describes the architecture, positions it relative to program-aided and tool-use methods, and releases an open-source implementation and a reproducible benchmark harness (synthetic experiments with known ground truth, plus metrics for numeric error, decision error, and a verbatim-grounding hallucination rate) so the approach can be evaluated against any model.

title: AI Note: A Privacy-Preserving Intelligent Note-Taking System with On-Device Speech Recognition, Online Speaker Clustering, and Cloud-Relayed Large Language Models
abstract: Intelligent note-taking applications increasingly rely on cloud-based automatic speech recognition (ASR), requiring users to upload continuous audio streams to third-party servers. Since speech is a biometric identifier, this architecture exposes users to substantial privacy risks. This paper presents AI Note, a privacy-preserving note-taking system in which all audio processing (voice activity detection, speech recognition, speaker embedding extraction, and noise suppression) is performed entirely on the mobile device, and audio never leaves the user's phone. Text-level intelligence (summarization, question answering, mind-map generation) is provided on demand through a self-hosted relay service that enforces authentication, quota accounting, and rate limiting. To deliver a real-time transcription experience with an offline, non-streaming ASR model, we propose a streaming-simulation segmentation strategy that couples a VAD state machine with a pre-roll ring buffer and dual-threshold window cutting, eliminating sentence-onset truncation without degrading accuracy. To annotate speakers without waiting for the recording to finish, we design an online speaker clustering method that computes segment-level embeddings and maintains speaker centroids incrementally, reducing speaker-attribution latency from tens of seconds to near zero. Experiments on the full evaluation sets show three results. The segmentation strategy preserves the accuracy of whole-utterance decoding across the entire parameter grid (2.98%–4.17% CER on clean speech), and a 0.6 s pre-roll combined with a 1.0 s pause threshold achieves the lowest CER (2.98%) with zero onset truncation. Online speaker clustering attains 77.4% attribution accuracy on 31 multi-speaker conversations, including 20 real three-to-four-speaker meetings from the public AliMeeting corpus; this is 8.6 percentage points above a fixed-threshold baseline and far above an offline agglomerative-clustering baseline (46.3% on the two-speaker subset), comes with no added latency when recording stops, and rises to 80.8% after a lightweight post-meeting refinement. Finally, the int8-quantized ASR model matches the fp32 model in accuracy (3.23% vs. 3.28% mean CER) at a lower real-time factor (0.34 vs. 0.38) and one quarter of the model size. A sixth experiment adapts a 1.7B LLM into an on-device meeting-minutes model: trained on a three-layer recipe of real-meeting distillation, synthetic expansion, and boundary negatives, one defect-driven data iteration raises the clean rate on fabricated to-dos and fabricated owners from 20% to 80% at 98% token-level digit fidelity, and the model quantizes to 1.03 GiB, closing the remaining text-level privacy gap at draft quality. The complete system has been deployed and validated in real-world usage, including hour-long full-load recordings on a commodity phone.

title: Fast Simulation Algorithms for OLH using Binomial Modeling
abstract: Optimized Local Hashing (OLH) is a widely used hash-based Local Differential Privacy (LDP) protocol, and simulation-based experimentation is the standard approach for evaluating OLH and OLH-based applications in research. However, the existing OLH simulations have $O(nd)$ computational complexity, where $n$ is the user population size and $d$ is the domain size, and can lead to significant execution times as $n$ and $d$ grow. In this paper, we propose two fast simulation algorithms for OLH (2-Binom and 3-Binom) grounded in Binomial modeling. Our key insight is that, for any domain value $v$, the total number of users whose perturbed reports support $v$ can be decomposed into a sum of two or three Binomial random variables. Using this insight, our algorithms reduce the simulation complexity to $O(n + d)$ without hurting statistical equivalence. In particular, we theoretically prove that both algorithms yield unbiased frequency estimations with variances identical to those of the original OLH simulations. Experiments on real-world datasets confirm that both approaches reduce execution times from several minutes to milliseconds, yielding significant speedups with no change in utility.

title: Fixed-Marginal Quantum Instruments and Hidden Feedback Frames
abstract: We construct equiprobable qubit instruments whose outcome probabilities and non-selective channel remain fixed while a hidden conditional feedback frame changes. The archive contains exact tight-frame and recovery results, a self-calibrated character-spectrum readout, verification code, and an unmitigated Rigetti endpoint benchmark. The benchmark is explicitly not treated as path-level monodromy or topology evidence.

title: Unified Computational Value Theory
abstract: Unified Computational Value Theory (UCVT) proposes a formal framework that integrates optimization objectives, reward structures, human preferences, scientific selection principles, and intelligent decision making into a single computational paradigm. By postulating that the value of a computational process is determined jointly by the information processed, the experience accumulated, and the context in which the computation occurs, UCVT establishes a concise mathematical relationship: (Information + Experience + Context) -> Computational Value. This relationship is further extended to link value with subsequent action selection, yielding (Information + Experience + Context) -> Value -> Action. UCVT aims to fill a conceptual gap in computer science that has historically focused on "How to compute?" and artificial intelligence on "How to learn?" but has yet to address the deeper question of "What is worth computing?" The theory offers a potential foundation for next‑generation computational sciences, complementing classical theories such as computation theory, information theory, and learning theory. The paper develops the core principles of UCVT, presents a rigorous mathematical formalism, discusses possible applications across autonomous systems, economic modeling, and human‑machine interaction, and outlines future research directions including the emerging field of Computational Personality Science.

title: Computational Self-Forgetting Theory (CSFT-3)
abstract: The rapid growth of data streams and the increasing demand for lifelong learning in autonomous systems necessitate mechanisms that can maintain model relevance over time. Computational Self-Forgetting Theory (CSFT-3) proposes that adaptive systems should actively delete outdated internal representations—so‑called self‑models—rather than passively accumulating knowledge. CSFT-3 formalizes self‑forgetting as an optimization problem where the system evaluates the marginal utility of each component of its internal state and prunes those that no longer contribute positively to future performance. This paper develops the mathematical foundation of CSFT-3, presents an algorithmic architecture that integrates self‑forgetting into standard machine learning pipelines, and demonstrates its potential impact on long‑term adaptability, resource efficiency, and alignment with Turing Award‑level research on artificial general intelligence.

title: Unified Computational World Model Theory (UCWMT)
abstract: The evolution of computing has followed a linear trajectory: data → information → knowledge → intelligence. The next logical leap is knowledge → world model → understanding. Unified Computational World Model Theory (UCWMT) proposes a rigorous mathematical framework that unifies perception, learning, reasoning, simulation, and scientific discovery into a single computational process. The theory is grounded in the core hypothesis that intelligence is the continual refinement of a compressible, predictive, and controllable world model. UCWMT formalizes this as the mapping (Observation + Knowledge + Interaction) → World Model → Prediction → Discovery. The theory integrates existing computational paradigms while predicting novel computational phenomena such as automatic paradigm discovery and self‑generative algorithmic exploration. This paper lays out the mathematical foundations, explores implications for artificial intelligence and cognitive science, and outlines a research agenda that extends UCWMT to a science of computational paradigm discovery.

title: The Null Token Knows: Reducing Message-Free Hallucination in ASR and NMT
abstract: Modern encoder-decoder systems can produce fluent text even when their input contains no recoverable message. We study this failure in ASR and NMT through the models' reserved null tokens, asking whether the score for ending generation already carries a usable abstention signal. Across speech recognizers and translation models, we audit native null-token scores and scalar logit shifts. In Whisper, we additionally probe decoder states and compare supervised row edits with conventional external gates. The evaluated models often expose a useful abstention signal, but stock decoding does not reliably act on it. Raising the null-token score can sharply suppress fabrication, but aggressive intervention also deletes valid speech or shortens legitimate translations. These findings turn the null token into a diagnostic lens on hallucination and motivate evaluating abstention methods by both suppression and deletion costs, rather than by hallucination reduction alone.

title: Computational World Model Singularity Theory (CWMS)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational World Model Singularity Theory (CWMS), a framework for understanding how autonomous systems that iteratively refine their internal representations of the environment can approach a singularity in model quality. We formalize the notion of a world model as a mapping function M_t that predicts future observations given current states and actions. The core innovation is a recursive enhancement loop in which each updated model M_{t+1} is used to generate new training data for the next iteration, yielding an exponential growth in predictive accuracy. By analyzing the convergence properties of this loop, we derive conditions under which the model quality Q(M) reaches a fixed point or diverges toward a superintelligent regime. The theory bridges concepts from reinforcement learning, probabilistic modeling, and computational complexity, suggesting a pathway to Turing Award level contributions. We discuss the implications of CWMS for the emergence of artificial general intelligence, the ethical considerations of rapidly improving models, and potential future research directions.

title: Iterative Self-Learning for Expressive Text-to-Speech Synthesis
abstract: Expressive text-to-speech (TTS) systems that use explicit conditioning labels provide direct and interpretable control over expressive attributes, in contrast to reference-based or prompting-based approaches, but require labeled data. Obtaining these labels at scale is costly and time-consuming, yet no prior semi-supervised framework addresses this specific bottleneck. Existing semi-supervised TTS methods instead target scarcity of paired speech-text data or transcriptions. To address the scarcity of expressive labels, we propose an Iterative Self-Learning (ISL) framework for expressive TTS, built on Invert-Classify, a classifier-free method that recovers discrete expressive labels by inverting a frozen generative model. The framework iteratively pseudo-labels unlabeled speech using the current model, retrains on the combined labeled and pseudo-labeled data, and repeats, progressively refining label quality and synthesis. We validate on two expressive tasks, word-level prominence and utterance-level emotion, across multiple low-resource data splits. We find that iterative refinement can improve pseudo-label accuracy over single-pass baselines. Furthermore, we observe that these improvements in pseudo-labeling of expressivity translate to gains in expressive label adherence and synthesis quality, confirmed by objective metrics and human listening tests. In the most data-scarce conditions, ISL-trained models outperform single-pass pseudo-labeling and further approach fully supervised performance, demonstrating that gradient-based ISL is an effective solution to expressive label scarcity in low-resource TTS.

title: Computational Representation Fusion Theory (CRFT)
abstract: Computational Representation Fusion Theory (CRFT) introduces a unified mathematical framework for integrating heterogeneous representations—namely vectors, graphs, and logical expressions—into a coherent new form that preserves semantic fidelity while enabling novel computational capabilities. By formalizing a fusion operator that maps tuples of representations into a joint space, CRFT establishes algebraic properties such as associativity, distributivity, and invertibility under specific constraints. This theory offers a principled basis for designing next‑generation artificial intelligence systems that can seamlessly combine low‑level perceptual embeddings, relational knowledge graphs, and symbolic reasoning modules. The paper presents the core principles, formal definitions, illustrative examples, and discusses the potential impact of CRFT on AI architecture and its candidacy for transformative recognition within the field.

title: A Silent Diacritic-Collapse Regression in the Ollama Runtime (mxbai-embed-large), Surfaced by Latent Space Cartography of Wikidata
abstract: We report a previously undocumented defect in how the Ollama runtime serves mxbai-embed-large,one of the most widely used open-source text embedding models: on every release from v0.14.0(2026-01-10) onward, diacritic-bearing input collapses into a single [UNK]-dominated attractor re-gion, producing 969,622 cross-entity embedding pairs at cosine similarity ≥ 0.95 in our 100,113-embedding Wikidata corpus. "Hokkaid¯o", "Éire", "Djazaïr", and "Filast.¯ın" — unrelated words indifferent languages — do not merely embed similarly: the runtime returns byte-identical vectorsfor them (cosine similarity exactly 1.0, because the returned floats are equal), while "Hokkaid¯o" hascosine similarity of only 0.45 with its own ASCII equivalent "Hokkaido". The failure is silent (theruntime returns a confident-looking vector and raises no error) and benchmark-invisible (MTEB andsimilar suites do not probe diacritic-rich input at scale), so any RAG system, semantic search engine,or knowledge graph application serving this model through an affected Ollama version has silentlydegraded on non-ASCII text since 2026-01-10. Crucially, the defect is not in the model: the iden-tical registry blob is healthy on Ollama ≤ v0.13.4 (diacritical collision rate ≈ 0, indistinguishablefrom an ASCII control), and a version bisection over 21 Ollama releases localizes the regressionprecisely to the v0.13.4 → v0.14.0 runtime boundary.We found this defect not by targeted fuzzing but as a byproduct of latent space cartography —the systematic mapping of structure in pre-trained embedding spaces (Liu et al., 2019). We applystandard TransE-style relational displacement analysis (Bordes et al., 2013) to frozen (non-KGE)embeddings, sweeping over all predicates reachable by breadth-first traversal of a Wikidata knowl-edge graph; seeding from a Japanese historical text (Engishiki) naturally reaches the romanized,diacritic-rich terminology that standard benchmarks never touch. Applied to mxbai-embed-large(1024-dim), nomic-embed-text (768-dim), and all-minilm (384-dim) — all three embedding thebyte-identical frozen text set — the procedure identifies 33 relations that encode as consistent vectordisplacements across all three models, confirming these are properties of the semantic relationshipsrather than artifacts of any single model. A correlation between geometric consistency and predic-tion accuracy holds in mxbai-embed-large (r = 0.882, 95% CI [0.803, 0.940]) and reproduces inall-minilm (r = 0.804), more weakly in nomic-embed-text (r = 0.430). The same systematic probingthat maps an embedding space's relational structure also surfaces the regions where it silently fails.All code, data, and the version-bisection harness are publicly available.

title: Designing Quantum Error Correcting Codes to fit decoders via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We present a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to the co-design of stabilizer sets of Quantum Error Correcting Codes (QECCs) and decoders. We show how to produce a generative model that produces Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes based on the choice of decoder. Specifically, we fix a decoder architecture and use Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) to train an agent over BB codes to maximise decoder performance under a depolarising channel noise model.

title: 未提供标题
abstract: Aiming at scattered knowledge sources, inconsistent entity expressions and insufficient relation extraction accuracy in food pairing, this paper proposes a food pairing knowledge graph construction method integrating large language models and relation completion.A domain ontology covering dishes, ingredients, nutrients, dietary restrictions, applicable populations and health goals is designed.Candidate entities and relations are then extracted from recipe texts, nutrition descriptions and dietary-restriction materials using a large language model, and entity normalization is performed through a domain dictionary and semantic embeddings.Finally, a relation scoring function integrating LLM confidence, semantic similarity and domain rules is used to filter, review and complete candidate triples.Experiments on a food pairing corpus show that the proposed method achieves a relation extraction F1 score of 88.71%, which is 6.05 percentage points higher than direct LLM extraction, and obtains a human-verified accuracy of 87.33% for completed relations.The results indicate that the proposed method can provide a reliable structured knowledge base for healthy diet recommendation and food pairing question answering.

title: Computational Causal Singularity Theory (CCS)
abstract: Computational Causal Singularity Theory (CCS) proposes a unified mathematical and algorithmic framework for modeling, discovering, and manipulating causal structures in high‑dimensional data streams. The theory integrates recursive machine learning with formal causal calculus to achieve a self‑enhancing causal inference system. At its core lies a simple yet powerful recursion: Cause → Better Cause, whereby a system refines its causal understanding by repeatedly applying causal discovery algorithms to its own output. CCS formalizes this recursion using a family of transformation operators T_k that map a causal graph G_k to a more accurate graph G_{k+1}. The theory further introduces the concept of a causal singularity, defined as a fixed point of the recursion where additional iterations produce no measurable improvement. We demonstrate that under mild conditions the recursion converges to a singularity that captures the true underlying causal mechanisms. The implications of CCS for artificial general intelligence are profound: a system that can autonomously refine its causal model may achieve a level of reasoning comparable to human experts, thereby opening the door to Turing Award‑worthy contributions. This paper develops the formal foundations of CCS, discusses its potential impact on AI, and outlines future research directions.

title: Quantum Bridge
abstract: Professional Biophysics Platform for Preventive Precision Medicine An advanced hybrid computational engine that models, evaluates, and corrects microscopic mechanical strains in genetic switches. Quantum Bridge integrates QED-grounded tensor analysis, Shannon entropy topography, and Riemannian manifold monitoring with direct hardware execution on IBM Quantum QPUs via Qiskit Runtime. Featuring real-time 3D Hilbert × lattice visualization, complementary state transformations, and thermodynamic stability governance, it provides researchers with an academically defensible platform for precision genomic stability.

title: Risk-Aware Density–Boundary Graph Reweighting for Rare Event Detection in Intelligent Risk Monitoring Systems
abstract: Rare-event detection is a critical task in intelligent risk monitoring systems, where missed minority events may lead to financial loss, security threats, or operational failures. Existing imbalance-handling methods frequently apply one class-level correction and therefore ignore the heterogeneous geometric roles of minority observations. This study presents density–boundary graph reweighting (DBGR), a unified sample-level weighting framework that combines continuous minority sparsity and majority-boundary exposure and regularizes the resulting scores through a minority-only K-nearest-neighbor graph. Its methodological contribution lies in this joint pre-training formulation and in producing classifier-compatible weights, rather than in claiming novelty for density estimation, graph propagation, or weighting individually. Two variants are considered: DBGR-Safe for sparse and relatively safe minority prototypes and DBGR-Danger for sparse boundary observations. Experiments on financial fraud detection, industrial fault diagnosis, and network intrusion detection show recall-oriented gains with XGBoost and reduced variability for the tested LightGBM setting, while the benefit is limited for Random Forest. On Creditcard, DBGR-Danger improves Recall from 0.8223 to 0.8949 and F2 from 0.8410 to 0.8931. On NSL-KDD U2R, focal loss remains better in Recall, F2, and PR-AUC, whereas DBGR-Safe achieves the best F1. DBGR is therefore positioned as a complementary, classifier-compatible strategy rather than a universally superior imbalance-handling method.

title: Comprehensive Benchmarking of Deep Learning Architectures for Lung Cancer Histopathology
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, while histopathological diagnosis is often affected by inter-observer variability and the substantial workload associated with manual slide examination. Although deep learning has shown considerable potential in computational pathology, comprehensive benchmarks that integrate tissue classification and region segmentation within a unified analytical framework remain limited. This study presents a two-stage deep learning framework for multi-class tissue classification and pixel-level histopathological region segmentation, accompanied by a systematic comparison of state-of-the-art architectures at each stage. For tissue classification, six models, a custom convolutional neural network, VGG16, DenseNet, MobileNetV3, a custom Vision Transformer, and YOLO11, are evaluated on a combined dataset of 39,000 images derived from LC25000 and LungHist700. The models distinguish between adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and normal lung tissue. YOLO11 achieves the best classification performance, with an accuracy of 98.38%, a five-fold cross-validation accuracy of 98.21 +/- 0.35%, and a macro F1-score of 0.98. For region segmentation, U-Net, ResNet-encoder U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and YOLO11-seg are evaluated using the GlaS gland segmentation benchmark. DeepLabV3+ obtains the highest Intersection over Union of 0.80 and a Dice score of 0.89, while YOLO11-seg achieves a comparable Intersection over Union of 0.79 using approximately 14x fewer parameters. The best-performing classification and segmentation models are subsequently integrated into an end-to-end framework, providing an accurate, computationally efficient, and reproducible baseline for automated histopathological image analysis.

title: BreakRL: Reinforcement Learning Fundamentals
abstract: A Chinese-language, ablation-driven textbook on reinforcement learning. Each of the 14 chapters pairs a written derivation (PDF) with reproducible experiments in which key mechanisms are removed so readers can watch the algorithm fail. Covers bandits, MDPs, temporal-difference learning, DQN, policy gradients, Actor-Critic, PPO, SAC, offline RL (CQL/IQL), model-based RL (Dyna-Q), Decision Transformer, and the LLM post-training trilogy (RLHF, DPO, GRPO/RLVR), plus a 17-entry failure atlas organized as symptom, mechanism, reproduction, and fix. Text is CC BY 4.0; notebook code is MIT.

title: Computational Goal Ecology Theory: A Framework for Understanding Multi‑Goal Dynamics in Intelligent Systems
abstract: The rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence demands a unifying theory that can capture the complex interactions among multiple goals pursued by autonomous agents. Computational Goal Ecology Theory (CGE) proposes such a framework by modeling agents as goal‑oriented entities operating within a dynamic ecosystem of competing, cooperating, and eliminating forces. In CGE, a global goal set G = {g1, g2, …, gK} is shared among agents, each with a private utility function Ui(G). The state of each agent i at time t is represented by Si(t), and its action Ai(t) drives the transition of state according to a function Fi. The theory formalizes competition through pairwise utility differentials, cooperation via joint utility maximization, and elimination when an agent's utility falls below a threshold. The dynamics of the system are captured by the differential equation dUi/dt = α Σj wij (Uj − Ui) + β Ci − γ Ei, where w is an interaction weight matrix, Ci denotes cooperative benefits, and Ei represents elimination pressures. By analyzing the stability of equilibria and the conditions for emergent coordination, CGE provides a mathematical lens through which to predict collective behavior in heterogeneous agent populations. The theory's potential for addressing fundamental questions in autonomous system design, its alignment with core principles of artificial general intelligence, and its capacity to guide the development of future intelligent societies underscore its significance. This paper presents the core ideas of CGE, develops its formal underpinnings, explores its dynamical properties, and discusses its implications for the broader AI community, including its potential to contribute to the next Turing Award.

title: Computational World Model Boundary Theory (CWMBT)
abstract: Computational World Model Boundary Theory (CWMBT) proposes a unified framework for understanding the limits and capabilities of models that attempt to comprehend the world. By formalizing the boundary between the known and unknown aspects of reality, CWMBT offers a set of principles that delineate what a model can and cannot capture. The theory is built upon a rigorous set of definitions, axioms, and derived theorems that explore the interaction between model structure, data availability, and epistemic uncertainty. The goal of this work is to provide a conceptual foundation that can guide the design of intelligent systems, highlight the potential for Turing Award‑level contributions, and illuminate the ultimate boundaries of machine understanding.

title: Computational World Model Causal Generation Theory (CWMCGT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational World Model Causal Generation Theory (CWMCGT), a framework that transforms observational correlations into actionable causal models suitable for intervention planning. By formalizing the progression from correlation to causation through a set of mathematically grounded operators, CWMCGT constructs a generative world model that can simulate the effect of arbitrary interventions. The theory leverages structural causal modeling, counterfactual inference, and reinforcement learning concepts to produce a unified representation of the environment that can be queried for both predictive and prescriptive purposes. The core contribution lies in the explicit definition of the causal generation operators and the algorithmic pipeline that realizes them, enabling an AI system to understand and manipulate its world in a principled causal manner. This capability addresses one of the most persistent challenges in artificial intelligence—deep understanding of causal mechanisms—and has the potential to elevate AI systems to a level of reasoning comparable to human causal inference, thereby positioning the framework as a candidate for high-level recognition such as the Turing Award.

title: Deep Learning-Assisted Accuracy Improvement in Bladder Cancer Staging of Spectrum-Aided Visual Enhanced Cystoscopy Images
abstract: Recent statistics reported by the World Health Organization and the International Agency for Research on Cancer indicate that the global incidence of bladder cancer has continued to increase in recent years, particularly in industrialized countries. Therefore, the timely diagnosis of early-stage bladder cancer is of great clinical importance for improving patient prognosis and treatment outcomes. In this context, computational optical sensing frameworks that integrate Spectrum-Aided Visual Enhancer (SAVE) technology with cystoscopy have attracted significant attention to overcome the limitations of conventional visual data interpretation. In this study, an AI-driven optical biosensing framework was evaluated using 1372 white-light cystoscopy (WLC) images of bladder cancer (RGB-WLC) collected in collaboration with Chung Shan Medical University Hospital. Hyperspectral conversion technology was applied to extract precise spectral information from the white-light images. Subsequently, dimensionality reduction was performed based on the characteristic wavelengths of narrow-band imaging cystoscopy at 415 nm and 540 nm to generate hyperspectral reconstructed narrow-band images. The images were categorized into Ta stage (Ta), above T1 stage (Above T1), and four additional classes. The dataset was divided into training and testing sets to establish both a standard white-light cystoscopy model (RGB-WLC) and an advanced hyperspectral biosensing model utilizing the YOLOv8 architecture for enhanced pattern recognition. Model performance was evaluated using sensitivity, F1-score, and overall accuracy. The standard RGB-WLC model achieved an accuracy of 0.852, whereas the SAVE-based biosensing model achieved an accuracy of 0.948, representing an improvement of approximately 11.27%. The results demonstrate that combining algorithmic hyperspectral reconstruction with deep learning architectures effectively addresses the challenges of clinical data interpretation and significantly enhances the detection and staging performance of bladder cancer imaging.

title: Beyond Independence: Learning Correlated Views for Variational Incomplete Multi-View Clustering
abstract: Incomplete multi-view clustering (IMVC) aims to uncover shared cluster structures from data with partially observed views. Although recent imputation-free methods based on variational inference demonstrate robustness to missing views, they commonly rely on a conditional independence assumption across views in the posterior aggregation stage, which fails to capture the inherently structured and potentially correlated nature of multi-view data. In this paper, we propose a variational framework that explicitly goes beyond this assumption by introducing a learnable cross-view correlation structure. Specifically, we explicitly model and learn correlations between views by utilizing the covariance structure of posterior estimation errors during aggregation. To facilitate robust and efficient learning, the correlation matrix is parameterized through a normalized Cholesky decomposition, ensuring positive definiteness and enabling the entire model to be trained jointly through a unified variational objective. Extensive experiments on multiple IMVC benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse missing-view settings while introducing only a negligible number of learnable parameters. These results highlight the effectiveness of adaptive correlation modeling in variational IMVC, demonstrating the need to go beyond the independence assumption in IMVC. The code is available at https://github.com/zmxu196/ACOVA.

title: CRESCENDO Control-Transform Certificates: Machine-Checked Dispatch Elimination (Isabelle/HOL)
abstract: Machine-checked Isabelle/HOL proofs that dispatch elimination — specializing an interpreter on a fixed run-time-loaded program by removing opcode dispatch — is exactly correct for programs of arbitrary length, proved by induction. Covers an accumulator machine and a stack bytecode VM (with an explicit well-formedness side condition and stack-shape invariant). The control-specialization analogue of the CRESCENDO div-specialization (value) certificate. Verified under Isabelle2021, zero sorry, clean from-scratch build. Toy interpreter models demonstrating the certificate methodology transfers from value to control specialization.

title: Git-Style DAG-Based Branching Reasoning Architecture
abstract: This is an informal short note / early draft.This short note proposes a dual-model agent architecture. A main model follows a main reasoning branch; an evaluator model reviews key decisions and greedily spawns optimized branches that evolve alongside the main branch and periodically promote or merge back. The reasoning trace forms a Git-style DAG, with each node as one user-model conversation linked by parent pointers. Branches are first-class objects the model can read, write, and manage. Branch value combines quality, novelty, and UCB-style exploration bonus.

title: Reproducibility Artifacts for Semantic Representation and Rule-Based Interpretation of Finite Element Simulation Evidence
abstract: This repository contains reproducibility artifacts supporting the study “Semantic Representation and Rule-Based Interpretation of Finite Element Simulation Evidence.” The package provides an RDF/Turtle knowledge graph, executable SPARQL competency queries, query-result files, a validation summary, and a Python script for regenerating and validating the semantic artifacts. The RDF graph contains 221 triples representing 16 memory-parameter simulations, three graphite-surrogate simulations, and four direct-versus-recursive timing experiments, together with numerical observations, computational-method relations, and rule-derived semantic interpretations. The accompanying Python script rebuilds the RDF graph, executes the three SPARQL competency queries, regenerates their result files, and checks the expected graph size, query memberships, and rule outcomes. The package is intended as an implementation-level reproducibility resource for the numerical-to-semantic workflow described in the associated study.

title: Code and experiment archives for "Enforcing Graph-Relative Structural Compliance in LLM-Based Industrial Anomaly Explanation via Causal Graph Grounding"
abstract: Code and experiment archives for the manuscript "Enforcing Graph-Relative Structural Compliance in LLM-Based Industrial Anomaly Explanation via Causal Graph Grounding". The package contains the full research pipeline: a synthetic SCM generator; the PCMCI causal-discovery pipeline with exact-reproduction scripts for the SWaT and WADI discovery runs (51->28 retained dimensions, 230 cross-variable edges); an LLM backend implementing edge-set grounding (enum hard constraint via JSON-schema structured output with client-side validation, plus soft-prompt variants); run scripts for all reported experiments, including 30-seed degree-matched random-graph controls, the honest-boundary audit, evidence-table injection, and four-vendor cross-replication (Alibaba, DeepSeek, Zhipu, Moonshot); per-run JSON and log archives; and the raw per-rater CSV files of the human study (14 raters). The synthetic benchmark is self-contained; SWaT and WADI require a licence from iTrust, SUTD and are not redistributed. All seeds are fixed; see README.md for entry points and results/RUNS_2026_METADATA.md for model snapshot identifiers. License: MIT.Version 2 adds per-seed experiment archives and scripts E32-E41 (evidence-table CI re-run, rewire-overlap audit, agreement coefficients, structure-fault arms, allowed-set coverage with wrong-candidate sensitivity, honest-boundary reconstructions, cap-policy and prompt-metric comparisons, size-matched correlation control, and seed extensions). Version 3 accompanies the revised, retitled Expert Systems submission: it adds the WADI variable re-selection with unit-invariant criteria and the first WADI event-level evaluation (E42), a graph-drift probe (E43), structured numeric-claim fields (E44), an abstention 15-window extension (E45), the WADI unit-invariant compliance arm for the main table (E46), a root-incident-edge true-gap probe (E47), a unified WADI A1/A2 pipeline (E48), the extended WaDi.A2 release evaluation (E49), and the revised manuscript sources.
