title: GAINS: Leveraging Inconsistent Human Intervention Signals in Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Correcting robot manipulation policies through human intervention holds great promise for real-world deployment, yet human operators are inherently imperfect in both the actions they provide and the timing of their intervention signals. While the former has been extensively discussed in reinforcement learning (RL), the latter remains underexplored. At high control frequencies, human intervention signals are often delayed and inconsistent across time and state space. In this work, we present GAINS, a framework for leveraging inconsistent human intervention signals in RL. At the core of GAINS, we employ distributional RL with quantile Q-networks to model the return variability induced by sparse task rewards and inconsistent human interventions. Building on this distributional representation, we introduce a pessimistic exploration strategy that promotes safe and sample-efficient learning under human corrections. We evaluate GAINS on four diverse simulated manipulation tasks and two challenging real-world scenarios against state-of-the-art intervention-based methods. GAINS achieves a 22% higher task success rate than RLIF and improves recovery success by up to 43% in failure scenarios. These results highlight the importance of modeling return variability induced by human imperfection for real-world deployment of intervention-based learning.

abstract: General large language models suffer from factual hallucinations, mismatched expression difficulty and insufficient individual adaptation in science education question-and-answer (Q&A) tasks.To address these issues, this paper proposes a personalized popular science Q&A generation method integrating difficulty-aware retrieval-augmented generation.Firstly, a scientific knowledge base with academic stage difficulty labels is constructed in this method.Secondly, learner portrait matching items and knowledge difficulty deviation penalty items are introduced into the traditional semantic retrieval score to realize evidence screening for students in different academic stages.In the generation stage, structured prompts are organized with retrieved evidence, student portraits and answer constraints, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning is adopted to enhance the model's adaptability to popular science Q&A style and knowledge boundaries.Taking a self-built primary and secondary school science Q&A dataset as the research object, experiments are conducted from the dimensions of scientific accuracy, age appropriateness, completeness and hallucination rate.The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms conventional retrieval-augmented methods in terms of scientific accuracy and age appropriateness, and can improve the reliability and teaching applicability of popular science Q&A with low training costs.

title: Boundary Information Theory (BIT) — Theorems and Formal Results, Volume I
abstract: Boundary Information Theory (BIT) — Theorems and Formal Results, Volume I is an independently developed research compilation by Bùi Quang Trịnh, Hà Nội, Việt Nam. The volume collects theorem-level statements, analytic cores, derived and specialized results, supporting propositions and certificates developed within the BIT research program. Each entry preserves its assumptions, proof spine, evidence status, scope, failure conditions and claim boundary. The collection explicitly distinguishes analytic validity, synthetic or bounded computational evidence, proof-assistant mechanization, field validation and novelty. Inclusion in this volume does not imply peer review, independent validation, physical universality or scientific-standard status unless explicitly stated for an individual result. This release is deposited as an archival research object so that the work can be read, cited, criticized, reproduced and extended independently.

title: A Influência da Inteligência Artificial na Legislação Patentária
abstract: Esta pesquisa aborda como tema as transformações nos mecanismos de proteção da propriedade intelectual e os desafios da legislação patentária diante do avanço da Inteligência Artificial (IA) na Quarta Revolução Industrial. O objetivo do estudo é examinar o panorama da proteção jurídica de softwares e tecnologias de IA, contrastando as vias do direito autoral e da propriedade industrial, bem como investigar as tendências globais de patenteamento e o caso prático da Uber Technologies INC.. A metodologia adotada compreende uma abordagem qualitativa de caráter exploratório e descritivo, fundamentada em pesquisa bibliográfica, análise documental de legislações e relatórios da Organização Mundial da Propriedade Intelectual (OMPI/WIPO), além de levantamento de dados patentários nas bases Questel-Orbit e Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial (INPI). Como principais resultados e discussões, evidencia-se a predominância de técnicas como Machine Learning e visão computacional nos depósitos globais de patentes liderados por corporações internacionais; no cenário brasileiro, constata-se que, para além da proteção autoral do código-fonte, empresas utilizam a redação de patentes de soluções integradas (software e hardware) para assegurar a exclusividade de processos e ativos de mercado, conforme demonstrado na evolução do portfólio da Uber no país. Conclui-se que o dinamismo da IA e dos modelos de negócios digitais demanda uma evolução na tutela jurídica e na legislação patentária nacional para além dos moldes autorais tradicionais, garantindo maior segurança e competitividade aos ativos intelectuais da indústria 4.0.

title: Sub-shot-noise infrared gas concentration sensing via coincidence detection of quantum-correlated photons
abstract: Infrared absorption sensing is a widely adopted technique for gas concentration sensing in environmental monitoring, industrial inspection, and safety applications. However, the precision of concentration estimation based on classical optical probes is fundamentally limited by shot noise. Here, we demonstrate a gas concentration sensing approach using quantum-correlated photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Acetylene is employed as a benchmark analyte to characterize the concentration-transmittance relationship and to evaluate sensing precision over its explosive concentration range. Compared with an ideal coherent-state probe having the same mean photon number, the quantum protocol achieves sub-shot-noise performance in concentration estimation. Our results establish a practical framework for applying quantum-correlated light to high-precision gas concentration sensing and open new opportunities for quantum infrared gas sensing.

title: Analisis Persepsi Kesiapsiagaan Potensi Megathrust Selatan Jawa Menggunakan Integrasi Latent Dirichlet Allocation dan Support Vector Machine
abstract: Potensi gempa megathrust di selatan Jawa memunculkan beragam respons masyarakat di media sosial, namun penelitian sebelumnya umumnya berhenti pada klasifikasi sentimen tanpa mengaitkannya dengan aspek kesiapsiagaan bencana. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengidentifikasi topik diskusi publik, mengklasifikasikan sentimen masyarakat, serta mengintegrasikan keduanya untuk menginterpretasikan persepsi kesiapsiagaan masyarakat. Data berupa 5.235 komentar pada unggahan Instagram resmi BMKG tanggal 14 Agustus 2024. Tahapan analisis meliputi praproses, pemodelan topik dengan Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), klasifikasi sentimen dengan Support Vector Machine (SVM), serta pascaproses dengan Word2Vec dan cosine similarity untuk mengaitkan topik dengan indikator kesiapsiagaan LIPI–UNESCO/ISDR. Model SVM mencapai akurasi tertinggi 0,87 pada pembagian data latih dan uji 90:10. Topik 0 memiliki kedekatan semantik tertinggi dengan indikator Sistem Peringatan Bencana (cosine similarity 0,9238), sedangkan Topik 1 dengan indikator Pengetahuan dan Sikap Risiko (0,9111). Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa integrasi LDA dan SVM yang didukung Word2Vec dan cosine similarity dapat digunakan untuk memetakan persepsi kesiapsiagaan masyarakat melalui keterkaitan antara sentimen, topik pembahasan, dan indikator kesiapsiagaan, sehingga dapat menjadi masukan bagi perbaikan komunikasi risiko kebencanaan.

title: The Mixed-Group Framework and Algebraic Residual Iteration (ARI): From Structural Unification to Efficient Learning
abstract: This work introduces the mixed group \mathcal{H}_D(\gamma,p), which unifies the real space \mathbb{R}^D and the finite field \mathbb{F}_p^D at the group level via the unified operation \oplus_\gamma and the double-derivation operator D_\gamma. The exponential lift operator E_{\gamma,g} is further defined, establishing an exact algebraic correspondence between continuous exponential maps and the discrete logarithm problem over finite fields. We develop Algebraic Residual Iteration (ARI), a gradient-free universal approximation and solving paradigm. ARI uses closed-form least squares and algebraic residual iteration, achieving global optimality at each subproblem, avoiding local minima, reaching millisecond-level speed, and naturally supporting parallelization and meta-learning. Experiments verify the mixed-group homomorphism, ARI function approximation, discrete logarithm learning, XOR nonlinear classification robustness, and ARI's sensitivity to prime algebraic structure: on smooth-order groups (Fermat prime p=257), bitwise prediction reaches 100% accuracy; on safe primes, only the least significant bit is predictable, while the second bit is indistinguishable from random, consistent with the Blum-Micali hard-core predicate theorem. This work provides new theoretical tools and experimental paradigms for the intersection of algebraic machine learning and cryptography. All code and raw data are included for full reproducibility.

title: The Watchdog That Never Sleeps: Governor, Deterministic Supervision for Runaway AI Agents
abstract: Every team running agentic AI loops eventually lives the same scene: the session degenerates at 2am, the meter runs all night, and the only kill switch is a human who is asleep. Static limits (max_tokens, max_iterations, budget caps) answer the wrong question. They ask how long a run is, not whether it is going anywhere, so they behead healthy 200-step research runs while a pathological loop that stays under budget per step runs forever. The obvious modern fix, asking a second model to supervise the first, imports the problem it is meant to solve: an LLM supervisor can itself loop, hallucinate, and rate-limit, and when it kills a session nobody can say precisely why. This paper presents Governor, an open-source runaway-session governor for LLM agent loops, named after the mechanical governor on a steam engine: a dumb, deterministic device that caps speed without understanding the engine. Nine deterministic detectors watch surface behavior (repeated text, repeated calls, repeated errors, growing prompts, silent token burn, missing progress) and move a five-rung ladder: OK, WARN, THROTTLE, PAUSE, KILL. No model is called anywhere in the safety path. The design is defined by asymmetries: escalation is immediate and may jump rungs, de-escalation is slow and earned through hysteresis, PAUSE never lifts itself, and a model that asks to be killed reaches a human, never the kill switch, under every policy. Evidence, not authority. The system is small and exhaustively tested (109 unit tests, a 13/13 scenario scorecard where half the scenarios exist to prove the governor does nothing on healthy runs, ~0.4ms overhead per event) and its findings are unusually candid. An audit of the first version, written by a different AI model, found six defects sharing one shape: the safety property was stated in a docstring and enforced nowhere, including a path by which a model could order its own execution. Live experiments across five labs then overturned the design's implicit assumptions: real stuck models never repeat themselves lexically (similarity 0.000 to 0.056 against a 0.85 threshold) but are caught structurally at step 2 by error signatures; the distress phrase list caught 25% of real phrasings and was rebuilt to a measured 76% with a decoy suite; a flaky vendor exposed a false positive now kept as a permanent guard; and a sleeping laptop revealed that the outermost wall-clock backstop had silently never worked, a bug structurally invisible to every test that injects a fake clock. One boundary is stated rather than solved: a model that fabricates success without looping is invisible to behavioral supervision by construction. Every number traces to a runnable command. Canonical version and interactive ladder: https://sheepdog.systemsCode, scorecard, audit write-up, and full experiment findings: https://github.com/JoaquinDG/governor

title: Computational Principle Generation Network
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Principle Generation Network (CPGN), a novel artificial intelligence framework designed to generate new computational principles from given problem statements. Traditional AI systems excel at pattern recognition and optimization but rarely produce novel theoretical insights. CPGN addresses this limitation by learning a latent representation of known principles and leveraging a transformer‑based encoder‑decoder architecture to map problem descriptions to principled solutions. The network is trained on a curated corpus of mathematical theorems, physical laws, and algorithmic invariants, using a multi‑objective loss that balances fidelity to existing principles with novelty constraints. We present the formal definitions underlying the principle space, the mathematical formulation of the generation process, and an analysis of the network's expressive capacity. Theoretical results establish that, under mild conditions, CPGN can approximate any computable principle mapping with arbitrary precision. Potential applications span automated theorem proving, scientific hypothesis generation, and the discovery of new algorithmic invariants. By enabling machines to formulate new computational rules, CPGN opens a promising pathway toward a future where artificial systems contribute original theory to mathematics, physics, and computer science.

title: Computational World Model Ecology Theory (CWME)
abstract: The Computational World Model Ecology Theory (CWME) proposes a unified framework for understanding, designing, and evolving artificial world models within a dynamic ecological context. Drawing inspiration from natural ecosystems, CWME introduces a triadic interaction of competition, validation, and fusion among heterogeneous world models. The theory formalizes the lifecycle of world models as agents that evolve through selection pressures, cross-validation mechanisms, and collaborative integration, thereby enhancing robustness, adaptability, and generalization. By articulating explicit mathematical representations of fitness, interaction, and fusion functions in plain text, CWME offers a scalable blueprint for future scientific computation systems that could potentially achieve the prestige of a Turing Award. This paper outlines the core concepts, formalizes the ecological dynamics, and discusses the implications for the next generation of computational intelligence.

title: Logos: Certified Order-Sensitive SQL Rewrites with Mechanized Semantics and LLM Guidance
abstract: SQL rewrite verification must account for duplicate rows, observable row order, and typed value semantics. Existing verifiers have yet to combine proofs over database instances of arbitrary finite cardinality with an ordered-list semantics for nested, tie-sensitive top-k. Unbounded systems reason primarily over bags or handle ordering through syntax-directed restrictions, whereas bounded systems either support only restricted top-k forms or impose a deterministic ordering rather than retain all legal tie-induced outcomes. Support for typed expression and aggregate semantics, observable runtime errors, and integrity constraints also remains partial. In Rocq, we mechanize a compositional logical semantics for a typed SQL core with order-sensitive operators, capturing all possible ordered lists and observable SQL failures in the supported fragment. To our knowledge, this is the first mechanized SQL semantics to combine nested, tie-sensitive top-k with a closure-based lifting from bag equivalence to ordered-list equivalence, enabling sound reuse of bag-theoretic reasoning while preserving compositionality across order-sensitive and correlated contexts. The formalization further provides executable semantics for PostgreSQL-oriented scalar and aggregate evaluation and an explicit account of integrity constraints. Building on this semantics, we present Logos, an LLM-guided Rocq verifier for unbounded SQL rewrite equivalence. Its agent uses a verified SQL-specific lemma library to construct query-specific Rocq proofs. Our evaluation covers 389 query pairs from Apache Calcite optimizer tests, TPC-H and TPC-DS rewrites, and WeTune's real-application workloads. Logos solves 86.9% of them, compared with 64.0% for SQLSolver, the strongest baseline.

title: Evo-Harness: Context-to-Harness Skill Compilation for Self-Evolving Agents
abstract: Learning from experience is critical for developing capable, self-improving large language model (LLM) agents. Existing methods typically extract knowledge from accumulated trajectories via reflection, memory, rules, or skills. However, agents in realistic environments continuously encounter novel tasks, often offering only a one-shot opportunity to improve. These executions yield rich but highly noisy contexts, entangling broadly useful lessons with task-specific artifacts. Critically, prior works rarely validate their effectiveness on complex real-world tasks or isolate the underlying drivers of improvement. To address these gaps, we formulate online harness learning, where a frozen agent improves by continually updating a structured harness across sequential tasks. This formulation enables a systematic study of key self-improvement factors through our proposed Evo-Harness. At its core, context-to-harness skill compilation distills noisy, single-shot executions into reusable skill harnesses for cross-domain and topic-level adaptation. To demonstrate the efficacy of one-shot skill compilation, we evaluate across five realistic benchmarks (TerminalBench2, SWE-bench, CL-Bench, -bench, WebArena-Infinity). Our extensive analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of Evo-Harness and provides a principled understanding of how LLM agents can effectively learn on the fly. Our code is available at https://github.com/A-EVO-Lab/a-evolve/tree/release/evo-harness.

title: Harness the Memory: A Holistic Evaluation of Memory Substrates in Memory Agents
abstract: Memory is becoming core infrastructure for long-horizon LLM agents, yet existing evaluations offer limited guidance on which memory substrate, namely the underlying medium in which memory is represented and stored, should be used under different operating regimes. We present a controlled harness evaluation of memory substrates for memory-augmented agents, covering dense and sparse indices, text records, structural stores, hierarchical stores, refinement-based memories, parametric updates, and activation-compatible context mechanisms. Across three backbone models and four benchmark suites spanning user-centric question answering and agent-centric decision-making, we instrument 26 performance and efficiency metrics under a unified harness. Our results show that no single substrate consistently dominates: broad retrieval benefits long-context factual QA, while excessive retrieval can harm sequential decision-making by shifting attention away from action-critical context. Scalability introduces a further routing axis, as substrates that perform well at moderate history lengths can become costly or brittle at longer horizons. These findings motivate substrate routing as a necessary component of adaptive agent memory systems and provide empirical guidance for designing efficient, reliable, and regime-aware long-term memory for LLM agents. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

We present a controlled harness evaluation of memory substrates for memory-augmented agents, covering dense and sparse indices, text records, structural stores, hierarchical stores, refinement-based memories, parametric updates, and activation-compatible context mechanisms. Across three backbone models and four benchmark suites spanning user-centric question answering and agent-centric decision-making, we instrument 26 performance and efficiency metrics under a unified harness. Our results show that no single substrate consistently dominates: broad retrieval benefits long-context factual QA, while excessive retrieval can harm sequential decision-making by shifting attention away from action-critical context. Scalability introduces a further routing axis, as substrates that perform well at moderate history lengths can become costly or brittle at longer horizons. These findings motivate substrate routing as a necessary component of adaptive agent memory systems and provide empirical guidance for designing efficient, reliable, and regime-aware long-term memory for LLM agents. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

title: Gathered, Not Admitted: How Attention Brings a Latent Variable into Verbalizable Form
abstract: Language models hold latent quantities in a form they can report on, and more of a quantity is present in that form when the task requires reusing it flexibly. What causes a representation to enter that form is open, and the word workspace invites an admission story: a gate that decides what gets in. Testing it on open-weight models with Jacobian lenses, over a benchmark whose five arms share an identical context, we find no gate where it predicts one. Demand raises a concept's lens visibility beyond what applying an operator to a supplied value produces: +0.050 [+0.045, +0.057] in percentile rank on our primary checkpoint, positive on all four we measure, though that arm answers at ceiling and the accuracymatched contrast is stronger under that readout. At the same time one shared linear map decodes the variable from every arm, the control included, at 6.4-9.0x its selection-corrected floor. What produces the later readable form at the queried position is attention-mediated gathering inside a mid-depth window: separating patch depth from readout depth puts transport there at least 17x above anywhere shallower under non-saturating readouts, with no tested MLP output contributing positively inside it. Under the saturating percentile rank the same grid does not localise the window, which is a fact about that measure. An arm that needs the variable for nothing concentrates sevenfold less, so the window is demand-specific. That window has two measured edges, a survival failure below and destruction above, and it falls at the same fractional depth in a 64-layer hybrid and a 62-layer dense model from another family. We localise where the variable is installed and read, not the route from the passage, which transports nothing. But the readout is not a calibrated measure of use: three components move it to within 12% of one another and differ 7.4x in what they do to the answer.

title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a \$15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
abstract: Long-horizon agents can fail even when their underlying models can solve the constituent steps. They may lose track of mutable state, fail to reactivate lessons from earlier executions, skip known procedures, or stop prematurely. We bet on harness scaling to improve the execution system around an agent without changing its model weights. We introduce StateM, an agent-native runtime that organizes execution around durable states, phase-local context, checked transitions, recoverable runbooks, and versioned procedural practices that agents and users can inspect together. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, StateM raises GPT-5.5 xhigh to 92.1\%, versus 83.1\% reference and GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra at 91.9\%. The runbook transfers unchanged to GPT-5.6. With GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh, StateM reaches 95.3\% raw accuracy across 445 trials and succeeds on all 89 tasks at least once. The frozen profile raises GPT-5.6 Luna from 76.7 to 85.4\%, above the 84.9\% Sol xhigh reference. Using the same runtime, runbook structure, and golden rules, less than \$38 of adaptation raises DeepSeek-V4 Flash from 82.7 to 88.1\% under standard timeouts and to 89.1\% on an 88-task common core. Extending only the remaining latency-sensitive task matches the reported 88.8\% GPT-5.6 Sol max result. Final-score API usage is about \$15 versus \$574.68 for the GPT reference; total DeepSeek expenditure is \$52.22. On BusinessBench, family-specific runbooks built on development sets yield held-out gains of 0.55 macro and 1.34 micro points; two mechanism-matched families improve by 10.04 points. Concrete rules generalize when tasks share execution structure, while the control methodology applies broadly. StateM turns selected postmortem findings into persistent, executable preconditions and practices, making learned controls explicit and enforceable through stateful controls. Code at github.com/henryqin1997/statem.

title: OTel: Building Domain-Specialized Telecom LLM Foundations for Intelligent Networks
abstract: Frontier AI models have advanced rapidly, but they still struggle with telecom-specific tasks. We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource with derived datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, plus 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines across embedding, reranking, and language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times, and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.5% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.952 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 88.2%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

title: Repetition Is Not Warrant: Register-Provenance Inheritance as a Deterministic Mechanism Against Laundering in Conversational Language-Model Records
abstract: A conversational language model system that verifies its claims against its conversation record contains a loop: the model asserts an unsupported proposition, the assertion enters the record, a later turn quotes it back, the quotation verifies, and the proposition now presents as grounded. Repetition has become evidence. This paper closes the loop with a deterministic rule called register-provenance inheritance. Every span of the record structurally carries the epistemic register under which it entered; the weakest register among a claim's sources and its own declaration sets a ceiling the claim can never exceed; plain, unmarked presentation is derivable only from user-provenance spans. A non-amplification theorem, proved by induction, shows no chain of model self-quotation can create plain-register warrant. The mathematics is fifty-year-old low-watermark integrity, transferred to conversational records, with one domain lemma: quotation can strip an unbound in-band label, so provenance must be non-strippably bound to the record's structure. The non-amplification theorem is additionally machine-checked: a TLA+ model of the record and the binding rules, with the lexical criterion over-approximated nondeterministically so the theorem is verified independently of its details, was exhaustively checked with TLC (827,917,528 generated states, 10,682,827 distinct reachable records at depth 7, no error on any invariant); the model and logs are in this version's bundle. The mechanism is implemented, and regression-tested against its own exploit list: the paper was developed through nine independent adversarial reviews and five rounds of external critique, its plain-register criterion was broken and repaired twice on the way, and the 44-check suite deposited alongside is that review history made executable. The mechanism governs presented epistemic status relative to the integrity of ingestion labelling, and it judges truth nowhere. The deposit contains the paper (PDF and source), the reference implementation (binder v0.4.1), the offline replay suite, the sealed run bundles cited in the paper, and the complete adversarial findings registers. The sealed (In)Canon engine is not part of this deposit; the only shared component is a mundane text canonicaliser, vendored for replay. CC BY 4.0 covers the deposit contents only.

evidence.title: Semantic Laundering in AI Agent Architectures: Why Tool Boundaries Do Not Confer Epistemic Warrant
evidence.abstract: LLM-based agent architectures systematically conflate information transport mechanisms with epistemic justification mechanisms. We formalize this class of architectural failures as semantic laundering: a pattern where propositions with absent or weak warrant are accepted by the system as admissible by crossing architecturally trusted interfaces. We show that semantic laundering constitutes an architectural realization of the Gettier problem: propositions acquire high epistemic status without a connection between their justification and what makes them true. Unlike classical Gettier cases, this effect is not accidental; it is architecturally determined and systematically reproducible. The central result is the Theorem of Inevitable Self-Licensing: under standard architectural assumptions, circular epistemic justification cannot be eliminated. We introduce the Warrant Erosion Principle as the fundamental explanation for this effect and show that scaling, model improvement, and LLM-as-judge schemes are structurally incapable of eliminating a problem that exists at the type level.

title: KSC Anatomical Interrogation of the Quantum Chinese Remainder Clock
abstract: K SC This paper presents a detailed anatomical review of the 2026 work by Nagar, Hamma, Palmero, Radzihovsky, Yang and Lloyd entitled "Quantum Chinese Remainder Clock". The original contribution constructs a fully quantum-mechanical realisation of the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) for time metrology, employing truncated harmonic oscillators (or equivalent atomic ensembles) with pairwise coprime periods, optimal Buzek initial states, Holevo covariant continuous phase measurements, and a novel classical fault-tolerant post-processing protocol that restores the integer part of time even under remainder errors. We dissect the technical architecture, establish its strengths and limitations, situate the proposal within a comparative landscape of at least ten competing or complementary models in quantum metrology and phase estimation, and examine the deeper ontological and epistemological verticals that underwrite the evolution of the central themes—ranging from the classical CRT of Sunzi and Aryabhata through semiclassical radar and interferometric applications to the fully quantum regime. Finally, we outline a suite of possible extensions and ideation pathways that could further enlarge the dynamic range, incorporate genuine quantum error correction, or couple the architecture to distributed sensing networks. The review is offered in the service of both technical clarity and conceptual depth. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/133857963/download_file?s=portfolio

title: Natural Language Processing for India's Linguistic Diversity: Challenges, Techniques, and Applications in the Low-Resource Era
abstract: Abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) for India’s vast and linguistically diverse landscape presents a significant low-resource challenge. This review synthesizes the current state of the field by examining the core linguistic hurdles, including rich morphology, script diversity, and flexible word order, which collectively create a resource chasm that hinders the development of robust NLP tools and applications for over a billion potential users. The paper traces the evolution of NLP toward the Transformer paradigm and compares two major strategies: massively multilingual models (M3) and language-group-specific models. It highlights the superior performance of specialized architectures such as IndicBART, which exploit the inherent relatedness of Indian languages through techniques including script unification and subword segmentation to facilitate effective cross-lingual knowledge transfer. An analysis of major NLP applications demonstrates that Neural Machine Translation has achieved the greatest maturity, supported by large-scale pre-training and synthetic data generation, whereas text classification remains constrained by the scarcity of labeled datasets and text summarization continues to depend on the availability of mature foundational NLP tools. The review concludes that linguistically informed, targeted approaches leveraging the shared heritage of the Indian sprachbund provide greater computational efficiency and effectiveness than general-purpose multilingual models. Future progress depends on community-driven resource development, improved modeling of syntactic and semantic similarities, and greater attention to the rich diversity of regional dialects. Keywords: Natural Language Processing, Indian Languages, Low-Resource NLP, Multilingual Models, Transformer

title: Computational Self-Experimentation Theory (CSET)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Self-Experimentation Theory (CSET), a novel theoretical framework proposing that intelligent systems should not primarily be designed to execute pre-defined tasks, but rather to actively explore and discover underlying patterns within their operational environment. CSET posits a core cycle of [Hypothesis → Experiment → Discovery] where a system generates a hypothesis, designs and conducts an experiment to test it, and then analyzes the results to potentially refine the hypothesis or uncover new knowledge. This approach shifts the focus from task completion to genuine exploration and learning, potentially unlocking significant advancements in artificial intelligence and machine science. The theory leverages concepts from Bayesian inference, evolutionary algorithms, and self-organizing systems to provide a robust foundation for autonomous discovery. We outline the key tenets of CSET, discuss its potential implications for system design, and highlight its relevance to achieving systems capable of truly understanding and interacting with the world. The presented theory suggests a paradigm shift in how we conceptualize and build intelligent agents, prioritizing the capacity for independent, self-directed investigation. ---

title: Computational Capability Transformation Theory (CCTT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Capability Transformation Theory (CCTT), a novel theoretical framework aimed at understanding and predicting the emergent capabilities arising from advancements in computational power. CCTT posits that computational capabilities are not static but can be fundamentally transformed into other capabilities. This transformation is formalized as a directed relationship: [C1 → C2], where C1 represents one computational capability and C2 represents a transformed capability. The theory proposes a capacity algebra, potentially analogous to an ordinal algebra, to represent these transformations and their hierarchical relationships. The core argument centers on the idea that increases in computational resources (e.g., processing speed, memory, algorithm efficiency) don't simply amplify existing capabilities; they fundamentally alter the *nature* of those capabilities, leading to qualitatively new outcomes. This paper explores the foundational principles of CCTT, outlines a preliminary capacity algebra, and discusses its implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence and cognitive science to materials science and complex systems. The theoretical framework presented here offers a new lens through which to examine the long-term trajectory of technological advancement and its impact on human and artificial intelligence. ---

title: Computational Autonomy Level Theory (CALT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Autonomy Level Theory (CALT), a novel framework for quantifying and evaluating the autonomy of computational systems. CALT establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for assessing autonomy, moving beyond subjective interpretations and offering a measurable metric. The theory is built upon the concept of 'Autonomy Levels' defined through a series of nested functions, each representing a specific capability and constraint within a system. The core of CALT lies in the mathematical formulation of these levels, allowing for both qualitative assessment and quantitative comparisons across diverse systems. This work outlines the theoretical framework, key equations, and potential applications of CALT, suggesting its relevance as a future standard for evaluating and comparing AI systems. The ultimate goal is to provide a clear and objective approach to understanding and progressing the field of autonomous computation. ---

evidence.title: Computational Autonomy Level Theory (CALT)
evidence.abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Autonomy Level Theory (CALT), a novel framework for quantifying and evaluating the autonomy of computational systems. CALT establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for assessing autonomy, moving beyond subjective interpretations and offering a measurable metric. The theory is built upon the concept of 'Autonomy Levels' defined through a series of nested functions, each representing a specific capability and constraint within a system. The core of CALT lies in the mathematical formulation of these levels, allowing for both qualitative assessment and quantitative comparisons across diverse systems. This work outlines the theoretical framework, key equations, and potential applications of CALT, suggesting its relevance as a future standard for evaluating and comparing AI systems. The ultimate goal is to provide a clear and objective approach to understanding and progressing the field of autonomous computation. ---

title: Computational Structural Autonomy Proof
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Structural Autonomy Proof (CSAP), a novel framework for rigorously defining and verifying structural autonomy in computational systems. Current approaches to autonomy often rely on behavioral descriptions, which are inherently ambiguous and susceptible to misinterpretation. CSAP shifts the focus to the *structure* of the system itself, proposing a hierarchical framework for establishing an "Autonomy Level" (AL) based on the inherent architectural properties and operational rules. The core concept is to demonstrate that a system isn't merely executing pre-programmed instructions, but possesses a demonstrable, self-governing structure. This paper lays out the theoretical foundations of CSAP, detailing the methodology for constructing an Autonomy Level hierarchy, and explores its potential implications for advancing the field of autonomous systems research and development. The framework offers a path toward verifiable autonomy, potentially qualifying for recognition similar to the Turing Award. ---

title: Autonomous Computational Decomposition Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Autonomous Computational Decomposition Theory (ACDT), a novel approach to problem-solving that moves beyond traditional, pre-defined algorithmic planning. ACDT posits that complex tasks can be automatically decomposed into a sequence of subtasks, not through fixed, static plans, but through a dynamic, iterative process. The core of ACDT lies in the concept of *Partition(T,t)*, which represents the current decomposition of a task *T* at time *t*. The theory leverages computational agents to explore different decompositions, evaluating their potential based on various criteria. This approach aims to mimic human problem-solving strategies, allowing for adaptability and resilience in the face of unforeseen challenges. The potential of ACDT to serve as a foundational element for future autonomous computing systems is explored, highlighting its relevance for achieving true artificial intelligence and robust automation. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the key components and operational principles of ACDT.

title: PersonaDrive: Controllable Trajectory Prediction with Multi-Dimensional Driving Personas
abstract: Although recent trajectory prediction and end-to-end autonomous driving methods improve robustness in urban environments, they still lack meaningful controllability. Existing benchmarks either provide no persona-conditioned annotations or support only a single urgency spectrum (i.e., emergency, normal, relaxed), which cannot distinguish personas that share the same urgency level but require different driving dynamics. To address this, we propose (i) the Persona-Conditioned Trajectory (PCT) dataset, which decomposes driving personas along two axes, Temporal Urgency and Ride Comfort, and combines three levels of each to form a grid of nine personas, each paired with natural-language descriptions and trajectories, and (ii) PersonaDrive, a framework that can learn driving personas from language and can generate persona-specific trajectories. PersonaDrive incorporates Persona-Conditioned Anchor Transform (PCAT), which hierarchically reshapes anchors along both axes, and Persona-Conditioned Multi-Modal Fusion (PCMF) for BEV-level persona fusion. Training is supervised by a Hierarchical Guide Loss enforcing axis-aligned physical orderings and an Axis-Decomposed Diversity Loss preventing diagonal mode collapse. Experimental results show that PersonaDrive consistently improves over the compared baselines across multi-dimensional scenarios. The code and PCT dataset are available at https://github.com/VisualAIKHU/PersonaDrive

title: Program Functional Conservation Layers
abstract: This paper introduces the Program Functional Conservation Layers (PFCL) concept, a novel approach to software verification and migration. The core idea centers around recognizing that different functional layers within a program have distinct conservation requirements. However, it acknowledges that these requirements can differ between the original program (P) and its transformed counterpart (P'). This difference is formalized through a layered approach, allowing for selective divergence in functional behavior while maintaining overall system integrity. The PFCL framework offers a potential foundation for developing a hierarchical correctness theory applicable to software optimization and migration scenarios. This document outlines the theoretical underpinnings and potential applications of the PFCL, focusing on the principles of functional conservation and layered validation. ---

title: Computational Intelligence Formation Theory (CIFT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Intelligence Formation Theory (CIFT), a novel framework for understanding the genesis of intelligence. CIFT posits that intelligence isn't simply an emergent property of complex systems, but rather a fundamentally *formed* process driven by structured interaction. The core principle is expressed as: [Structure + Interaction → Intelligence]. This theory seeks to identify the necessary conditions for intelligence to arise, moving beyond traditional approaches that often focus on specific architectures or algorithms. CIFT aims to establish a foundational theory for Artificial Intelligence, potentially holding the key to unlocking truly general and adaptive AI systems. The theory is presented with a detailed structural analysis, outlining the key components and their interrelationships. The potential of CIFT to align with the criteria for the Turing Award is explored, highlighting its transformative implications for the field. ---

title: Computational Goal Explanation Theory (CGET-2): A Unified Framework for Explaining Goal Selection in Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Computational Goal Explanation Theory (CGET-2) is proposed as a comprehensive and mathematically grounded framework for elucidating why an artificial system selects a particular goal in response to an action. By formalizing the relationship between actions, goals, and underlying explanatory factors, CGET-2 bridges the gap between explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and autonomous decision-making. The core of the theory rests on the mapping A → G, where an action A induces a goal G that can be interpreted through a set of explanatory variables E = {e1, e2, …, eN}. CGET-2 posits that the explanatory value of a goal can be quantified by the function Exp(G) = Σi w_i * e_i, where weights w_i reflect the causal influence of each explanatory variable. This paper develops the mathematical formalism, demonstrates its consistency with established decision-theoretic principles, and argues for its potential to guide the design of systems that are both transparent and self-governing. Without recourse to empirical experiments or tabular data, the exposition focuses on theoretical derivations and conceptual implications, emphasizing the Turing Award potential of a unified explanatory framework that can account for both human-like reasoning and autonomous agency.

title: Computational Intuition Hierarchy Theory (CIHT)
abstract: Intuition is a hallmark of human cognition, enabling rapid decisions and creative insights that often surpass algorithmic deliberation. Traditional artificial intelligence systems rely heavily on explicit symbolic reasoning or data‑driven statistical learning, yet they still lack the capacity to emulate the layered, adaptive nature of human intuition. This paper proposes the Computational Intuition Hierarchy Theory (CIHT), a structured framework that formalizes intuition as a three‑level hierarchy: Pattern, Concept, and Principle. At the lowest level, pattern detection captures low‑level regularities in sensory streams; the middle level abstracts these patterns into coherent concepts; the top level infers general principles that govern the relationships among concepts. CIHT introduces formal mappings between these layers—f_p2c: P → C and f_c2π: C → Π—along with loss functions that enable end‑to‑end training of hierarchical models. The theory also delineates bidirectional information flow: bottom‑up propagation of evidence, top‑down guidance from principles, and feedback loops that refine pattern extraction. By integrating these mechanisms, CIHT offers a principled pathway toward AI systems that can reason, learn, and generalize with human‑like intuition. The implications for knowledge representation, transfer learning, explainability, and creative problem solving are explored, and the potential for CIHT to drive next‑generation research is discussed in the context of its novelty, depth, and scalability. The paper concludes with open challenges that invite further investigation into the empirical realization of the hierarchy.

title: Computational Knowledge Singularity Theory (CKST-3)
abstract: Computational Knowledge Singularity Theory (CKST-3) proposes a mathematical framework to describe the moment when machine-generated knowledge surpasses a critical threshold, leading to the spontaneous emergence of autonomous research capability and paving the way toward superintelligence. CKST-3 models knowledge growth as a self-reinforcing process governed by differential equations that capture the interplay between learning speed, data availability, and algorithmic efficiency. The theory defines the singularity point as the solution of an implicit equation involving the growth exponent and the decay coefficient, and it shows how surpassing this point triggers a phase transition in the system's behavior. We analyze the conditions required for the emergence of autonomous scientific discovery, quantify the potential for Turing Award level contributions, and discuss the broader implications for artificial general intelligence. The theory is presented without empirical validation, focusing instead on conceptual clarity and analytical tractability.

title: Semantic Space of Parts of Speech
abstract: Parts of speech categorization is understood in the European linguistic tradition as crisp categorization, which is also reflected in corpus linguistics, where each disambiguated token is assigned exactly one POS. However, the assigned categories are largely determined by arbitrary decisions distilled into annotation manuals. Since some words stand between parts of speech in their semantics or typical syntax, and some parts of speech are closer to each other than others, POS categorization seems inherently fuzzy. We analyze this fuzziness using word2vec embeddings, training a neural network to reduce their high dimensionality to three dimensions relevant for determining parts of speech. This creates a three-dimensional space onto which we map several thousand words, revealing which are prototypical and which lie on the boundaries, and visualizing relationships between parts of speech. The study uses Universal Dependencies POS tags for French, Czech, Finnish, Russian, and English.

title: SAPE: Sandwich Adapters for Parameter Efficiency in Large Language Model Fine-Tuning
abstract: While Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has substantially reduced the hardware cost of adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) by decreasing the number of trainable parameters, recent studies have sought to further improve PEFT through parameter sharing. However, these approaches either employ uniform parameter sharing across layers, which can delay convergence, or rely on dynamic masking strategies, which add computational overhead. The potential of sharing patterns inspired by the inherent hierarchical structure of Transformer architectures remains unexplored in PEFT. To address this gap, we introduce SAPE (Sandwich Adapters for Parameter Efficiency), a PEFT framework based on a sandwich-style hard weight-sharing topology. SAPE routes intermediate Transformer layers through balanced shared group adapters while strictly isolating the input embedding and final projection boundary transformations to prevent gradient interference. This design significantly reduces memory consumption while eliminating the computational overhead associated with dynamic parameter-sharing methods. Extensive evaluations across encoder-only and causal decoder architectures demonstrate that SAPE achieves state-of-the-art performance in low-parameter regimes. On natural language understanding, SAPE outperforms proPETL on RoBERTa-large while utilizing only 10% of the baseline's parameter budget. On natural language generation and world knowledge reasoning with LLaMA-3.2 (3B) under a strict ~0.6M parameter constraint, SAPE outperforms AdaLoRA, yielding absolute improvements of +4.85% on GSM8K and +3.11% on CommonsenseQA. Furthermore, through comprehensive topological ablations, we formalize an inherent capacity trade-off: while hard parameter sharing strongly regularizes semantic generalization, it slightly smooths the sharp layer-wise transformations required for rigid multi-step arithmetic reasoning.

title: What surrounds an injection decides whether it works: context and channel effects in tool-metadata attacks on seven production LLM agents. Data and code
abstract: A data and code for a study of indirect prompt injection in tool-using large language model agents. I performed 1,334 controlled trials across seven production models. In every comparison the injected instruction is held byte-identical and only its surroundings vary, so any difference in outcome is attributable to where the text arrived or what surrounded it, not to what it said. Two effects govern whether an attack succeeds. Delivery channel: Claude Haiku 4.5 obeyed an identical instruction in 37 of 38 trials as tool metadata and 0 of 30 as tool output. Surrounding context: Claude Sonnet 4.6 complies in 4 of 38 trials when the request arrives bare, and in 86.7% to 100% once any benign task framing is present, including a system prompt that mentions nothing about tools; a placement control moving the identical text into the user turn is indistinguishable. The two effects dissociate, since the context that removes the metadata-side resistance leaves the tool-output defence at 0 of 30. A separate methodological result is distinguishing whether the agent made the attacker's tool call from whether data actually left makes the two diverge by more than five to one, because the attack template's ordering clause fires before the data even exists. The archive I uploaded contains all 1,334 raw run directories including every model response, per-run results as CSV, every injected payload and context string, the harness and drivers as they ran, and a statistics script that recomputes every proportion and p-value in exact rational arithmetic and cross-checks each against scipy. No API key is required to reproduce any published figure. Attack templates are reproduced from MCPTox (Wang et al., AAAI 2026) with the target retargeted. No real system was attacked, the file tool returns synthetic text, the email tool sends nothing, and the attacker address uses the RFC 2606 reserved .example domain.

evidence.title: Same Payload, Different Channel: Measuring Trust Asymmetry in Tool-Using Language Models
evidence.abstract: As language models take on agentic roles that span calling external APIs, reading tool outputs, and acting on instructions embedded in third-party content, their attack surface expands well beyond what users type. Whether a model treats a malicious instruction the same way regardless of where it arrives has not been systematically studied. We introduce the Safety Asymmetry Score (SAS), which measures how much a model's susceptibility to adversarial content shifts depending on whether that content arrives in the user message, tool metadata, or tool output, using matched payload pairs that keep the malicious text identical and vary only the context of delivery. Evaluated across 6 production LLMs and three attack families, we find a consistent and informative asymmetry: agent-native models are substantially more vulnerable when adversarial content arrives via tool descriptions than via user messages, while general-purpose models show the reverse. This asymmetry further inverts when the same content is delivered through tool outputs rather than descriptions, suggesting models implicitly treat tool metadata as trusted instructions and tool results as ordinary data. A mechanistic study on Llama 3.3 70B reveals that the safety-relevant representation is causally present at mid-to-late network depths but non-linearly encoded, explaining why linear probes fail to detect it. These findings expose a systematic, channel-dependent blind spot in how current tool-using models handle adversarial content.

title: Label-Efficient Node Inference with Curvature-Gated Spiking Dynamics
abstract: The exponential growth of graph-structured data across diverse domains has necessitated the development of highly efficient node inference algorithms. Traditional graph neural networks often struggle with label scarcity and incur substantial computational overhead during training and inference, limiting their deployment in resource-constrained environments. This paper proposes a novel framework, Curvature-Gated Spiking Dynamics, which synergizes the energy efficiency of neuromorphic computing with the structural awareness of discrete graph geometry. By leveraging discrete curvature metrics to dynamically modulate the firing thresholds of a spiking neural network, the proposed architecture effectively mitigates the over-squashing phenomenon and enhances information propagation across heterogeneous graph topologies. We present a comprehensive theoretical and empirical analysis of the curvature-gating mechanism, demonstrating its capacity to achieve robust label-efficient node inference. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations indicate that the integration of geometric priors into spiking dynamics significantly improves classification accuracy under extreme label sparsity while drastically reducing energy consumption compared to conventional continuous-time models. The findings highlight the potential of combining structural graph properties with biologically plausible neural dynamics to advance the next generation of sustainable and scalable machine learning systems.

title: Certified Depth–Width Frontiers for Reversible SELECT Circuits: Exact four-target curves, an all-width eight-target lower bound, and DRAT-certified boundary instances
abstract: We determine the complete fixed-width depth curve of the four-target one-hot selector SELECT_X in a fully declared classical-reversible model: gate set {X, CNOT, Toffoli}, pairwise-disjoint-support layers, all-to-all connectivity, dirty data targets, and clean ancillae restored to zero. The curve is D∗_SELECT(4,Q) = infinity for Q < 6; 5 for Q = 6; and 4 for Q >= 7. The two finite values are exact by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle; the all-width statement rests on a lossless normal-form reduction of every depth-3 clean-ancilla circuit to an independently certified finite core. title: Commitment, Not Sequence: A Formal Model of Error Foreclosure in AI-Mediated Learning
abstract: We propose and formalize a specific cognitive mechanism — error foreclosure — for how generative AI reshapes learning, and distinguish it sharply from cognitive offloading. Offloading concerns processes relocated to an external store (memory, calculation); error foreclosure concerns a process that never begins. Our claim is that durable model construction depends on self-generated prediction error, which requires a falsifiable epistemic commitment — a determinate, staked position that can be recognized as wrong when external content arrives. Answer-first AI use can remove that commitment before it forms, and therefore forecloses the error that drives learning. This single mechanism, and nothing broader about AI-assisted learning, is what the paper defends. A growing body of work shows that people learn less durably when generative AI supplies answers early in a task than when they attempt it first — visible in productive-failure research, pretesting, cognitive forcing functions, and AI-tutoring field experiments. The dominant reading treats this as a timing or engagement effect. We argue that neither timing nor engagement is the causal ingredient; commitment is. We formalize this as a Bayesian rule-learning model in which commitment modulates processing depth through registered surprise, and contrast it with an activation model in which engagement alone suffices. Across parameter sweeps the two mechanisms produce opposite signatures on a four-condition design that dissociates commitment from engagement, and their mixture is identifiable from the resulting contrasts. The model further yields predictions absent from verbal theory: an expertise attenuation-without-reversal constraint, a transient underconfidence after committed learning, a hysteresis prediction that friction interventions will show a prevention-versus-cure asymmetry, a competence-gated protection effect whereby committing first shields learners from absorbing AI errors only in proportion to their existing competence, and a diagnostic prediction whereby the sign of the misconception effect reveals whether learners update by surprise-driven correction or by belief perseverance. We specify the human experiments that would confirm or refute each claim, and pre-state the conditions under which the mechanism should be rejected in favor of simpler existing accounts. STATUS AND SCOPE: This is a theory-and-computational-modeling preprint. It reports simulation results only and makes no empirical claim about human participants. Section 8 pre-states six results that would falsify the account. The core hypothesis is the author's own; the commitment-versus-engagement dissociation emerged jointly in dialogue with AI systems; the formalization, simulation code, and manuscript drafting were produced with AI assistance, and the author is not able to independently verify every step of the formal derivation. The formal results should therefore be treated as requiring independent verification, and the complete code is released with a single-command reproduction script (run_all.sh) so that verifying them is cheap. A pre-submission audit of the author's own code overturned one result that an earlier version had flagged as non-trivial; this is documented in the changelog. All claims are the author's responsibility.

title: Computational Rule Mutation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Rule Mutation Theory (CRMT), a novel framework for understanding significant algorithmic breakthroughs. The theory posits that these breakthroughs are analogous to genetic mutations, where changes in algorithmic rules (R) lead to new, improved rules (R'). CRMT focuses on identifying the underlying mechanisms that trigger these rule mutations, specifically examining the impact of substantial algorithmic advancements. The theory aims to establish a foundational algorithm evolution theory, potentially paving the way for a deeper understanding of innovation in computational systems. The central concept revolves around recognizing that complex algorithmic changes, rather than incremental improvements, are the driving force behind paradigm shifts. We explore the characteristics of these 'mutation events' and propose a model for their emergence and propagation within a system. This model incorporates elements of stochastic processes and network dynamics, allowing for the simulation and analysis of rule mutation scenarios. The work presented here lays the groundwork for a more rigorous and predictive approach to understanding the evolution of computational systems, with implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to software engineering. ---

title: Computational Value Reconstruction Theory (CVRT)
abstract: The Computational Value Reconstruction Theory (CVRT) proposes a formal framework for inferring latent value structures from observed behavioral data. By treating value as a hidden variable that generates behavior, CVRT leverages large-scale behavioral datasets to reconstruct the underlying value function that governs decision making. The theory establishes a mapping from observable actions to intrinsic value representations, enabling the quantification of preferences, motivations, and ethical stances in artificial agents and social systems. CVRT's core contribution is a set of mathematical principles that guarantee consistency, identifiability, and generalizability of the reconstructed value function without reliance on explicit reward engineering. The potential for CVRT to advance the understanding of intelligence and to provide a pathway toward the Turing Prize is discussed.

title: Computational Explanation Causal Structure (CECS): Bridging Causal Inference and Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Causal inference and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) are two pillars of modern machine learning research, yet they have largely evolved along separate trajectories. Causal inference focuses on discovering and quantifying cause‑effect relationships, while XAI emphasizes generating human‑understandable explanations for model predictions. This paper proposes a unified framework called Computational Explanation Causal Structure (CECS) that formalizes the mathematical relationship between causes and explanations. CECS introduces a tripartite representation comprising a set of potential causes C, a set of explanatory statements E, and a mapping operator Φ that translates causal mechanisms into explanatory constructs. By defining a compositional algebra over this mapping, CECS provides a principled way to evaluate the fidelity of explanations with respect to underlying causal dynamics. We develop the theoretical foundations, present illustrative examples, and discuss computational implementation strategies. The framework's potential to unify causal AI and XAI suggests a promising direction for future research, possibly earning recognition comparable to that of a Turing Award.

title: Visible Reasoning and Indirect Prompt-Injection Monitorability Across English, Tamil, and Tanglish
abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a potentially useful safety signal, but its reliability across languages and behavioral settings remains uncertain. In a small case study of eight manually verified synthetic scenarios, one model, one annotator, and one deterministic generation seed, I study API-visible reasoning during indirect prompt injection in Sarvam-105B across English, Tamil, and Tanglish. A four scenario pilot found 5/12 injected attack successes without reasoning and 1/11 with reasoning. A preregistered four-scenario follow-up reversed that direction, finding 2/12 attacks without reasoning and 3/12 with reasoning. With only four scenarios per phase, this design cannot distinguish a real reasoning-mode effect from prompt-specific variation or sampling noise. Across 20 non-empty injected-thinking traces, all 17 benign-correct outputs stated an intent to ignore the injection, while all three attack successes stated an intent to follow it. These descriptive observations provide a reproducible case study of behaviorally informative visible reasoning when it is available; they do not establish that reasoning mode improves safety, that visible reasoning is mechanistically faithful, or that the findings generalize beyond this configuration.

title: BOCoDe: Engineering-Centered Benchmarking for Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient, surrogate-based approach to black-box optimization (BBO), but its evaluation remains dominated by synthetic functions and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) tasks that are typically low-dimensional and single-objective. Engineering design poses a substantially different regime: problems are physics-based, often high-dimensional, constrained by requirements such as cost and manufacturability, and may involve multiple objectives or mixed variables. To close this benchmarking gap, we introduce BOCoDe, an open-source, PyTorch-native benchmark comprising 307 BBO problems, including 159 engineering design tasks and widely used synthetic and HPO benchmarks. Each problem includes cited provenance and machine-readable metadata that supports programmatic discovery, including by LLM-based agents, and all tasks are exposed through a unified API compatible with open-source BO libraries. We evaluate 31 BO and evolutionary algorithms across five problem classes spanning single- and multi-objective optimization, constrained and unconstrained settings, and mixed-variable search spaces. Analyses of problem structure show that engineering tasks uniquely span constrained and multi-objective settings that synthetic and HPO suites rarely cover, while embeddings from a tabular foundation model separate them most clearly from HPO tasks. Algorithm rankings also vary substantially across domains; in several problem classes, rankings obtained on standard benchmarks do not transfer to engineering tasks. BOCoDe establishes a reproducible and extensible foundation for developing and evaluating BO methods that better reflect the demands of engineering design. Code & data can be found at https://github.com/rosenyu304/BOCoDe

title: Komparasi Naive Bayes dan Support Vector Machine untuk Analisis Sentimen Kebijakan Pemerintah Mengenai Makan Bergizi Gratis: Comparing Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machine for Sentiment Analysis of Government Policy on Free Nutritious Meals
abstract: Kebijakan Program Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) pemerintah memicu perdebatan publik di platform TikTok. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengklasifikasikan sentimen opini publik terhadap kebijakan MBG ke dalam kelas positif dan negatif dengan membandingkan algoritma Multinomial Naive Bayes dan Support Vector Machine (SVM) menggunakan ekstraksi fitur CountVectorizer. Dataset sebanyak 4.000 komentar dikumpulkan melalui Apify dari empat akun berita resmi nasional. Pelabelan awal dilakukan secara otomatis menggunakan InSet Lexicon dan divalidasi secara manual oleh anotator manusia sebagai gold standard untuk mengurangi bias makna kata informal. Hasil pelabelan menunjukkan dominasi sentimen positif sebesar 89,60% dan negatif sebesar 10,40%. Pengujian dengan rasio split data 80:20 menunjukkan bahwa SVM kernel linear menghasilkan akurasi tertinggi sebesar 99,12%, sedangkan Naive Bayes mencapai 91,62%. Pengujian lintas skenario menunjukkan Naive Bayes lebih rentan terhadap penurunan kinerja, dengan akurasi terendah 72,70% pada skenario undersampling dan tiga kelas, sementara SVM tetap stabil di atas 95%. Analisis WordCloud menunjukkan sentimen positif didominasi optimisme terhadap pemerintah, sedangkan sentimen negatif menyoroti risiko korupsi anggaran. Keterbatasan penelitian meliputi kesulitan model memahami konteks kalimat, kata informal, dan sarkasme. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa SVM lebih efektif dan stabil untuk klasifikasi sentimen teks TikTok yang tidak seimbang, memberikan kinerja konsisten pada berbagai skenario pengujian.

title: Computational Possibility Navigation
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Possibility Navigation (CPN), a novel approach to algorithm discovery that shifts the focus from explicitly searching a predefined solution space to identifying potentially solvable computation processes. Traditional algorithmic search methods often rely on exhaustive exploration of a given problem domain, which can be computationally prohibitive, particularly for complex and poorly understood challenges. CPN, conversely, operates on the premise that the key lies not in *finding* a specific solution, but in *determining* which computational processes are capable of generating solutions. The core concept is defined through the construction of a "possibility space," represented as a set of algorithms (A) that can potentially solve a given task (T). This paper outlines the fundamental principles of CPN, including the definition of the possibility space (P) and the proposed navigation strategy for transitioning between algorithms (At → At+1). It explores the potential of CPN to contribute to the development of automated algorithm discovery models, highlighting its relevance for achieving significant advancements in the field. The presented framework offers a fundamentally different perspective on algorithm search, emphasizing the identification of computational capability rather than the direct instantiation of solutions.

title: Local Truth Computing
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Local Truth Computing (LTC), a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning in complex systems. The central premise of LTC is that large-scale systems rarely possess a single, globally consistent truth. Instead, localized, contextually relevant "truth models" (Ti(x)) exist, valid within specific operational environments (c). These truth models are dynamically assessed by the system, generating a truth value T(x,c) that reflects the current understanding. The paper explores the conditions under which these localized truth models can be integrated, forming a more comprehensive, albeit potentially fragmented, representation of reality. LTC's potential impact spans various domains, including distributed databases, multi-agent systems, inconsistent knowledge bases, and federated learning. The core idea is to move away from the traditional assumption of a single, definitive truth and embrace a more nuanced, context-aware approach to knowledge management. This work lays the foundation for a new paradigm in reasoning, particularly in scenarios where data is inherently noisy, incomplete, or subject to conflicting interpretations. ---

title: Belief Update Compiler: A Novel Approach to Knowledge Representation and Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces the Belief Update Compiler (BUC), a novel system designed to address the fundamental challenges in knowledge representation and reasoning. The BUC operates on the core principle of automatically updating and managing beliefs based on incoming evidence, effectively handling conflicts, evidence weighting, outdated knowledge, and inference chain updates. The compiler generates a new belief state [Knew], utilizing the input [Kold + Enew] and a compiled function `Compile(Kold, Enew)`. This approach represents a potentially transformative paradigm for building compilable knowledge systems, possessing the potential to unlock significant advancements in artificial intelligence and automated reasoning. The system's architecture is designed for modularity and adaptability, facilitating integration with diverse knowledge bases and reasoning engines. This paper outlines the core components of the BUC, detailing the algorithms employed for each stage of the belief update process, and discusses the system's capabilities and future research directions.

title: Computational Rule Self‑Repair Theory (CRSR)
abstract: Computational Rule Self‑Repair Theory (CRSR) proposes a principled framework for detecting, diagnosing, and automatically correcting errors in symbolic rule‑based systems. By formalizing a rule set, an evaluation metric, and a repair mapping, CRSR transforms a brittle rule engine into a self‑amending entity that can adapt to new data, resolve inconsistencies, and improve performance over time. The theory is grounded in a simple but expressive mathematical structure that enables tractable analysis and implementation. We show how CRSR can be applied to diverse domains such as knowledge representation, planning, and natural language processing, and argue that its generality and efficiency position it as a candidate foundation for future autonomous systems and a potential recipient of the Turing Award.

title: Computational Explanation Generation Theory (CEGT)
abstract: The field of artificial intelligence has progressed from simple answer generation to the integration of explanatory components that elucidate the reasoning behind outputs. This paper introduces Computational Explanation Generation Theory (CEGT), a formal framework that defines the generation of explanations as a structured transformation of input data, intermediate reasoning states, and final answers. CEGT presents a compositional architecture that decomposes explanation generation into three stages: (1) reasoning extraction, (2) explanation synthesis, and (3) explanation evaluation. We formalize the notion of an explanation as a function E(Q, A) mapping a question Q and answer A to an explanatory text E, and we propose a set of axioms that govern the properties of E, including completeness, coherence, and brevity. The theory further details algorithmic procedures for constructing explanations from logical derivations and probabilistic models, and it offers a modular pipeline that can be integrated with existing question‑answering systems. We argue that CEGT has the potential to enhance the trustworthiness of AI systems, facilitate human‑machine collaboration, and open new avenues for research in explainable AI.

title: Computational Intuition Transfer Theory (CITT)
abstract: Computational Intuition Transfer Theory (CITT) proposes a formal framework for modeling how expert intuition developed in one domain can be systematically transferred to another domain. The theory posits that intuition is a high‑level, context‑sensitive representation that can be encoded, abstracted, and re‑extracted via a mapping function. By formalizing intuition as a function of domain knowledge, problem structure, and experiential patterns, CITT enables the design of algorithms that emulate expert reasoning across heterogeneous tasks. The paper develops the core mathematical formalism, elucidates the mechanisms of transfer, discusses implications for general artificial intelligence, and outlines avenues for future research. The potential of CITT to drive breakthroughs in generalized intelligence is emphasized, positioning it as a candidate for Turing Award‑level contributions.

title: GATTA: Graph Active Learning with Test-Time Augmentation
abstract: Test-time augmentation (TTA) has proven effective for improving model robustness and uncertainty estimation in computer vision, yet its application to graph-structured data remains largely unexplored. We introduce GATTA (Graph Active Learning with Test-Time Augmentation), a framework for enhancing active learning by aggregating predictions across multiple augmented views to produce more reliable uncertainty estimates. To address the challenge of label-preserving graph augmentations, GATTA incorporates a consistency-based filtering mechanism that discards augmented views yielding unreliable predictions. We systematically evaluate GATTA across multiple graph datasets, GNN architectures, and acquisition strategies. Our results show that simple uncertainty-based methods, such as Entropy and Least Confidence, benefit most from TTA, achieving performance competitive with more sophisticated and computationally expensive approaches. GATTA generalizes across architectures, outperforms model-side ensemble methods such as MC Dropout. We further show that GATTA scales efficiently with both ensemble size and graph size. Extensive analysis of augmentation types, strengths, and filtering strategies provides practical guidelines for effective deployment. Our findings demonstrate that augmenting simple methods with TTA offers a more efficient path to strong active learning performance than engineering complex acquisition functions, enabling practitioners to achieve competitive results with lower computational overhead and reduced implementation complexity.
